## Getting it running

### Which version of the game do I need?

**1.9.0**, and only 1.9.0. Support for 1.8.2 ended with Savage Wind 0.5.1: if your copy is older, update it on your own
console and extract it again. [Why only one version?](#why-only-one-version-of-the-game)

### What do the game files need to look like?

Folders named `exefs/` and `romfs/`, already extracted and decrypted. Savage Wind doesn't decrypt anything and doesn't
accept a cartridge image or an installation package. The exact layout, and how to add the DLC, are in
[Game files](game-files.md).

### Setup says "No game files found in that folder"

Check that the folder you chose directly contains `exefs/` and `romfs/`, and not one more folder that holds them.

If you are reusing an install, extract the new Savage Wind in the same place and accept without choosing a folder: it
reads the `extracted` folder that is already there. If that fails, use a separate folder for the new Savage Wind and
copy `extracted` into it ([#590](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/590)).

### "The game code has no address for opt_two_redraw", or setup says the version is wrong

Your game files are not version 1.9.0. Update your copy on your console and extract it again. We can't help you get a
newer copy, and asking for one in an issue gets the comment removed.

### Setup says "It has N files; with the update applied it has 41062"

Your extracted RomFS is incomplete: a complete 1.9.0 RomFS, with the update applied over the base game, has 41,062
files. Setup refuses fewer, because the game crashes as soon as it reads a missing file. Extract your copy again. How you
extract it is up to you, and we can't help with that part ([why](#how-do-i-get-the-game-files)).

### The loading screen never ends after boarding a Divine Beast

Your DLC is merged into `romfs`. Set the game up again with the DLC in its own folders, as
[Game files](game-files.md#the-dlc) shows: with it merged, the loading screen after boarding a Divine Beast never ends.
Keeping the DLC separate fixes it, and your saves stay.

### Setup stops at 5%, 10% or "The game code didn't build"

That step runs a compiler over your files, so it needs free space and a working toolchain. Check that:

- you have about 20 GB free on that drive;
- Savage Wind is in a folder you can write to, not Program Files or a synced folder such as OneDrive;
- your antivirus didn't quarantine anything from the Savage Wind folder.

If it still fails, [open an issue](#reporting-a-problem) with `savagewind.log`
([#618](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/618)).

### How long does setup take?

About 15 minutes on a 12-thread CPU, and longer on fewer threads: a Steam Deck needs around 15 for the game code
alone. It only happens once, and again only if an update changes the game code.

### Do I have to extract the game again after updating Savage Wind?

No. The files you set up stay in the Savage Wind folder. An update can ask you to rebuild the game code from them, but
it doesn't need your original copy again.

### How do I update?

From 0.5.1 on, Savage Wind updates itself in one click from Savage Wind Configuration, on Windows and in the Linux
AppImages. If you are on 0.5.0 or older, install the latest version by hand once, by extracting the zip over the old folder
or by using the new AppImage. Your game files, saves and settings stay.

The first start of a new version empties the shader caches and precompiles them again, and it rebuilds the game code
only if that version needs it.

### Why is the first time I play slow or stuttery?

Shaders are built for your graphics card the first time they are needed. The precompilation step covers most of them,
and the rest appear as short stutters that go away once they are cached. On NVIDIA, a small driver cache can throw this
work away between sessions: in NVIDIA Control Panel > Manage 3D settings, raise **Shader Cache Size**
([#468](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/468)).

### How much disk space and memory does it need?

About 20 GB of disk and 16 GB of RAM.

### Where are my saves? Can I bring saves from the Wii U or Cemu?

See [Saves](saves.md). Wii U and Cemu saves can be imported from **Savage Wind Configuration > Settings > Saves**.

### Can I keep the game files on another drive?

Yes: [Moving the data folder](data-folder.md).

---

## Crashes

### "Savage Wind stopped because of an error"

Attach the log and your zipped `save` folder as described in [Reporting a problem](#reporting-a-problem). The numbers in
the message are useful to us, even when they mean nothing to you.

Before reporting, check that you are on the latest release and on game version 1.9.0. Many old crashes are already
fixed.

### Crashes with `exception c0000005` on an Intel GPU or a GPU that shares system memory

Close the game, open `savagewind.ini` (next to `savagewind.exe`) and set:

```
sparse_heap = off
```

Then play again. If it still crashes, post the `savagewind.log` of that run on your issue
([#619](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/619),
[#596](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/596)).

### "Vulkan device lost" or "the GPU stopped responding"

Update your graphics driver first. Then lower the resolution and the shadow quality: running out of video memory is one
of the known causes on cards with little of it. If it keeps happening, report it with your log.

### It crashes while saving

Another program may be holding the save files, usually OneDrive or an antivirus. Keep the Savage Wind folder out of
synced folders and add it to your antivirus exceptions.

### It crashes after playing for hours

Long sessions are still being worked on, and memory use can grow as you play
([#640](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/640)). Save often during long sessions, and tell us how
long you played and attach the log.

### A cutscene froze or broke

Set the frame rate to 30 fps for that scene, then raise it afterwards. Then tell us which scene it was on
[#425](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/425).

### The game seems to keep running after I close it

Check your task manager for `savagewind.exe` and end it if it's there. If it comes back or won't end, report it.

---

## Graphics

### The window stays black on Windows with an AMD card

From 0.5.1 on, the first start of a new version tries to clear AMD's shader cache once. If it still happens, reset it by
hand:
in AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition, go to **Gaming > Graphics > Advanced** and click **Reset Shader Cache**, then start
Savage Wind again. AMD's driver can keep a damaged cache from an older version. Renaming the Savage Wind folder also
gives the driver a fresh cache.

### The sky is black, dark or wrong on my AMD card

Fixed in Alpha 6: 3D textures are now cleared when they're made, which AMD's Windows driver needed (RX 6000 cards
and older, Vega included). If the sky is still wrong on Alpha 6, add your card, driver, screenshots and log on
[#359](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/359).

### The water is white, milky or transparent

Milky water after a loading screen was fixed for Alpha 5, and transparent water for Alpha 6
([#649](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/649)). If you see either on the latest version, add your
GPU, driver and position.

### Which upscaler should I use?

Since Alpha 6, Video > Upscaler offers FSR 1, FSR 3, FSR 4 (AMD Radeon RX 9000) and NVIDIA DLSS (RTX cards; Savage
Wind Configuration downloads NVIDIA's library). They gain the most where the graphics card is the limit: 4K, the Savage
preset, Extreme shadows. Where the CPU is the limit (1080p on a fast card), they cost about as much as they save, and
their anti-aliasing is the reason to use them there. DLSS and FSR 3 look best in Quality or Native mode; Ultra
Performance is only offered on a 4K window.

### Does frame generation work everywhere?

It works on Windows. Linux and the Steam Deck aren't tried yet. It adds a cost of its own, and on some systems it is
slower instead of faster ([#635](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/635)). Turn it off if that happens.
Don't combine it with the NVIDIA app's or your driver's own frame generation.

### Why does TAA cost so much?

It uses the same motion vectors as FSR 3, so it has the same cost, with the same redesign planned
([#654](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/654)).

### Which GPU does it use? Can I choose?

See [Choosing the GPU](#choosing-the-gpu).

---

## Performance

### My PC is weak. Where do I report how it runs?

On the pinned issue: **[#589, performance or graphical issues on integrated or older GPUs](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/589)**.
Please don't open a new issue for it. Attach:

- your `savagewind.log`, from a run where you got to the world;
- your CPU, GPU and amount of RAM;
- your settings and window size;
- where you were in the game.

In the game, press F12 (or the key below Esc, left of 1), type `report`, and paste what it copies. This helps a lot.

Reports like these decide what gets optimized next, so they are the most useful thing an owner of an older PC can send.

### What should I change first on a weak PC?

1. **Video > Graphics preset > Potato.** It lowers draw distance and shadows below the console's.
2. **Frame rate limit at 30.** A steady 30 fps feels better than a jumping 45.
3. **Lower the internal resolution, with FSR 1.**

If the resolution makes no difference, your CPU or driver is what limits you, and it is worth telling us on #589.

### What is the slowest setting?

Shadow resolution at Extreme, by far: in forests it can cut the frame rate to a third. After that, try lowering the
draw distance.

### What hardware is the minimum?

A GPU with a Vulkan 1.3 driver, a CPU with SSE4.2 and 16 GB of RAM. Without AVX2 and FMA the game code runs in a slower
compatibility mode. GPUs with only Vulkan 1.2, such as the GT 730 and the oldest Radeons on Windows, aren't supported.

### Is this faster than an emulator?

It depends on your PC, and we have no finished comparison to quote. Your CPU no longer translates the game while it
plays, but all the graphics work still has to be done, and the Vulkan drivers matter a lot.

### Things slow down at random or when I use a rune

Short drops right after a loading screen or when a rune starts were reduced in 0.5.1 by waiting less on the GPU
([#639](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/639),
[#672](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/672)). If you still see them on the latest version, report
how long they last and attach the log.

### It uses a lot of RAM

We are looking at reports of high use. Please post your log on the issue ([#525](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/525)).

### Something behaves wrong above 30 or 60 fps

The game was made to run at 30 fps, and Savage Wind corrects each system that assumes that as it's found. Some still
break: physics puzzles, doors, platforms or scripted scenes. Tell us which one on
**[#425](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/425)**, with a save from just before it. Going down to 30
fps gets you past it.

---

## Controls

### Can I change the keys and buttons?

Yes, every action in **Options > Key bindings**. Default keys are in [Controls](controls.md).

### Which controllers work?

Any controller SDL knows. Button prompts follow the device you use, set in **Controls > Button icons**.

### Does gyro work?

Yes, with any controller SDL reads a gyro from: DualSense, DualShock 4, Switch Pro and Joy-Con, the Steam Deck, and
others such as the 8BitDo Ultimate 2 in its Switch or DInput mode. **Options > Controls > Motion source** says where the
motion comes from right now, or why there is none.

| Your controller | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| DualSense, DualShock 4, Switch Pro, Joy-Con | Nothing. With Steam Input on, the game opens the controller behind it for its gyro. |
| Steam Deck | Nothing, in Gaming mode or Desktop mode. |
| Steam Controller | Close Steam before starting the game, or set its gyro to act as a mouse in Steam Input. |
| Xbox and other XInput pads | XInput has no gyro. If yours has one, switch it to its Switch, DS4 or DInput mode. |
| ROG Ally, Legion Go, MSI Claw and other PC handhelds | Run Handheld Companion (or the handheld's own tool) with its DSU server on, or have it show a DualShock 4 with gyro. A DSU server that answers comes before the sensor SDL lends the handheld's gamepad. |
| A DSU server (DS4Windows, BetterJoy, SteamDeckGyroDSU...) | Start it; the game finds it at 127.0.0.1:26760 when the controller has no gyro. Motion source: DSU server takes it first. |
| Streaming (Moonlight, Artemis) | Have the host (Sunshine, Apollo) emulate a DualShock 4 or a DualSense, which carry the gyro. |

Sensitivity, vertical sensitivity, inversion and Lean to turn are in Options > Controls; they change motion aiming,
not shrine tilting. On a controller without a gyro, the sticks tilt the shrine apparatus, or hold T and move the mouse.
If the gyro still misbehaves, start the game with `SAVAGEWIND_MOTION_LOG=1` and attach `savagewind.log` to
[#136](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/136).

### Does it work with mouse aiming?

Yes, the mouse turns the camera directly with no acceleration, and sensitivity is in **Options > Controls**.

### The mouse cursor escaped, or I can't click

Esc frees the cursor, and clicking inside the window takes it back.

## Reporting a problem

1. **Use the [latest release](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/releases/latest)** and game version 1.9.0.
2. **Search the [existing issues](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues?q=is%3Aissue)** first.
3. **[Open a new issue](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/new/choose)** and attach:
   - `savagewind.log`. On Windows it's next to `savagewind.exe`, on Linux in `~/.local/share/savagewind/`. A new one is
     written at each start, so take it right after the bug.
   - For a crash or a cutscene bug, your `save` folder, zipped, after closing the game.

**Make a problem report**, in Savage Wind Configuration, gathers these into one zip for you.

Where each kind of report goes:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| Poor performance or broken graphics on an older or integrated GPU | [#589](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/589) |
| Something that breaks at high frame rates | [#425](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/425) |
| Anything else | [A new issue](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/new/choose) |
| Code, a patch or a fix | [A pull request against `test`](../CONTRIBUTING.md), not an issue |

Before opening one, read this page. An issue about something it already covers, including a new report of a
[known issue](#known-issues), is closed right away with the reason and a link to the answer. If what it says didn't help
on the latest release, say so in your report and attach the log, and it stays open. A closed one is reopened if you
comment with that.

Reports missing the log get a `needs-info` label and are closed after 24 hours without it. Never attach or link game
files, keys or firmware.

---

## Other settings

### Choosing the GPU

Close Savage Wind and edit `savagewind.ini`, in the same data folder as `savagewind.log`. Set `gpu = 1`, for example,
using the number printed beside your preferred adapter in the log's `[vk] gpu 0: ...`, `[vk] gpu 1: ...` lines, then
restart. `gpu = auto` (the default) prefers a discrete GPU. An unavailable adapter falls back to automatic selection
with a warning in the log. Adapter numbers can change after hardware or driver changes, so check the log again if
necessary. The `SAVAGEWIND_GPU` environment variable overrides this setting for one launch (an index or `auto`). This
selects the rendering GPU. The `display` setting selects the monitor.

### We asked you to try a test setting

Use the Launch options list on the start screen, so you don't need a terminal:
[launch-options.md](launch-options.md).

### What is `vk_pipelines.seed`?

A list of shader hashes and draw states met in a full playthrough, next to the executable (about 4,000 pipelines, 100
KB; it holds nothing of the game itself). The shader precompilation reads it so that the first boot already has every
pipeline that playthrough needed. Deleting it only costs some stutter on the first boots.

### Can I change the picture on the start screen?

Yes. Put your own next to `savagewind.exe` (on Linux, in the data folder) as `splash.jpg` or `splash.png`. It's only
read from your folder and is never part of Savage Wind.

### What are the F keys for?

F1 opens the overlay (with Cheats and more). F10 cycles the performance overlay. F12, or the key below Esc, opens the
[console](CONTROL.md). All the keys: [Controls](controls.md).

---

## How do I get the game files?

**We won't tell you, and nobody here will.**

Not how to dump a cartridge, not which tool to use, not where to get keys or firmware, not which guide to follow, and
not "just a hint in private". Questions like this in issues get removed, and accounts that keep asking are blocked.

That isn't unfriendliness, and there are good reasons for it:

- **The law.** Getting the game out of a console means getting past its technical protection. Many countries restrict
  circumvention and helping others do it, separately from whether you own the game. What is allowed differs from one
  country to another. We aren't lawyers, and we can't tell you what's legal where you live.
- **It would put the project at risk.** Savage Wind can exist because it's only code of its own, and because everything
  of Nintendo's comes from the player. Instructions for circumventing protection, or links to tools, are the kind of
  thing that gets projects like this taken down, and then nobody has it.
- **We can't tell who owns what.** A guide written for owners helps anyone at all, and the project doesn't support piracy
  in any form.
- **It has to stay clean.** For the same reason the repository has no game files, no keys and no generated game code,
  and Savage Wind doesn't include anything that decrypts.

**What you need to know:** Savage Wind needs your own copy, version 1.9.0, from your own console, already extracted to
`exefs/` and `romfs/` folders. Once you have that, we are glad to help with anything that goes wrong
([Game files](game-files.md)). What happens before that point is up to you.

**And "can you send me the files?"** No. Don't ask anyone here, and don't post links. See also
[Respect copyright](../README.md#respect-copyright).

## The recompilation

### What is a static recompilation?

An emulator translates a game's machine code while the game runs. A static recompiler does it once, ahead of time: it
reads the Switch executables, turns every function into C code and compiles that into a program for your PC. When you
play, your CPU runs native code.

### Is this an emulator?

No. There's no Switch being imitated while the game code runs. The game's code runs directly, and Savage Wind replaces
what is around it: the operating system services, the graphics API, audio and input. It keeps one thing an emulator also
needs, a translator for the game's GPU shaders.

### What does Savage Wind actually do at setup?

1. It checks your files are version 1.9.0.
2. It copies them to its own data folder.
3. It recompiles the executables into C on your machine, with a bundled compiler, and builds them into a game library.
4. It translates and precompiles the shaders for your graphics card.

### Why is the compile done on my PC and not shipped?

Because the result contains Nintendo's code. It's generated on your machine from your files, it's for your own use, and
you must not share it. Our releases only contain Savage Wind's own code.

### How does it draw the game?

The game talks to NVN, the Switch's graphics API. Savage Wind implements NVN on top of Vulkan, and has its own translator
from the Switch's Maxwell GPU shaders to Vulkan. That layer is where most of the graphics bugs live, and it's why a
problem can be specific to one vendor or one driver.

### Is it a decompilation? Does it use the decompilation projects?

No. The recompiler translates machine code automatically, and nothing is written from a decompilation project. Code from
those projects isn't accepted (see [CONTRIBUTING](../CONTRIBUTING.md)). The game's own behaviour is studied in our own
copy of the game.

### Why only one version of the game?

The recompiler, and the patches that add higher frame rates, wider screens, the options menu and more, are tied to exact
addresses in one build. Every other version would be close to a separate project to maintain. Version 1.9.0 is the
latest one, and is what you have after updating. For this reason, older versions and other sources of the game such as
the Wii U version won't be supported.

### Why do some glitches work differently?

They depend on the game version and sometimes on the frame rate. Savage Wind is 1.9.0, so what the official updates
removed stays removed, such as some windbomb variants
([#508](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/508)). There's a
[glitch compatibility tracker](glitch-compatibility.md) to record results.

### Why are there still bugs if the code is the original?

Because everything around it is new: graphics, OS services, timing. A real Switch does some things in an order or a time
that the game has silently come to depend on. High frame rates and huge resolutions are also things the game was never
written for.

### Can I use mods?

Partly, and not yet the way you would on Cemu. Language packs work: `lang/<language>.txt` in the data folder is read over
the built-in translations. A loader for other mods is planned, and because this isn't an emulator, Wii U and Cemu
packs need adapting. Mods must not ship game files
([#647](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/647),
[#645](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/645)).

### Does it support amiibo?

There's a virtual reader for your own figure dumps, in the overlay (F1 > amiibo). Savage Wind doesn't include any figure
data, and won't. Getting amiibo rewards without figures is planned.

### What is built on what?

Savage Wind is built on [LAS Recomp](https://github.com/peiikai/LASRecomp), with
[TotK Recomp](https://github.com/valentderah/totk-pc-recomp) and [Ryujinx](https://github.com/Ryujinx/Ryujinx) as
references. Details: [Credits](third-party.md).

---

## Platforms and requests

### Windows and Linux?

Both are maintained, on x86-64. On Linux use the AppImage ([linux.md](linux.md)).

### Steam Deck and handhelds?

The Steam Deck works and is the handheld that gets tested. Other PC handhelds are recognized and have a preset, but only
the Deck has been tried by us.

### Wine or Proton?

Not supported. The AppImage exists so that Linux doesn't need them
([#366](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/366)).

### macOS?

Not planned as a target. The Metal code inherited from LAS Recomp is still there, but nobody maintains it.

### Linux on ARM? Android?

The ARM AppImage is highly experimental. Android is outside the project's scope, though a good pull request would be looked at
([#433](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/433)).

### Tears of the Kingdom?

No plans. Savage Wind is only this game, at least until it ends its Beta phase. There are separate projects for that game.

### Multiplayer?

No. It's an open request ([#617](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/617)), but nothing like it is in the
game.

### What's planned next?

The [Status](STATUS.md) page shows every part, how far it is and what's planned. Alpha 6 has the motion vector redesign
for FSR and TAA as its main job.

---

## Philosophy

### Why does this project exist?

To give a game that deserves it a real PC version, on real PC terms: native code, any frame rate, any resolution, proper
keyboard and mouse. And to make sure nobody with an old PC is left out, which is why Alpha 5 was the "Potato" update.

### Why is it made with AI?

Because that's how a project this size can be made by one person. Nearly all of the code, tooling and reverse engineering
is written by an AI (Anthropic's Claude, through Claude Code), directed, tested and reviewed by a human. We say so up
front, because people have a right to decide with that information. If you don't trust code written by AI, you can
simply ignore this project.

### Why is it free? Can I donate?

It's free, and there's no way to donate, on purpose. Nintendo still sells this game, and a fan project that takes money is
a different thing, legally and morally, from one that doesn't. There are no paid versions, no early access and no
sponsors. The best way to help is a good bug report.

### Why do I have to own the game?

Because it's the only honest way to do this. Savage Wind is a new way to play a game you already have, not a replacement
for buying it. If you like what it does, Nintendo made the game, and they deserve the sale.

### What does the project refuse to do?

- Ship, host or link game files, keys, firmware or translated game text.
- Help anyone circumvent anything.
- Take money.
- Add its cheats into the game's own menus. They stay in the overlay and the console, so the game looks as it should.

### How is the Status number calculated?

It's a weighted average, and how it's weighed is on the [Status](STATUS.md) page. It is an estimate of how far the project
has come against what it set out to do, not a promise.

### How can I help?

- **Report bugs well.** A log and a save are worth more than a long description.
- **Test on hardware we don't have**, especially older GPUs, Intel and AMD on Windows.
- **Write code:** read [CONTRIBUTING](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first. Open pull requests against `test`, keep each one to one
  change, and say how you tested it. Every pull request is tested by the maintainer before it goes in, and its author is
  credited.

### Why do you close issues so fast?

Because one person reads all of them. Anything this page already answers is closed at once with the reason, duplicates
point to one place, reports without a log can't be acted on, and every closed issue can be reopened by commenting with
new information.

`docs/LAUNCHER-SIZE.md`:

```md
# Launcher game-file size

Settings and Game Files share one lazy background size calculation. Opening
either page starts it; later visits reuse its result. The size label reads
"Calculating..." while pending and "Unavailable" if enumeration or thread
creation fails. Partial totals are not displayed as complete measurements.

The cache owns a copy of the scan path. A generation counter cancels and rejects
old results after invalidation or a root/session change. Setup suspends scanning
and clears the result; deletion and DLC removal invalidate it. The next request
after the operation starts a new scan. Starting the game cancels the worker
and joins it; quitting ends it with the process. Cancellation is checked
between filesystem operations; it does not interrupt an OS call that is already
blocked.

The total is logical file length, limited to the same setup-created entries as
the deletion allowlist in `runtime/game_files.h`. Links are skipped. The size
is informational and does not authorize deletion. The cache lasts for one
launcher session and is refreshed by its setup/removal actions, without a
filesystem watcher for external edits.

- Windows reads file sizes and reparse attributes from native directory
  enumeration. Paths use UTF-8, wide APIs and extended-length absolute paths.
- Linux performs one directory-relative metadata lookup per entry and opens
  child directories without following symlinks.
- macOS retains portable traversal, now on the worker. Native macOS bulk
  enumeration and multi-worker Linux scanning are deferred.

## Verification

`make test-game-file-size test-file-size-cache` runs synthetic filesystem and
worker tests without game files or a GPU. Scanner tests cover exact totals,
empty trees, Unicode names/roots, paths over 260 characters, sizes over 4 GiB
and cancellation. POSIX checks include symlinks, unreadable directories, files
whose contents are unreadable, and deletion. Cache tests hold a scan while
servicing requests and verify reuse, invalidation, stale completed results,
root changes, suspension, incomplete results, cancellation, restart and thread
creation failure.

Verified 2026-10-30 against upstream `test` at `0dece28`:

- Full Linux ARM64 and Windows x64 runtime builds pass. The generated game-code
  library and its ABI were not changed or rebuilt.
- Scanner: 22 Linux checks and 15 Windows checks. Cache tests pass on both.
  Linux AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer for the
  cache, and Clang static analysis pass. Portable scanner tests pass on Linux;
  a native macOS build/run remains unverified.
- Existing binding-capture and vibration tests pass on both hosts. Linux RomFS
  regression passes. All 12 language tables have zero missing/unused entries.
- Windows ACL fixtures verify that an unreadable directory reports an
  incomplete result and denied file-content access does not prevent measuring
  accessible metadata. A junction fixture preserves the expected total.
- The real Windows game folder returns 15,157,992,803 bytes in 126-145 ms,
  including console-process startup, over three runs. The Linux warmed
  41,067-file synthetic tree measures about 75 ms including process startup.
- Five diagnostic Windows launcher runs cover normal scanning, an artificial
  two-second worker delay, Game Files first, empty data and access denial. Each
  process performs one shared scan across repeated page switches. CPU UI
  construction remains below 4.5 ms, with pending/ready/unavailable states and
  25 screenshots checked from logs; representative screenshots inspected.
  An explicit worker-stop diagnostic cancels a 30-second delayed scan and
  exits normally without waiting for the delay.
- Linux launcher screenshot smoke passes with software Vulkan.

The UI diagnostics force page transitions/readiness without loading game code;
they measure UI construction, not full presented-frame or physical input
latency. Timing/page-selection instrumentation and artificial delays are only
in ignored verification copies, not the runtime sources committed here.

`docs/PC_MOUSE_CONTROLS.md`:

```md
# PC mouse controls

Mouse pointer controls for menus, inventory, quick equipment and map are enabled by default. Open the executable directly; no custom launcher or environment variables are needed. The native mouse camera already exists upstream and is not reintroduced here. Virtual gyro changes remain separate.

## Options

In the game's **System > Options > Controls** (also in the configuration UI):

- **PC mouse pointer**: hover/click menus, inventory and map. With it on, **Esc** opens pause or goes back and **F2** frees the cursor. Click once inside the window to take it back; that click is consumed. With it off, Esc retains upstream cursor-release behavior.

The switch applies immediately and is saved as `pc_cursor` in `savagewind.ini`. Existing files without the key default to on. `SAVAGEWIND_PC_CURSOR=0/1` is an optional startup override; Controls can change it during the session.

Bow controls are outside this contribution. The normal bindings remain: F for the bow, right mouse for shield/lock-on, and left mouse for attack.

## Pointer behavior

In native Options pages, the wheel scrolls the view without generating d-pad
input. Hover activates the native row highlight and its localized help text; left-click operates its
toggle, button or choice arrow. Hover does not recenter the scroll view. These
controls use **PC mouse pointer**, including immediate disable and reboot reset.
Mouse and keyboard/controller share one native highlight and help text. Options does not draw a separate mouse highlight. Keyboard/controller navigation retains focus until the mouse moves, clicks or scrolls again, including when Options captures the game button state. Rebuilt pages start at the top, so returning from a long key-binding list cannot carry its scroll offset into the parent menu.

Inventory categories support clicking their icons, wheel navigation and horizontal dragging. Quick equipment supports wheel and drag selection, retaining the selected item when its selector closes. The current `test` defaults remain **1 weapons / 2 shields / 3 runes / 4 whistle**. Saved custom bindings are not overwritten.

Adventure Log and Ability Controls hover select through their registered native row lists, keeping their details and shared highlight synchronized. The outer category list is kept separate from its nested row lists. Hover uses cursor selection rather than the scroll-page selection function, so it does not rebuild or recenter the view. A stationary mouse retains focus until keyboard/controller input takes over; new mouse input takes it back. Clicking a category icon switches the native list while retaining disabled/locked categories. Hover preserves the viewport and does not repeatedly select the same quest. Cursor hit-testing clips visible bounds without calling the native clipping callback, which clears focus for offscreen rows. Category hit areas use their 32 px cursor panes rather than their overlapping 211 px containing layouts. Clicking the upper Adventure Log / Inventory / System labels uses the normal section transition, with a hover frame and pressed feedback; modal submenus retain input priority.

Map navigation supports wheel zoom (the map grows around the pointer, so the spot under it stays under it), left-drag panning, WASD and progressive edge scrolling. Marker hover has a small attraction radius without recentering the map. Stamp placement stays anchored while choosing an icon, and Edit/Delete/Cancel accepts pointer input. Coordinates account for resolution, aspect ratio and letterboxing.

Direct panning closes the native unbounded vertical sentinel using the opposite zoom-dependent extent. Dragging, WASD and edge scrolling stop at that boundary, and a viewport left outside by an older revision is recovered. Synthetic limit/zoom tests pass, and the contributor confirmed this follow-up in game on the previously validated local pointer base. Full gameplay validation of the latest upstream integration remains pending.

The system cursor is hidden while keyboard/controller navigation owns menu focus, and over the map canvas while the game pointer is active, without enabling relative mouse mode there. It is restored for host UI, cursor release, loss of focus and when pointer mode is off. Controllers and existing bindings remain available.

Controller button presses and stick movement outside the configured dead zone release the PC map adapter, including the button that opens the map. While the controller owns input, native map pan/zoom/focus helpers run unchanged and cached mouse viewport, drag and stamp state are discarded. Mouse movement, clicks or scrolling reclaim pointer control; WASD retains PC map navigation. Host tests exercise these transitions and out-of-window cache invalidation. Physical-controller gameplay validation is pending.

The specialized map/inventory adapters target BOTW 1.9.0. Optional generator sites validate instruction prologues; missing groups disable their adapters instead of guessing addresses. Reboot clears cached guest pointers and gesture state.

Dialogue pointer input uses the shared conversation screen: left-click advances text when no responses are selectable, while response clicks use their native cursor channel. It also advances shop dialogue while the background item screen remains allocated.

Shop purchase lists and selling grids share native list selection, so the item highlight and details follow hover instead of returning to the old keyboard selection. Quantity entry uses the game's existing number and arrow panes: click minus/plus, hold to repeat, or click the number to type. Hover highlights the available arrows and number; number editing has a blinking caret. Native menu cues provide hover and activation feedback. Typed values and held arrows clamp to the dialog's native minimum and maximum without confirming a transaction. An additional affordability cap derived from rupees has not been implemented or verified.

The button prompts at the bottom of the pause menu (Sort, Select, Back, Rotate...) and the Back prompt of Rotate mode are clickable: a click presses the prompt's own button, read from its glyph. Left click stays the pointer's click elsewhere, so Sort (Y, bound to left click by default) is reached through its prompt instead. Middle click and the side buttons keep their bindings while the pointer is on, as with it off: middle click is the right stick press, which enters Rotate. In Rotate mode, a left-button drag turns Link through the right stick, as the mouse camera does with the pointer off; right click or the Back prompt leaves Rotate mode.

Dragging horizontally over Link's inventory preview adjusts its native yaw targets without modifying the actor's translation or entering the Rotate mode that hides inventory information. The gesture retains its original owner, so crossing into the item grid cannot start a page drag. Inventory category clicks rebuild the three-page ring around the destination with the screen's own open-time routine (pages, their visibility and the neighbours' positions) rather than stepping through intermediate categories, so keyboard/controller paging continues from there. Header and category buttons use native menu hover/confirmation sounds. The map pointer is confined to the map edge zone and released in other screens or host UI.

## Validation

Updated onto `test` at `ed9279a`, retaining upstream changes. The Windows host executable builds. After synchronization, pointer, input-focus, control, console and gyro host tests pass; localization checks report no missing/unused keys, and game-site checks pass. The in-game checks below cover the pre-sync pointer build; full gameplay validation of this latest integration remains pending. Automated coverage includes:

- `make test-pc-controls`: actual host cursor-update transitions (including map entry while relative mode is already off), focus, overlay/F2 policy, number-key defaults, options persistence across boots and startup overrides.
- `tests/test_options_pointer.c`: synthetic Options viewport scrolling without d-pad/selection changes, scroll limits, transformed hover rectangles, direct row actions, native focus activation without auto-scrolling, input ownership, disabled pointer behavior and reboot reset. The contributor also checked Options hit detection, wheel scrolling, help text, keyboard/mouse focus transfer and returning from binding subpages in game.
- `tests/test_cursor_math.c`: seven resolutions/aspect ratios, letterboxing, 1,200 pan/zoom samples, time-based WASD/edge navigation.
- `tools/test_game_sites.py`: 45 checks.

The contributor tested the final local Windows/BOTW 1.9.0 revision in game, covering Adventure Log and Ability Controls hover/category selection, shared input focus, upper section buttons and sounds, inventory categories and Link rotation, NPC dialogue and responses, shop hover and dialogue, quantity typing/held arrows/feedback, and map navigation/stamps. The maintainer previously tested the earlier menu, Options, inventory and map revision on Windows. The bow override has been removed: ordinary gameplay bindings remain unchanged.

Synthetic host tests also cover stationary list hover, the derived purchase-list type, locked categories, viewport preservation, quantity repeat timing/limits/release, native preview yaw changes without actor translation or UI-mode changes, and reset behavior. These tests supplement gameplay checks; Steam Deck and broader controller testing remain pending.

build/test_cursor_math
python tools/test_game_sites.py
```

`docs/PERF-ROUTES.md`:

```md
# Performance routes

`tools/perf_routes.py` measures the same six views the same way every time, so a change can be judged in fps and
milliseconds against a baseline. It needs a game build with the control endpoint (`threads`, `gpuprof`, `memstats`,
`frametrace`; docs/CONTROL.md), Windows for the thread shares (the stack sampler; Linux uses CPU time per thread), and a
scratch copy of a save that is not the player's.

## The routes

Each route is its own boot. `SAVAGEWIND_TEST_WARP=<place>` (runtime/services/test_warp.c) rewrites where the save puts
Link, scripted input picks Continue, and the game loads straight into the place. A long `teleport` is not used: far from
the loaded area it leaves the game waiting on its loading spinner. Two routes then hop a short way, inside the loaded
area, and hover there with fly mode.

| route | place | view |
|---|---|---|
| plateau | Great Plateau, outside the Shrine of Resurrection | north-east over the grass to Hyrule Castle (yaw 150, pitch -3) |
| kakariko | Kakariko Village, horse gate | north into the village, NPCs (yaw 180, pitch -10) |
| field | Riverside Stable, Hyrule Field | north over the field (yaw 180, pitch -3) |
| rito | Rito Village, hovering 75 m south of the goddess statue | north at the village spire (yaw 180, pitch -8) |
| castle | above castle town, hovering 145 m south of the castle gate | north at Hyrule Castle (yaw 180, pitch 0) |
| hateno | Hateno Village, goddess statue | east over the village (yaw 90, pitch -8) |

Every route: hour 10:00, held (`time set 10`, `time freeze`), clear weather (`SAVAGEWIND_TEST_WEATHER=0`), camera set with
`look`, then 12 s to settle. Each run keeps a screenshot of its view next to its log, to check it is the same view.

## What is measured

1. 20 s with nothing else running: `frames` (average fps, frame time p99 and max; "1% low" is 1000 / p99), the
   `[vk] t=...` lines of `SAVAGEWIND_VK_PROF=2` (GPU time of the submissions per frame, compiles, `[hitch]` lines over
   34 ms) and `threads` (CPU time per thread), with `nvidia-smi` read once a second (GPU clock, load, power).
2. `gpuprof`: the GPU time per pass of one frame; the top three labels (same label summed) go in the CSV. Pass sizes in
   the labels are the game's own (1600x900 docked), before the runtime scales them.
3. 4 s of `sample` stack samples every 2 ms. Per thread they give the share of time working or waiting:
   - main thread (the game's first thread, handle 0x101): busy, waiting for the render thread (`queue_wait`), waiting
     for the GPU (`vk_wait_seq`, `renderer_sync`) or another wait (other game threads, sleeps, a free core);
   - render thread (the NVN queue thread, 0xf000: translation and command recording): busy, waiting for the GPU or idle.

4. Memory: `memstats` once a second through the timed window (a few tens of microseconds on the presenting thread):
   process RAM (working set / RSS: peak and median over the window; `ram_hwm_mb` is the process's high-water mark
   since boot), memory in use system-wide, GPU memory per heap (`VK_EXT_memory_budget`: the whole process's use of
   each heap; `gpu_local` the device-local heaps, `gpu_host` the others) and texture memory by kind at the end of the
   window: native ASTC, ASTC decoded to RGBA8 on the CPU (GPUs without ASTC; with the ASTC size it came from), BC,
   render targets (depth formats and the NVN compressible or display flag), other. `astc_ms` is the CPU time spent
   decoding ASTC in the window.
5. Hitches: `frametrace` records every frame of the window: its time and what happened in it (pipelines and shaders
   built, on any thread, and their ms; draws that waited for a pipeline and how long; upload and texture MB; ASTC
   decode ms; GPU waits; guest file reads; `vkAllocateMemory`; the present; page faults; CPU ms of the main, render and
   recorder threads). Each run keeps `<tag>_frames.csv`. A hitch is a frame over twice the window's median frame
   time; `<tag>_hitches.csv` lists them with a cause: the largest stall (pipeline wait, ASTC, GPU wait over the
   window's median wait, file reads, `vkAllocateMemory`, present over its median) if it explains a quarter of the
   frame's excess over the median or more; else `pipeline_build` if the frame's pipeline builds do (synchronous
   shaders, the default, build on the render thread inside the frame); else the thread whose CPU time rose most over
   its median (`main_cpu`: game logic; `render_cpu`: translation; `recorder_cpu`: Vulkan recording), by the same quarter
   rule; else `builds` (some built in that frame), `upload` (4 MB or more), `faults` (over 4x the median), or
   `unknown`. `table` prints a memory table and a hitch-cause table after the speed table; `rehitch <dir>` works the
   hitch columns out again from the kept traces.

`game_ms` and `render_ms` are those busy shares times the frame time. **limiter** is the largest of main busy, render
busy and GPU time as a share of the frame time ("none" under 80%). The stack samples slow the game a little, which is why
they come after the timed window. CPU time from `threads` is not used for the limiter: three game threads spin while
they wait (an SDK event thread, the audio render thread and one game thread), so they always show 100%.

## Running it

```
python tools/perf_routes.py run --save <scratch save folder with save_0> --ini <savagewind.ini to start from> \
    --out <dir> --size 1920x1080 2560x1440 --runs 3 [--config <label>] [--affinity 0xff] [--env VAR=value ...]
python tools/perf_routes.py table <dir> [<dir> ...]     markdown table: median and spread over the runs
python tools/perf_routes.py boot --save ... --out <dir> --place kakariko    start one place and leave it running
```

The settings are the given ini with the frame cap off, vsync off, frame generation off, the perf overlay off and the
window size of `--size`; the game runs hidden (`SAVAGEWIND_HIDDEN=1`) on port 7790. `--affinity` starts the game on
those logical processors only (the mask is set before any thread runs). Results append to `<dir>/results.csv`, one row
per run and route; each run's folder holds the log, the settings and the screenshot. A route whose game crashed or
lost its camera is tried once more, in a `<run>_attempt2` folder (the failed one keeps its log).

`--potato` imitates a weak PC: one logical processor on each of 4 cores, 1280x720, a 4 GB hard cap on the game's
working set (`--ram-mb`, Windows; pages over it go to the standby list, so it shows trimming, not a slow page file) and
a 2 GB card (`--vram-mb`: the budget the VRAM trim sees and the heap copy's plan), with the console's shadow
resolution whatever the ini says. Each of the limits can be given on its own. The GPU itself stays as fast as it is.

### On the Steam Deck (Linux)

The script runs on the Deck itself (its python3; it needs only `tools/perf_routes.py`, `swctl.py` and
`profile_samples.py`), started as a user systemd unit in the desktop session so it outlives the SSH session, under
`systemd-inhibit --what=sleep:idle`. It takes the game as an AppImage with a data root of its own, set up once from
the game files with `SAVAGEWIND_SETUP_FROM`:

```
python3 tools/perf_routes.py run --tree ~/sw-bench --exe ~/sw-bench/SavageWind-igpu.AppImage \
    --data-root ~/sw-bench/data --save ~/sw-bench/save-src --ini ~/sw-bench/deck-default.ini \
    --out ~/sw-bench/runs/deck --size 1280x800 --runs 3 --visible --fullscreen
```

There is no stack sampler on Linux: main and render busy ms are their CPU time per frame (`busy_from` = cpu; neither
thread spins while it waits). The GPU clock, load and power come from amdgpu's sysfs files. Before each boot the
script waits while any `savagewind` it did not start runs (the player's game). `--cache-reset <dir>` puts the data
root's `cache/` back to a copy of `<dir>/cache` before each boot and starts the driver's on-disk shader cache (Mesa)
from `<dir>/mesa`: a player's first boot after setup (copy both right after setup). `--visible` shows the window (a hidden window on a
Wayland desktop is not a fair measure); `--fullscreen` keeps fullscreen, as a Deck player has it.

Hidden runs get background GPU clocks while someone uses the desktop: compare interleaved runs, and look at the
`gpu_clock_mhz` column (about 1950 MHz on an RTX 3060 when nobody is at the PC). The `others` column counts other
`savagewind.exe` processes seen during the run; a run with any is not comparable.

## Steam Deck baseline (2026-11-01)

The iGPU reference: Steam Deck (RADV VANGOGH, 15 W APU, 16 GB shared), Desktop mode (KDE Plasma), plugged in, 0.4.1-alpha.4
plus the counters of this tool; fresh-install settings (upscaler and AA off, shadows console, FOV 100, synchronous
shaders), fullscreen 1280x800, uncapped; the recorder thread off (it does not start on Linux builds: glibc puts the
1.14 MB of static TLS, 1 MB of it `ms_guarded`'s buffer in `runtime/memscan_os.c`, inside its 1 MB stack, and
`pthread_create` returns EINVAL). Warm caches, 3 runs, median (min-max):

| route | fps | 1% low | p99 ms | main ms | render ms | GPU ms | GPU clock | limits |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| plateau | 51.4 (51.2-51.9) | 34.6 | 28.9 | 12.65 | 18.52 | 16.53 | 643 MHz | render 95%, GPU 85% |
| kakariko | 53.4 (52.8-53.4) | 43.4 | 23.1 | 13.97 | 17.99 | 16.79 | 672 MHz | render 96%, GPU 90% |
| field | 67.3 (67.0-68.4) | 52.8 | 18.9 | 12.12 | 13.88 | 13.28 | 792 MHz | render 93%, GPU 89% |
| rito | 39.6 (39.5-39.7) | 26.6 | 37.6 | 13.51 | 23.64 | 20.98 | 518 MHz | render 94%, GPU 83% |
| castle | 55.5 (55.5-55.6) | 44.1 | 22.7 | 12.98 | 17.50 | 15.82 | 681 MHz | render 97%, GPU 88% |
| hateno | 52.6 (52.4-52.9) | 41.5 | 24.1 | 12.96 | 18.36 | 16.81 | 660 MHz | render 97%, GPU 88% |

- The APU sits at its 15 W cap in every view; the GPU runs at 520-790 MHz (of 1600), 94-98% busy. CPU time saved is
  also GPU clock gained.
- Memory: RSS 1.0-1.2 GB, GPU device-local 777 MB, GPU host 3.14-3.19 GB (the 3120 MB guest heap as a dma-buf; the host
  heap is 3072 MB, so it is over budget), system 7.6-7.8 GB of 14.8 in use. Textures: BC 141-234 MB, render targets
  96-98 MB, other 56-58 MB, **ASTC 0 MB** (no ASTC texture in any view, so no CPU decoding).
- Hitches: none over twice the median in 24 warm windows. A first boot after setup (traced 45 s from the first world
  frame) has 4-16 per view: GPU waits after new pipelines (33 of 59, 1.5 s) and pipelines linked on the render thread
  (20, 1.4 s, up to 170 ms with 99-236 builds in one frame; 270-706 built in 45 s despite setup's precompile).

The full report (PC comparison, hitch lists, targets) is in the maintainers' Alpha 5 notes.

`docs/RECOMP-LOCALS.md`:

```md
# Registers and flags in C locals (`gen.py --locals`)

`make RECOMP_LOCALS=1` (the generator's `--locals`; the default since Alpha 5, `RECOMP_LOCALS=0` turns it off) turns on two passes ported from
[TotK Recomp](https://github.com/valentderah/totk-pc-recomp) (MIT, commit f469c5a; `third_party/totk-pc-recomp/LICENSE`):

- `tools/regs.py`: each generated function copies its 6 most used X registers (or SP) into C locals at its entry and
  works on those. It stores the ones it changed (a forward "dirty" plan over the function's flow) before a call, an
  SVC, a trap, a patch site, a return or a tail exit, and loads them again after: after a call only X0-X18 and X30
  (AAPCS64: the callee keeps X19-X29 and SP), after an SVC, a patch site or a setjmp all of them.
- `tools/flags.py`: NZCV lives in a local `Flags F` (`runtime/cpu.h`). A compare of a known kind keeps its operands, so
  `cmp; b.lt` becomes one C compare; the packed form is computed only where something needs it.

Without the passes every guest instruction loads and stores the Cpu, and clang can keep nothing in host registers,
since every guest store may alias the Cpu. The switch is part of `GAMELIB_ID` (Makefile) and reaches the start
screen's build of the game code (`runtime/gamebuild.c`, `GAMELIB_GENARGS`): a library built one way is never loaded
for the other, and players set up again when it changes.

## Where Breath of the Wild differs from TotK, and what the passes do there

- **setjmp / longjmp.** `main` imports both; libjpeg and libpng in `sdk` use them. A call to the guest setjmp
  (`gen.py setjmp_call`) runs on the Cpu: every dirty register is stored before it, its C (the host setjmp, the guest
  setjmp call) is left on the Cpu, and every local is loaded again after it, on both returns. The HLE longjmp
  (`runtime/hle/setjmp.c`) writes X19-X30 and SP and never returns to its caller, so the trust below never sees it.
  The flags after a setjmp are a call's: read from `c->nzcv` if anything reads them.
- **Patch sites** (`tools/patches.py`). Their hand-written C calls the runtime with `c`, reads and writes any register
  (`c->sp -= 0x30`, `c->x[0] = ...`), returns, calls guest functions and jumps to labels. It runs on the Cpu: dirty
  registers are stored and the flags published before it, its text is left as it is (`regs.OPAQUE`), and every
  register and `F.nz` are loaded again after it and before each of its `goto`s.
- **Other runtime calls with `c`.** SVCs store before and reload everything after. BRK and undefined words store
  before (they do not return). `rt_dispatch` (blr, br, jump table misses, calls outside the module) is a call or a
  tail exit. The cold `<name>_r` copy and functions with an unresolved computed `br` (all-instruction fallback) keep
  everything in the Cpu, as do functions with FP/SIMD inline asm (`--simd asm`, arm64 hosts).
- **Callee-saved trust.** Runtime writes to a running thread's X19-X29/SP: `hle_longjmp` (above); full-Cpu save and
  restore around a guest call (`runtime/pc_cursor.c`, `runtime/hle/nvn_boot.c`), which puts back what it found;
  `runtime/hle/movie.c` and `runtime/nvn/cmdbuf.c` restore X0-X7 only. Kernel threads each have their own Cpu, there
  are no guest fibers, and `ExitThread` / the unwind at shutdown leave by longjmp without returning. `sdk`'s C++
  unwinder (`_Unwind_*`, `__cxa_throw`) has no callers in `main`. So the trust is on; `--no-callee-saved-trust`
  reloads X19-X29 and SP after every call too.
- **Flags after a call.** Unlike TotK Recomp's, a read that can see a callee's (or a patch site's) flags reads them
  from `c->nzcv` (`flags.Plan.load`): what the function does stays the same as without the passes there. A callee
  still does not publish its flags when it returns, so code that reads a callee's flags (no AAPCS64 code does) would
  see the older ones.
- **Spin waits.** Guest code polls memory with plain loads in a loop (`ldr; cmp; b.eq` back to the load) and counts on
  the hardware to see the other core's store. Without locals the loop's own stores to the Cpu kept clang from moving
  the load out of it; with locals the loop stores nothing, clang hoisted the load, and the game hung at boot in
  `f_7000ef62dc` (found by bisecting main's functions). Every backward branch now carries a compiler barrier
  (`asm volatile("" ::: "memory")`), which keeps loads inside loops and leaves the locals in registers.
- **Diagnostics.** The hang watch and crash dumps (`runtime/kernel.c`, `runtime/dispatch.c`) read other threads'
  registers from the Cpu, which can now be older than the locals.

## Tests

- `tools/test_locals.py`: random hand-assembled functions (compares and their readers, stack loads and stores, a
  loop, calls, blr, SVCs, patch sites with a `goto`, setjmp/longjmp, tail exits through b, b.cond and br) generated
  through `gen.py` with and without `--locals`, compiled and run against Unicorn. `--no-callee-saved-trust` and
  `--reg-locals N` test the variants.
- `tools/test_lift.py <nso> <base> [count] [seed] --locals` and `tools/test_simd.py --locals`: every instruction as a
  one-instruction function with locals (`gen.single_with_locals`), against Unicorn.

## Measured (2026-11-01, Ryzen 5 5600X, RTX 3060, 1080p, tools/perf_routes.py, six routes)

- **Main thread:** 4-16% less busy per frame on the full CPU and 13-32% less on 4 cores / 4 threads.
- **CPU per frame:** 5-14% less on the full CPU and 3-17% less on 4 cores / 4 threads.
- **fps:** up 3-10% on the views the GPU or the render thread does not cap (field, castle, Hateno). The render thread
  is runtime code and does not change.
- **Code:** the library is 14% smaller (228 vs 264 MB) and compiles 12% faster.
- **Setup:** generation takes 3.5x as long in Python (main 179 s vs 49 s).

## Against PR #324 (flags only in a local, by Hiorac)

Measured 2026-11-01 on the same base and machine, interleaved, six routes at 1080p.

| | #324 | --locals |
|---|---|---|
| main-thread busy, full CPU | -3.5% | -8.2% |
| main-thread busy, 4 cores / 4 threads | -11% | -26% |
| CPU per frame, full CPU | -4.6% | -8.4% |
| CPU per frame, 4 cores / 4 threads | -6% | -10% |
| library | 241.5 MB | 227.6 MB |
| -O1 instructions, first 400 functions of main | -14% | -23% |

- Both flag passes reach about the same 57,000 functions.
- #324's one idea we lacked, that a jump out of a function stores the flags only when the code it goes to can read
  them, is in `gen.py` (`_entry_flags`).

`docs/SAVAGE-WIND.md`:

```md
# Savage Wind

Savage Wind (repositorio *Savage Wind Recomp*) es una recompilación estática de *Breath of the Wild* (Switch)
para Windows y Linux. Parte de LASRecomp beta 3 (MIT), la recompilación estática de *Link's Awakening*.

Notas de desarrollo. El README explica qué hace falta y las reglas de copyright para quien llega al repositorio.

## Reglas legales del proyecto

- El repositorio y cualquier build no contienen archivos del juego, código del juego (tampoco el C
  generado), assets, fuentes del sistema ni keys.
- Savage Wind no desencripta nada. La entrada son archivos ya extraídos por el usuario desde su propia
  consola y su propia copia del juego, en `extracted/` (ignorado por git).
- La recompilación corre en la máquina del usuario (`make gen` o la pantalla de setup), igual que en
  LASRecomp beta 3.
- No se usan marcas de Nintendo en el nombre, los íconos ni los binarios del proyecto.
- `.gitignore` bloquea `dump/`, `keys/`, `*.keys`, `*.xci`, `*.nsp`, `*.nca` y similares.

## Publicación

GitHub: `Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp` (remote `origin`, público desde el 2026-10-16). No se sube el historial
local: la importación de LASRecomp trae capturas de *Link's Awakening* y su randomizer. La rama local `public`
lleva un commit por publicación con el árbol de `main` y el email noreply de GitHub. Desde el 2026-10-21 se sube a
la rama remota `test`: el `main` remoto tiene un ruleset ("main": sin borrado, sin force push, cambios por pull
request y "Restrict updates" sin bypass), así que entra a `main` con un pull request de `test` (#1 para Alpha 2),
que solo se puede fusionar si el dueño del repo cambia ese ruleset:

```
export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=Revivedx GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=82332536+Revivedx@users.noreply.github.com
export GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=$GIT_AUTHOR_NAME GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=$GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL
git branch -f public $(git commit-tree "main^{tree}" -p public -m "<qué cambia>")
git -c credential.helper= -c "credential.helper=!gh auth git-credential" push origin public:test
```

Antes de cada publicación: `git ls-tree -r --name-only main` no debe tener archivos del juego, código generado,
keys ni rutas personales.

Issues y pull requests (#160, 2026-10-26): GitHub lee los formularios (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`) y los workflows
(`.github/workflows/`) de la rama por defecto, `main`, así que un cambio en ellos solo cuenta cuando llega a `main`.
`triage.yml` etiqueta `needs-info` los bugs nuevos sin log, de una release vieja o de 1.8.2 (con un comentario que
dice qué falta), `stale.yml` los cierra a las 24 horas sin cambios (corre cada hora) y `retarget.yml` pasa a `test` las pull requests de
forks abiertas contra `main`. Una etiqueta `triage-ok` deja un issue fuera del triage. **En cada release**: poner la
versión nueva como "(latest)" en el desplegable "Savage Wind version" de `bug_report.yml` (el triage marca solo la
opción "An older release").

Releases: el zip de `make dist` (ver `docs/BUILD-windows.md`) se sube con `gh release create v<versión>
--prerelease` sobre el commit de `public`. Alpha 1 (`0.1.0-alpha.1`, 2026-10-17) se probó como jugador: zip
extraído en una carpeta nueva, PATH sin MSYS2, preparación desde la pantalla de inicio (copia, `romfs.bin`,
generación y compilación con swgen + zig: 2308 s con 12 hilos) y PLAY hasta tener a Link en el Santuario, a 30
fps. La carpeta queda en ~30,5 GB (romfs 15 GB, `romfs.bin` 15,1 GB, `swgame.dll` 209 MB), ~32 GB durante la
compilación. Para la prueba sirve `SAVAGEWIND_LAUNCHER_AUTOPLAY=1` con `SAVAGEWIND_HOST_INPUT` (la tecla E es A)
y `SAVAGEWIND_SCREENSHOT_EVERY` (capturas en `build/` de la carpeta de trabajo).

Desde el 2026-10-18 `savagewind.exe` entra directo al juego si los archivos están preparados y `swgame` coincide con
este build; si no, muestra solo la preparación (modo setup) y al terminar arranca el juego. `--config` (lo que hace
`Savage Wind Configuration.exe`, runtime/platform/windows_config.c; en Linux la acción "Savage Wind Configuration"
del `.desktop` del AppImage; en macOS mantener Opción al abrir la app) muestra la pantalla de configuración completa;
"Quit to Start Screen" vuelve a ella. Las pruebas de la pantalla (`SAVAGEWIND_LAUNCHER_SHOT`, `_SETUP`, `_EXTRACT`,
`_DELETE`) la muestran siempre, en modo configuración, o en modo setup con `SAVAGEWIND_LAUNCHER_MODE=setup`. El fondo
(runtime/ui/splash.mm) es arte propio dibujado (un claro de bosque con la espada del icono en una piedra), o `splash.jpg` / `splash.png` del
jugador en la carpeta de datos (nunca en el repo ni en el zip).

Antes de copiar nada, la preparación comprueba el RomFS elegido contra la versión del `exefs/main`, con la columna de
ficheros del RomFS de `runtime/game_versions.h` (los que tiene con la actualización aplicada; 1.8.2: 41.056; 0: sin
recuento). El RomFS debe decir esa versión en `System/Version.txt` y tener al menos el 95 % de esos ficheros: así se
detectan el RomFS del cartucho sin la actualización (dice 1.0.0) y el RomFS de la actualización sola (muchos menos
ficheros).

## Estructura de entrada esperada

```
savage_wind/extracted/
  exefs/   main, main.npdm, rtld, sdk (y subsdk* si el juego los trae)
  romfs/   contenido completo de la romfs (base + actualización ya fusionadas)
```

BOTW 1.8.2 y 1.9.0 traen solo `subsdk0`. Otro `subsdk1`..`subsdk9` en una ExeFS de una versión conocida es de un mod o
de un cargador de mods copiado ahí (#165: el generador fallaba en `subsdk3`): `tools/layout.py` (`GAME_SUBSDKS`) lo
deja fuera del código y `runtime/loader.c` lo salta con un aviso en el log. Con una versión desconocida un subsdk sin
código sigue siendo un error ("build it again"). **Revisar al implementar el DLC o mods con código:** el DLC de BOTW es
contenido de datos (AddOnContent, sin código), pero un mod con código (exlaunch / skyline) sí trae un subsdk; si algún
día se soportan, `GAME_SUBSDKS` y el salto del loader tienen que dejarlos pasar.

La versión principal y la única con soporte es la 1.9.0 (2026-02-17, v1114112: texto en tailandés en Switch 2,
SDK 21.4.1), la última: un dump legal hecho hoy la trae. La 1.8.2 (versión de título v1048576) se sigue instalando y
funciona, pero sin soporte: un issue de 1.8.2 se arregla solo si también pasa en la 1.9.0 (decisión del usuario,
2026-10-22; ver "Versiones del juego"). El build id del módulo `main` identifica
la versión exacta; `tools/sw_probe.py` lo imprime.

## Cambios respecto de LASRecomp

Hechos:

- `tools/patches.py`: vacío. Los parches por instrucción de LASRecomp apuntaban a direcciones de
  Link's Awakening y habrían roto (o corrompido) la generación de BOTW.
- `tools/gen.py`: ya no carga `tools/rando/patch_variants.json` (sitios del randomizer de LA). El
  descubrimiento de funciones quedó en `discover()` para poder reusarlo desde otras herramientas.
- `tools/sw_probe.py`: nuevo. Mide el exefs sin escribir C (ver abajo).
- `.gitattributes`: finales de línea LF en checkouts de Windows.
- Runtime sin lo exclusivo de Link's Awakening (verificado con `make runtime-objs` en MSYS2 UCRT64:
  sin errores ni warnings, y el `.exe` enlaza):
  - Borrados: `runtime/rando.[ch]`; `runtime/ui/` `rando_tab`, `spoiler_view`, `tracker_overlay`,
    `inventory_overlay`, `pets_ui`, `chaos_overlay`, `save_editor`, `warp_tab`, `difficulty`, `cheats`,
    `shader_tour` (recorría los puntos de warp de LA) y sus datos `warp_data.h` / `item_names.h`;
    `runtime/hle/` `chamber`, `digs`, `doorjump`, `escape`, `flags_ext`, `hookshot`, `keysanity`,
    `miniboss`, `pets`, `pot_glow`, `qol`, `rescue`, `shopsanity`, `souls`, `warp`, `widescreen`;
    `runtime/nvn/texpatch.[ch]` (retoques de texturas de la UI de LA: iconos de botones Xbox/PlayStation,
    icono de Hero Mode, color de túnica y corazones, botella dorada).
  - Borrados fuera del runtime: `third_party/LAS-Randomizer`, `tools/rando/`, `tools/warp_table.py`,
    los objetivos `rando-helper` y `smoketest` del Makefile, `tools/linux/smoketest.sh`,
    `tools/doorjump_test.sh` y `tools/perf_sweep.py` (dependían del warp y del randomizer), keystone en
    `tools/build_deps_macos.sh`, el venv del randomizer en `tools/setup_windows.ps1`, y las capturas de
    LA de `docs/` (`ultrawide.jpg`, `start_screen.jpg`).
  - `make gen-helper` usa su propio venv (`build/gen-venv`: capstone, unicorn, lz4, PyInstaller);
    `tools/linux/rando_helper.sh` pasó a `tools/linux/gen_helper.sh` y solo congela el generador.
  - `tools/gen.py`: fuera el camino muerto de `rando_word()` (`RANDO_CODE` siempre estaba vacío).
  - Archivos genéricos revisados: `main.c` (sin seeds; `SAVAGEWIND_REBOOT_AT=<frame>:<game|title>`),
    `services/fs.c` (el overlay de la RomFS queda como herramienta de desarrollo:
    `SAVAGEWIND_ROMFS_OVERLAY=<carpeta>` reemplaza o agrega archivos; las partidas van siempre a `save/`),
    `hle/input.c` (sin ticks de LA; las variables de prueba que vivían en archivos de LA pasaron acá),
    backends Vulkan y Metal (sin pot/pets/widescreen/texpatch; la imagen queda siempre en 16:9 con
    barras), `settings.[ch]` (solo ajustes genéricos: video, audio, `dpad_move`, aviso del menú),
    `ui/menu.mm` (pestañas Controls, Video, Audio y Quit), `ui/launcher.mm` (sin selector de seeds,
    sin pregunta de aspecto, sin consulta de actualizaciones a GitHub de LASRecomp, sin fondo del video
    de título de LA; acepta cualquier `main` que sea NSO y muestra su build id). `paths.c`,
    `gamebuild.c`, `romfs_build.c`, `fnprof.c`, `hle/framepace.c` y `nvn/cmdbuf.c` no tenían ganchos
    de LA aparte de los nombres.
- Nombres: `savagewind[.exe]`, `savagewind.dll.a`, `swgame.{dll,so,dylib}` (entrada `swgame_tables`),
  generador congelado `swgen` (`tools/swgen.spec`), `savagewind.ini`, `savagewind.log`,
  `local.savagewind` (macOS), `~/.local/share/savagewind` (Linux), variables de entorno
  `SAVAGEWIND_*` (antes `LARECOMP_*`, incluida `SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT`), "Savage Wind" en la UI.
- Módulos en memoria (era el pendiente "ajustar `MAIN_BASE`/`SDK_BASE` y cargar `subsdk*`"): ya no hay
  direcciones fijas por módulo; las calcula `tools/layout.py` y se cargan todos los `subsdk*`. Ver abajo.
- Arranque con el `nn::init::Start` de 1.8.2 (`_ZN2nn4init5StartEmmPFvvES2_S2_`, tres callbacks; el de
  LA tenía dos). Desensamblado, hace: `_init_libc0`, `nnosInitialize`, **x2**, `_init_libc1`,
  `nninitInitializeSdkModule`, `nninitStartup`, `_init_libc2`, **x3**, `nnMain`, **x4**,
  `nninitFinalizeSdkModule`, `nnosQuickExit`. `runtime/main.c` busca primero esa firma (si no, la de dos)
  y pasa x2 = inicializar `sdk`, x3 = inicializar `subsdk9`..`0` y `main`, x4 = finalizarlos en orden de
  carga (`DT_FINI`, o `fini_array` al revés); los destructores del `sdk` no corren (la salida es rápida).
  Para llegar a x2 hicieron falta además `DT_RELR` (abajo) y `svcGetInfo` 28 (`AliasRegionExtraSize`, 0).
- Jump tables en `tools/gen.py` (era el pendiente de `printf_core`, ver abajo).
  - Antes, el descubrimiento de funciones tomaba como función nueva el destino de un `adr` hecho dentro de la
    misma función. Ese destino es la base de una jump table: 611 en el `sdk`, 953 en `main` y 334 en `subsdk0`.
    Así partía la función, y los cortes se encadenaban: `printf_core` quedaba en 38 pedazos. El `br` caía en
    un pedazo sin sus casos, y el `switch` de respaldo solo cubre el pedazo: "no function at 0x700292070c".
  - Ahora el rango de cada función sale de su FDE de `.eh_frame` (`analyze.eh_frame_extents`, el
    `pc_range`). Un `adr`/`adrp`+`add` a una dirección de la misma función es una etiqueta, no un inicio.
  - El resolver busca la guarda, la base y los casos en toda esa función, no solo en el pedazo. Emula la
    ventana en línea recta: los `cbz`/`tbz` que el compilador intercala siguen de largo, y el `cmp` puede
    tener `cbz`/`tbz` entre él y la guarda. Una lectura por un registro sin valor lee ceros. La guarda puede
    estar hasta 32 instrucciones antes del `br`. Cubre tablas `ldrb`, `ldrh` y `ldrsw`.
  - Si una función queda partida igual (una llamada a su mitad), los casos que caen en otro pedazo pasan a
    ser inicios, y el `br` llega a ellos con una llamada de cola.
  - Resultado: ninguna función con FDE del `sdk` ni de `main` queda partida. Antes eran 443 y 788
    funciones, en 6102 y 8361 pedazos de más. En `subsdk0` queda una, partida por un `adrp`+`add` que
    apunta a la mitad de otra función. El descubrimiento termina en 2 rondas (antes 17 en el `sdk` y 7 en
    `main`). Hay 40461 funciones en el `sdk` (antes 46563) y 122961 en `main` (antes 131322).
  - Las estadísticas de `gen.py` y `sw_probe.py` cuentan ahora los `br` de las funciones finales. Antes
    sumaban los de cada ronda. Sitios `br`, antes → ahora:

    | módulo | jump tables resueltas | `br_all_labels` | `br_dispatch` |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | `sdk` | 0 → 555 | 611 → 56 | 9695 → 9695 |
    | `main` | 266 → 1288 | 1063 → 42 | 6343 → 6342 |
    | `subsdk0` | 0 → 333 | 333 → 1 | 4022 → 4021 |

  - `br_dispatch` es un salto por un puntero cargado (vtables, stubs), no una tabla. El que cambia en `main`
    es una tabla `ldrsw` que el corte dejaba en un pedazo sin su `add`.
  - Los 56 + 42 que siguen sin resolver tienen la guarda en un bloque anterior, el índice recargado de otra
    ranura de la pila, o el índice acotado con `and`/`ubfx` sin `cmp`. Usan el respaldo de siempre: cada
    instrucción de la función es una etiqueta y el `br` salta por un `switch`. Como la función ya no está
    partida, igual llegan.
  - Ese respaldo depende de `computed_target`: busca hacia atrás desde el `br` la instrucción que escribe su
    registro y lo da por tabla si es un `add`/`sub` o un `adr`. Comparaba solo los 5 bits bajos de cada
    instrucción, que también son el registro que guarda un store y los destinos de FP/SIMD: en `main`, un
    `stp s9, s8, [sp, #0x80]` entre `add x9, x9, x10, lsl #2` y `br x9` lo cortaba (1.8.2 0x700109c950, 1.9.0
    0x70011b06e0, una tabla `ldrb` con base `adr` y sin guarda). El `br` quedaba como despacho simple y el
    juego moría al llamar al caballo ("no function at 700109c954", issue #22). Ahora `writes_gpr` mira con
    capstone qué registros escribe la instrucción. En la 1.9.0 cambian 2 `br` de `main`, ninguno del `sdk` ni de
    `subsdk0`, y ninguno deja de reconocerse; el otro (0x70003d7a84) ya se resolvía como tabla, así que el C
    solo cambia en esa función. `tools/test_layout.py` tiene su forma (la función K: falla con el `gen.py`
    anterior). En una prueba oculta (1.9.0) no se pudo llegar a esa función: hace falta un caballo que acuda al
    silbido, y ninguno de los saves de prueba tiene uno.
  - Costo: el C con todas las etiquetas crece en `main` de 312k a 485k instrucciones y en el `sdk` de 37k a
    171k. La función más grande sigue siendo la misma (11883 instrucciones, en `main`).
  - `tools/test_layout.py` agrega un módulo sintético con la forma de `printf_core`, y una función partida
    por una llamada a su mitad.

Pendiente:

1. Restos de LA conocidos, sin efecto en la compilación:
   - `ui/launcher.mm` no comprueba la versión: falta el build id del `main` 1.8.2 (`tools/sw_probe.py`).
   - `hle/movie.c` solo deja saltar `movie/opening.webm` (nombre de LA).
   - `hle/framepace.c` y `hle/heaps.c` explican sus valores con casos de LA (siguen siendo genéricos).
   - `CONTRIBUTING.md` es de LASRecomp. (El README y el ícono ya son propios: `docs/icon/icon.svg`, una montaña
     helada con una espada clavada en la cima, dibujo original; `icon_1024.png`, `icon.ico` e `icon.icns` salen de
     él con `rsvg-convert`.)
   - `tools/explore_far.sh`, `explore_input.sh`, `house_input.txt`, `dbgfs.sh`, `fresh_save.sh`: entradas
     de prueba pensadas para la pantalla de título de LA.
   - Pantalla ancha (aspecto desbloqueado) e iconos de botones por control: se fueron con
     `widescreen.c` y `texpatch.c`; para BOTW harían falta ganchos propios.
   - `runtime/nvn/metal.m` y `renderer.m` (solo macOS) se editaron sin compilarlos.
2. Arranque de 1.8.2: con el `sdk` generado entero, x2 corre los constructores del `sdk`.
   - Pasa por `printf_core`. Arreglado en `gen.py`: ver "Jump tables" arriba. Medido: entra 4 veces (dos
     `vfprintf` con `"%s"` y `"%02d - %s"`), y su tabla `ldrb` salta a 0x700292070c y a 0x700292063c.
   - Resuelto (2026-10-14), en orden de aparición:
     - TIPC: el `sdk` de 1.8.2 le habla a `sm:` por TIPC (tipo de mensaje 16 + comando; 15 cierra la sesión).
       `runtime/ipc.c` lo atiende con el mismo `sm_handler`: los argumentos son las palabras crudas, sin
       `SFCI`, y la respuesta lleva el resultado como primera palabra, sin `SFCO` ni alineación.
     - `romfs.bin`: el runtime lee la RomFS desde esa imagen, que arma la pantalla de setup. Para
       desarrollo sin launcher: `build/savagewind.exe extracted --build-romfs` (4,5 min, 15,1 GB).
       Desde #99 ya no hay imagen en disco: `runtime/romfs_image.c` la sirve desde `extracted/romfs/` (cabecera
       y tablas en memoria, los datos de cada fichero leídos del suyo) y la pantalla de inicio borra el
       `romfs.bin` de versiones anteriores. `--dump-romfs <fichero>` escribe la imagen para compararla.
     - `IApplicationFunctions` 210 (`GetHealthWarningDisappearedSystemEvent`): el juego espera ese evento
       antes del primer frame; el stub no devolvía handle y el juego sondeaba el handle 0 para siempre.
       Ahora devuelve un evento ya señalado.
     - Versión de NVN: `main` 0x7100d802e0 solo crea su sistema gráfico si el dispositivo informa API 55 con
       minor ≥ 15; con el 53.207 de LA seguía sin él y después leía un objeto nulo. Además pide las
       propiedades 82, 85 y 92 (tamaños por defecto de memoria de comandos, compute y control de la cola).
     - `NVNsamplerBuilder` mide 64 bytes en NVN 55. El HLE guardaba 80 (device + `NvnSamplerDesc`) y pisaba
       el frame pointer guardado del llamador (`main` 0x71000156f0 lo arma en la pila). El estado del
       builder ahora está empaquetado en 48 bytes.
   - Resuelto (2026-10-15 y 16), en orden de aparición:
     - Lista rota del heap de efectos (`main` 0x7100d8df90 giraba para siempre): la escribía
       `hle_nvnTextureViewSetDefaults`. `NVNtextureView` mide 16 bytes en NVN 55 y el HLE guardaba 0x28; el
       juego pone las vistas al final de bloques de un `sead::ExpHeap` y pisaba la cabecera del bloque
       siguiente. `NvnTextureView` ahora está empaquetado en 16 bytes. Lo encontró la trampa de escrituras
       por página (`SAVAGEWIND_WATCH*`, abajo).
     - Tamaños reales de NVN 55, leídos de los `SetDefaults`/`Initialize` del driver del `sdk` (sus funciones
       se ubican con `SAVAGEWIND_NVN_REAL=1`): `TextureView` 16, `SamplerBuilder` ≥ 48, `QueueBuilder` 60,
       `WindowBuilder` 48, `BufferBuilder` 40, `DeviceBuilder` 24, `EventBuilder` 16, `MemoryPoolBuilder` 64,
       `TextureBuilder` ≥ 104; objetos: `Sampler` ≥ 64, pools 32, `Event` 40, `Buffer` 48,
       `CommandBuffer` 160, `MemoryPool` 256, `Program` 128, `Sync` ≥ 56.
     - `nvnDeviceGetInteger`: la tabla de LA se reemplazó por la del driver 55.15 (`sdk` 0x71004c2c00 →
       0x71004c6310 → tabla 0x71004b6070); los valores que dependen del dispositivo son los de un Tegra X1.
     - Audio: con revisión ≥ 9 el SDK lee la versión 2 del estado de efectos (0x90 bytes cada uno) y la
       sección de rendimiento de 0x10; con otro tamaño abortaba la actualización (0x5299).
     - `nfp:user` (amiibo): `IUserManager` → `IUser` sin lectores; antes el juego leía un objeto nulo.
     - `svcGetInfo` 18 (`ProgramId`) sale de `main.npdm` y 20 (`UserExceptionContextAddress`) devuelve una
       zona de TLS: `SetDyingMessageRegion` la necesita no nula. El id base de `aoc:u` sale del program id.
     - Memoria de comandos: el juego graba cada display list una vez para medirla ("calc resource") y pide
       exactamente esa memoria al heap del modelo, que la `ResourceSizeTable` dimensiona para NVN real. Con
       los records de Savage Wind (≥ 80 bytes por comando) los heaps se quedaban cortos, la asignación fallaba
       y la lista llegaba con pool nulo. Ahora el juego ve un costo estimado por comando (≤ lo que escribe NVN)
       y los records van a memoria del host, en "sombras" por rango de memoria guest (`runtime/nvn/cmdbuf.c`).
     - Hilos: BOTW llama a NVN desde varios hilos. El renderer (submit, flush, present, texturas finalizadas)
       queda detrás de un lock recursivo (`gpu_lock`).
     - Texturas: los comandos guardan el `NVNtexture` del guest y lo resuelven al ejecutarse; el juego
       finaliza y vuelve a inicializar render targets en el mismo objeto, copia objetos `NVNtexture` y
       finaliza una copia mientras usa otra. `nvnTextureFinalize` solo suelta la imagen Vulkan; el objeto del
       host vive hasta un reinicio.
     - Buffers de onda fuera de la memoria guest se saltean en vez de leerse; pools de descriptores: hasta 64
       por envío.
   - Resuelto (2026-10-16, segunda tanda):
     - Shaders: `TLD4`/`TLD4S` (gather), `TMML` (LOD), formas bindless con el handle cargado de `c[2]` justo
       antes, y `LDS`/`STS` (memoria compartida de compute, tamaño en la sección de control +0x754). Todos los
       shaders del arranque traducen.
     - `nvnMemoryPoolMapVirtual`: el juego mapea su pool virtual de texturas (0x7300000) entero sobre uno físico;
       el pool virtual toma esa memoria.
     - Render targets re-creados cada frame: BOTW finaliza e inicializa otra vez sus targets en la misma memoria
       y muestrea los objetos viejos (entradas del texture pool, copias de `NVNtexture`). La imagen de una textura
       finalizada se estaciona y la toma la próxima textura con la misma memoria y forma; un objeto finalizado se
       resuelve a la textura hecha después en su memoria. Era la imagen "en bloques".
     - Cuelgue intermitente (la mitad de las corridas, entre los frames 280 y 1500): `svcWaitProcessWideKeyAtomic`
       soltaba el mutex antes de marcar el condvar, y quien señalaba se salteaba `svcSignalProcessWideKey`.
     - Entrada: BOTW lee los controles con `nn::hid::GetNpadStates` (plural), que el HLE no atendía.
     - Imágenes de texturas finalizadas que se seguían muestreando no se liberaban (el menú agotaba la memoria de
       video en 2 minutos).
     - Escala de render targets (la "resolución interna" de LA): apagada salvo `SAVAGEWIND_SCALE_TARGETS=1`; con
       ella el pipeline diferido de BOTW mostraba solo lo emisivo. Activa desde el 2026-10-19 (ver "Resolución
       interna y escalador").
