   Probar oculto: título, Continuar, mundo abierto, las páginas de Opciones (con Salir) y la frecuencia de frames
   (`SAVAGEWIND_CLOCK_PROBE` a 30 / 60 / 120: el reloj del juego igual).
6. Marcarla soportada en las dos listas. `python tools/game_sites.py find` debe salir sin errores para cada
   versión, y `tools/test_game_sites.py` y `tools/test_layout.py` pasar.

Con 1.8.2 el C generado es el mismo que antes de los sitios salvo `layout.c` (gana la versión y la tabla de
sitios).

La 1.9.0 (2026-10-22, rama `game-1.9.0`; archivos del usuario en `extracted-1.9.0/`, verificados): `main` 18,8 MB
(1.8.2: 17,8), `sdk` del SDK 21.4.1, layout `main` 0x70_0000_0000-0x70_01e9_8000 (30,6 MiB), `subsdk0` y `sdk` detrás.
- `game_sites.py find` encontró 29 de los 36 sitios de entonces tal cual. Los otros 7 (la actualización de Opciones,
  abrir una pantalla, el estado de Opciones de la pausa, los textos y el B del diálogo, la actualización del menú
  del título y "Ver.%s") no: las pantallas de UI de la 1.9.0 tienen 0x18 bytes más desde antes de +0x290 (la base
  abre con `strb wzr, [x0, #0x2a8]` en vez de #0x290; Opciones: filas en +0x36b0 / +0x36b8 en vez de +0x3698 /
  +0x36a0; menú del título: +0x3654 en vez de +0x363c; diálogo: +0x33c8 en vez de +0x33b0), y esos offsets estaban
  en los patrones. Se ubicaron votando ventanas cortas de la función de 1.8.2 contra la 1.9.0 y comparando lado a
  lado, y ahora tienen patrones comunes (`game_sites.py common`). Los dos campos que lee el runtime pasaron a ser
  sitios `imm` (`opt_screen_rows`, `title_options_state`), y el parche del B del diálogo toma su offset de la
  instrucción misma.
- Los 38 encuentran un solo lugar en cada versión, y cada uno coincide con el lugar que da un voto independiente
  (ventanas de la función de 1.8.2 buscadas en la 1.9.0) o con una comprobación a mano (`opt_create_rows` lee la
  tabla de opciones +0x10; la GOT que lee la pausa apunta a `screen_mgr`; "Ver.%s" está en 0x70_015c_d092).
- Iguales en la 1.9.0, mirados uno por uno en el código: `ksys::VFR` (+0x28 .. +0x150), el bucle de frames
  (+0x228 FC, +0x234 = FC +0xc, +0x250), ScreenMgr +0x28 / +0x30, la fila de Opciones (+0x50 .. +0x68) y su
  entrada de 0x30 bytes, 14 opciones del juego, la entrada de la pantalla (+0x38, bit 1 de +0x38), pantallas 0x34
  y 0x39, botones 0x6a y 0x6c, la vtable del diálogo (+0x4e0), el evento activo (+0x1d2b8), la respuesta del
  diálogo (0xd), PlayerInfo +0x88. El único símbolo HLE (`longjmp`) sigue en el `sdk` 21.4.1.
- La RomFS 1.9.0 tiene 6 ficheros más, el tailandés: `Pack/Bootup_THth.pack`, `Font/Font_TH.sbfarc` y cuatro
  fuentes `.sbfotf`. Savage Wind todavía no ofrece el tailandés como idioma del texto.
- Pruebas (ocultas; datos en `build/run190/extracted` con `exefs` y `romfs` enlazados a `extracted-1.9.0` y su
  `romfs.bin` hecho con `--build-romfs`; copia de `save/` del usuario): biblioteca generada sin que falle ningún
  parche (125144 funciones en `main`), título con "Savage Wind 0.2", Opciones desde el título (Vídeo, Fotogramas
  por segundo), Continuar al mundo abierto (la misma posición de Link que con 1.8.2), menú de pausa > Sistema >
  Opciones > Audio con la misma repetición (0,266 s y luego 0,200 s), Salir y B (las mismas pantallas que 1.8.2), y
  a 60 FPS 30,02 frames de consola y 1,00 minuto de juego por segundo, caminar 5,5 m/s, esprintar 8,1 m/s, estamina
  ~300 por segundo (como 1.8.2: 30,02 / 1,00 / 5,7 / 8,2 / 305). Las mismas llamadas sin implementar que con 1.8.2.
  La preparación acepta la carpeta 1.9.0 (versión "1.9.0", 39008+ ficheros) y rechaza `exefs` 1.9.0 con `romfs`
  1.8.2 y al revés.

## NVIDIA DLSS (Video > Upscaler)

Video > Upscaler: DLSS (`upscaler = dlss`; greyed where it can't run) renders the 3D scene smaller by the mode's factor
and NVIDIA's DLSS Super Resolution builds the full-resolution image from it, with the world camera's depth, motion
vectors, jitter and texture LOD bias (`runtime/nvn/vulkan/exec.c` `dlss_scene`). Windows, NVIDIA RTX graphics cards.
Elsewhere, or when NGX can't make the feature, a settings file asking for it gets FSR 1.

**No SDK.** Nothing of NVIDIA's SDK is compiled in, linked or shipped. `runtime/nvn/vulkan/dlss.c` finds the NVIDIA
driver's NGX core (`_nvngx.dll`, through `HKLM\SOFTWARE\NVIDIA Corporation\Global\NGXCore`), takes its Vulkan entry
points with `GetProcAddress`, and declares the few NGX types, values and parameter names it uses from the SDK's
documented interface. NGX's parameter object is a C++ class reached through its vtable (MSVC's layout: each group of
overloads in reverse order); a set-then-get round trip checks the layout first, and DLSS stays off if it fails. NGX is
loaded only when NVIDIA's `nvngx_dlss.dll` is next to `savagewind.exe`. The setup page's Download NVIDIA DLSS (on PCs
with an NVIDIA driver; `dlss_download = 1`, the default) and the game files page download it, with NVIDIA's
`LICENSE.txt` as `NVIDIA-DLSS-LICENSE.txt`, from NVIDIA/DLSS on GitHub at release `v310.9.16` (`runtime/dlss_fetch.c`:
WinHTTP; size and SHA-256 checked, written as `.part` and renamed only when both match). While it is missing on a PC
with an NVIDIA driver, the menus' greyed DLSS points at Savage Wind Configuration.

## FSR 3 upscaling: held back for now

AMD FSR 3.1 upscaling (PRs #194 and #195: per-object motion vectors, the five quality modes plus Ultra Performance) is
built in, but Video > Upscaler doesn't offer it yet (`fsr3_upscaler_enabled` in `runtime/nvn/output_scale.c`). On an
RTX 3060 the thread that records each frame for Vulkan limits 1080p and 1440p, and the motion vectors and FSR 3 add
about 1.1 ms there, so every FSR 3 mode ran slower than native at those sizes; only at 4K did Balanced and up gain.
It comes back with the redesign of the motion vectors planned for Alpha 6: recording them on the render thread costs
1.2 ms a frame for 2969 draws, spread out (constant buffers 0.35, matching 0.24, frame start 0.16, program 0.15, per-draw
setup 0.13, push 0.10), with no single defect. FSR itself costs next to nothing there (2026-11-09, 1440p Quality: 130 fps
native, 104 with FSR 3, 130 with FSR 3 and `SAVAGEWIND_MVEC=0`). That work has to leave the render thread.
Offered again since 2026-11-13: the vectors are worked out on a thread of their own (`runtime/nvn/vulkan/mvec.c`) and
the shadow cascades follow the upscaler's factor (same PC, Savage preset, 1440p, FSR 3 Quality over native: Great
Plateau 106 / 102, Kakariko 106 / 88, Korok Forest 67 / 40). `SAVAGEWIND_FSR3=0` hides FSR 3 and FSR 4 again; a
settings file with `upscaler = fsr3` then loads as AMD FSR 1 with the same quality mode.

## Frame generation (AMD FSR 3)

Video > Frame generation (AMD FSR 3) (Off by default; `frame_generation = 0|1`; `SAVAGEWIND_FG=0|1` overrides it in
tests) makes a frame between each two the game draws, with the frame interpolation and optical flow of AMD's
FidelityFX SDK 1.1.4 (MIT, `third_party/FidelityFX`, see its README). Windows and Linux (Vulkan); no row on macOS.

**Driving the SDK.** The SDK's own path is its frame interpolation swapchain: it replaces `vkCreateSwapchainKHR`,
`vkAcquireNextImageKHR` and `vkQueuePresentKHR`, wants a present queue and an acquire queue the game never touches,
paces the frames itself, and is Windows-only (`Windows.h`, Win32 threads and events). Savage Wind uses neither it nor
the ffx-api DLL layer: `runtime/nvn/vulkan/framegen.cpp` does in C++ what the ffx-api provider
(`ffx_provider_framegeneration.cpp`) does: a shared backend context for the resources the effects exchange (optical
flow vectors and scene change detection, two sets of dilated depth, dilated motion vectors and the previous frame's
reconstructed depth, which alternate), the optical flow context and the frame interpolation context. Per frame:
frame interpolation's prepare (dilates the depth and motion vectors), the optical flow over the HUD-less image, the
interpolation. All of it is recorded into the frame's own command buffer, on the game's queue, and the runtime keeps
its own present thread, its HDR10 pass, the VSync modes and the window's crop. The SDK's shaders are built by
`tools/ffx_shaders.py` (glslangValidator and a small SPIR-V reader for the bindings, in place of the SDK's
Windows-only FidelityFX_SC.exe), only the permutations used: wave32, 32-bit floats, render-size motion vectors without
jitter, both depth directions. `framegen.cpp` is the SDK's blob lookup (`ffxGetPermutationBlobByIndex`). The backend
asks for a few extension functions it then calls unchecked (debug labels, `vkGetBufferMemoryRequirements2KHR`):
`framegen.cpp` hands it no-ops or the core ones. Two changes to `ffx_vk.cpp`, for clang: the arrays in its scratch
memory are 64-byte aligned (they were 4: clang's aligned SSE stores faulted).

**Inputs** (`runtime/nvn/vulkan/exec.c`, "frame generation"):

- The camera. The world's draws into the 3D scene's depth read a context constant buffer (`c3` of the vertex stage)
  that holds, as floats, the view (0-11, a 3x4 matrix by rows), the view-projection (12-27), the projection (28-43,
  OpenGL style, z -1..1), the camera's own matrix (44-55: right, up, back and position in its columns) and near / far
  (56, 57). It was found by looking for the world camera's projection, known from `rt_persp`, in the bound constant
  buffers. The world camera's buffer is the one with a perspective projection (row 3 = 0 0 -1 0) and a far plane over
  10000 (25000; the HUD's layers and the menus' 3D models have 10000), on the depth target the most such draws use;
  the 58 floats are copied at its first draw of the frame.
- The depth: that target, at the 3D scene's size (`RS_SCENE`, the internal resolution), D32. OpenGL-style depth
  (0 near, 1 far: not inverted, not infinite).
- The motion vectors: BOTW has none. `fg_mv.frag` (`shaders.c`) takes each pixel's depth back to NDC, through the
  previous frame's view-projection times this frame's inverse to where that point was, and writes the difference in
  uv units (R16G16F, render size). Camera motion only: what moves on its own (Link, enemies, animals, grass and trees
  in the wind, water, particles) gets the vector of a still object at its place, and the interpolation's optical flow
  has to find the rest. Link gets his own: the camera orbits him, so on screen he stays where he is while the camera's
  vectors took him along with the world behind him, and players saw a smear around him whenever the camera turned
  sideways onto him (not from behind). His position (uking::act::PlayerInfo +0x88, read with the camera's buffer)
  gives a box around him, his feet + 0.1 to 1.9 m and 0.7 m to each side, projected to the screen and to a depth
  range; the pixels inside both (him, and a strip of ground at his feet) take the motion of his centre on screen
  between the two frames. His limbs and what he holds are still the optical flow's. `SAVAGEWIND_FG_MV_DEBUG=1` paints
  the box (red) and the pixels taken as him (yellow) into the motion vectors (dump them with
  `SAVAGEWIND_FG_INPUTS_AT=<n>`); `SAVAGEWIND_FG_NO_LINK=1` leaves him out. That is the default again.
  `SAVAGEWIND_FG_OBJECT_VECTORS=1` makes the per-object motion vectors too (`mvec.c`, from PR #194: every scene draw
  matched with the previous frame's and run again on its inputs, jitter taken out), and frame generation takes them
  when they are this frame's and at the depth's size (their .xy are clip-space NDC differences: FSR's motion vector
  scale (-w / 2, h / 2), as for the FSR 3 upscaler). Link running, enemies and animals then interpolate without the
  double image, but on grass and trees some draws match the wrong draw of the previous frame and get motion they
  don't have (2026-10-28: the dumped vectors showed motion on standing trees and a grass blade with the camera still),
  and the generated frames broke the grass around Link up while the camera turned: the flicker players saw. They also
  cost ~0.6 ms of GPU and ~1.5-2 ms of CPU a frame (2560x1440, RTX 3060, no limit: 52-57 drawn fps against 54-59
  with the camera's vectors). So they stay off for frame generation until the matching is right for foliage.
- The HUD-less image: BOTW composites the scene into a linear 10-bit image of the final size (A2B10G10R10), draws the
  HUD into that, then copies it sRGB-encoded into the 8-bit image it presents. The composite's target is copied right
  after the composite (`scene_composite`, the draw `scene_post` also uses), before the next draw, the HUD's first,
  with a blit into an sRGB image: that encodes as the game's copy does, and read through a UNORM view it matches the
  presented image bit for bit where there is no HUD. The SDK tells the HUD apart by comparing the two, so the HUD, the
  minimap and Savage Wind's overlay stay sharp in the generated frames (a raw copy of the 10-bit bits made everything
  look like HUD, and the "generated" frames were the game's next ones).
- A cut (a jump of over 10 m, or the view turned over ~35 degrees in a frame), a frame without all of the above, or
  the first frame after the menus: no history (the SDK's reset). Its own scene change detection catches the rest.

**Presenting** (`device.c` `present_locked`, `present_wait_turn`). The interpolated image is the game's final image
(`RS_OUT`), so it goes through the same path as the game's frames: the crop and placement in the window (Fill wide
screens, bars), SMAA or FSR 1 to the window's size, the F1 menu and performance overlay, the HDR10 pass. The display
shows a frame when the GPU has drawn it, not when the CPU hands it over: the GPU runs a frame or two behind (present to
shown ~33 ms at 50 drawn fps), and both frames of a pair are drawn within a millisecond of each other. So the present
thread waits for each frame of a pair to be drawn (the submission's timeline value), presents the generated one at
once and the game's half the time between generated frames later, as AMD's frame interpolation swapchain does. The
presents queue up for it (the game's frame waits there while the next frame is drawn; plain presents stay one at a
time, as before), and `vkAcquireNextImageKHR` / `vkQueuePresentKHR` share a lock (the swapchain is externally
synchronized); the swapchain has one image more for the queued pair. Same scene as below, hidden window at 120 Hz,
VSync On: presented every 8.6-9.6 ms with a standard deviation of 0.4-1.2 ms, present to shown 4-7 ms (17-20 ms
without frame generation, where the CPU runs ahead).

The first two versions spaced the presents by the CPU's clock (half the measured frame time, then whole refreshes):
on the user's G-SYNC display both frames of a pair showed together, then a long gap, and the picture ghosted while the
camera moved with VSync On, Fast or Adaptive (with Off, tearing hid it). The display's own times
(`SAVAGEWIND_PRESENT_CSV`, VK_KHR_present_wait) showed it: intervals of 7-15 ms, not whole refreshes (G-SYNC on).

**Frame rate.** Video > Frame rate counts the presented frames: with frame generation the game is paced at half of it
(`framepace_period_ns`, `g_fg_active`): 120 shows 60 drawn + 60 generated, 60 shows 30 + 30, no limit draws as fast
as it can (300 at most) and doubles that. The game's clock follows the frames it draws, as always. With VSync On or
Adaptive the presented rate stays under the display's refresh rate as without frame generation (116 at 120 Hz).

**When.** In play only: not on the start screen, in the pause menu or the map, or with the F1 menu open
(`fg_wanted`): there the picture mostly stands still, and the game's own frames keep its cursor crisp. Cutscenes and
talks are generated too. When it stops, the next frame starts without history.

Tests: `SAVAGEWIND_FG_SHOT_AT=<frame>,...` saves two presents in a row from there, each generated frame and the
game's frame after it (`build/frames/window_N_<0|1>_<gen|real>.png`); `SAVAGEWIND_FG_DEBUG_VIEW=1` shows the SDK's
debug view (motion vector fields, optical flow, disocclusion) instead of the generated frames; `SAVAGEWIND_FG_LOG=1`
why frames aren't generated; the `[fg]` lines count generated and presented frames every 2 s. `SAVAGEWIND_EXIT_AT=<frame>`
ends a scripted run.

**Measured** (2026-10-25, RTX 3060, Ryzen 5 5600X, hidden 2560x1440 window, HDR10 on, SMAA, no upscaler, VSync
Off; the Great Plateau by the Temple of Time's walls, standing, then turning the camera; each line the mean over 2 s,
from the runtime's `[vk]` and `[fg]` lines):

| Frame rate | Frame generation | Drawn by the game | Presented |
|---|---|---|---|
| 60 | Off | 60 | 60 |
| 60 | On | 30 | 60 (30 generated) |
| 120 | Off | 106-118 standing, 81-89 turning | the same |
| 120 | On | 60 standing, 59 turning | 120 standing, 117 turning |
| No limit | Off | 108-118 standing, 82-90 turning | the same |
| No limit | On | 71-78 standing, 56-59 turning | 142-155 standing, 112-118 turning |

So with frame generation the game draws about 4 ms longer per frame here. GPU time per frame
(`SAVAGEWIND_GPUPROF_AT`, which marks the frame generation steps): motion vectors 0.06 ms, the SDK's optical flow and
interpolation 3.4 ms, the generated frame's own present (SMAA, the HDR10 pass) about 0.4 ms. `SAVAGEWIND_FG_TEST=1`
makes the frame without presenting it, `=2` presents the HUD-less copy instead of interpolating (to tell the parts'
costs apart: no limit, 113 drawn fps off, 72 with the interpolation alone, 98 with the second present alone). The
SDK's 16-bit shaders (`FFX_HALF`, with shaderFloat16 on) were tried: no faster on the RTX 3060, so not kept.
The performance overlay counts the presented frames with frame generation on (generated ones included); its frame
time and graph are the game's frames. At 120 it
holds 120 presented where the game alone doesn't, at the cost of drawing 60 (and the controls answering as at 60,
half a frame later). Also tried: a 3440x1440 window with Fill wide screens and FSR 1 Quality (render 2293x960 -> 3440x1440,
112-116 presented at 120), HUD 16:9 in the middle, the generated frames right.

**What it looks like** (shots: `SAVAGEWIND_FG_SHOT_AT`, compared to the game's frames before and after; the generated
frame's PSNR against each is 1.5-2.5 dB over theirs against each other, so it lies between them):

- The camera turning, standing: clean. The world, Link standing, the HUD and the minimap as in the game's frames.
- Running: Link himself ghosts. His motion isn't in the vectors (camera only), the optical flow finds part of it, and
  what it misses is blended: at 30 drawn fps (60 presented) a clear double image of his legs, sword and bow in the
  generated frames; at 60 drawn (120 presented) the same, smaller (a soft second outline of the legs and the sword).
  On screen that shows as a faint shimmer around him while he runs. The grass in the wind moves too little to show.
- The HUD is the game's newer frame's in both, so its animations (the minimap turning) step at the drawn rate.
- Not looked at yet: enemies, horses, water, particles, fast cuts in cutscenes, and the image on a real display
  (VSync On / FIFO, VRR, HDR10 brightness): the shots are taken from the window image before the present. Not
  measured: the added latency. The Linux build of the SDK's sources (`ffx_compat.h` has what glibc lacks) isn't
  tried yet.

## Colour grading (Options > Colour)

Options > Colour (the game's own Options screen; also the F1 menu's Video tab, section Colour) grades the 3D image:
a preset, exposure (-2..+2 EV), contrast (-50..+50), saturation (-100..+100), temperature and tint (-100..+100), a LUT
and its intensity (0-100%). ini: `colour_exposure` (EV), `colour_contrast`, `colour_saturation`,
`colour_temperature`, `colour_tint`, `colour_lut` (`none`, `sw:<file>` shipped, `<file>` the player's),
`colour_lut_strength` (percent). Windows and Linux (Vulkan); no page on macOS. Code: `runtime/color_grade.c` (presets,
LUT folders and files), `exec.c` `scene_post` / `grade_lut` / `grade_wanted`, `shaders.c` `grade.frag`.

**Where.** One fullscreen pass on the 3D scene at the scene -> final image composite (`scene_composite`), at the
scene's own size and in its format (A2B10G10R10, or RGBA16F with HDR, linear light), before FSR 1's EASU / RCAS and
CAS; the composite then samples the result (`scene_up`). The game draws its HUD after the composite, so the HUD keeps
its colours (checked: the hearts' pixels are identical with every preset and LUT). Frame generation's HUD-less copy
and its final image come after it, so real and generated frames are graded alike. With HDR, the 3D scene's tonemap is
the extended curve and the present reads the float picture instead of the clipped 8-bit copy (`docs/hdr.md`); the
grade shader preserves values above 1.0, so the extended highlights survive it. With every setting neutral (or
`SAVAGEWIND_SCENE_GRADE=0`) the pass doesn't run.

**The pass.** In linear light: exposure x white balance as RGB gains (temperature moves red against blue by 0.3 x t,
tint green by 0.2 x t, then normalised to the same Rec. 709 luma), saturation around luma. Then sRGB-encoded, as the
picture is seen: contrast as an S curve through 0, 0.5 and 1 (slope 1 + contrast in the middle, so nothing clips),
and the LUT (RGBA16F 3D texture, trilinear, sampled at texel centres: `u * (n - 1) / n + 0.5 / n`, after DOMAIN_MIN /
MAX), mixed in by its intensity. Back to linear for the composite.

**Presets.** Natural (neutral), Warm, Cool, Vivid, Cinematic, Muted: slider values only (`g_color_presets`), set by
eye on the Great Plateau by day and in the evening. The preset row shows Custom when the sliders match none.

**LUTs.** `.cube` (LUT_3D_SIZE 2..64, DOMAIN_MIN / MAX, TITLE and comments; 1D LUTs refused) and ReShade-style PNG
strips (N*N x N: 1024 x 32, 4096 x 64; slice = blue, x = red, y = green). Listed: the shipped ones (`colour-luts/`
next to the executable; `third_party/luts` in a source build: three CC0 LUTs from FreshLUTs, see its README) then the
player's (`<data root>/luts/`, made at the first listing; rescanned each time the page opens). The first setup offers
Savage Wind's own look (`COLOR_LUT_RECOMMENDED`, the shipped `Savage_Wind.cube` at 50% intensity,
`COLOR_LUT_RECOMMENDED_STRENGTH`): the start screen's "Savage Wind colour look" toggle, on unless the ini already
names a LUT (`colour_lut`, `none` included). Players' third-party packs (e.g. Nexus ones whose licence forbids
redistribution) are never shipped: they load them themselves.

**Cost** (RTX 3060, Great Plateau, `SAVAGEWIND_GPUPROF_AT`, three frames each): 0.10 ms at 1920 x 1080, 0.13 ms at
2560 x 1440; the LUT adds 0.005-0.008 ms. Neutral: 0 (no pass).

**Tests.** `SAVAGEWIND_COLOUR_AT=<frame>:<exposure>/<contrast>/<saturation>/<temperature>/<tint>/<LUT %>/<LUT>,...`
(ascending; exposure in tenths of an EV; the LUT as the ini names it) changes the look during a run, for A/B shots of
one view with `SAVAGEWIND_WINDOW_SHOT_AT`. Checked hidden: neutral, each preset, five LUTs; with AMD FSR 1 (Quality,
1707 x 960 -> 2560 x 1440), with FSR 3 frame generation (generated and real frames graded alike) and with HDR10 on
(hidden runs on the test PC are HDR10; the shots are the SDR image before the HDR pass, so the PQ output itself was
not looked at on a display).

## Audio

El `sdk` de BOTW trae el AudioRenderer entero: el servidor (`nn::audio::server`: voces, mezclas, efectos,
generación de comandos) y el procesador de comandos del DSP (`nn::audio::dsp::CommandListProcessor`), código de
CPU que se recompila con el resto. Savage Wind lo usa en vez de reimplementarlo (`runtime/services/audio.c`):

- El cliente llega al servidor dentro del proceso (`CreateAudioRendererManagerByDfc`, `sdk` 0x7100224d00) cuando
  los parámetros piden el dispositivo de render CPU: `nn::audio::OpenAudioRenderer` (`sdk` 0x7100220a70) toma ese
  camino si `AudioRendererParameter` +0x2c es 1, y con +0x30 (modo de ejecución) en 1 lo abre en ejecución manual,
  sobre el work buffer del juego, sin transfer memory. Si no, abre `audren:u`.
- El HLE de `InitializeAudioRendererParameter` pide CPU + manual, así que el juego calcula su work buffer y abre el
  renderer con esos valores. El de `OpenAudioRenderer` guarda el handle y arranca dos hilos `nn::os` (el código
  del `sdk` busca su `ThreadType` en TLS +0x1f8): uno renderiza un frame de 5 ms
  (`AudioRenderSystem::ExecuteAudioRendererRendering`, en el objeto del renderer +0x70) cada vez que el stream de
  SDL baja de su objetivo, con el mutex del renderer (+0x2d0, el que toma `Update`) tomado; el otro señala el
  evento del juego, para que el render no espere el mutex del evento.
- Esos dos hilos hacen el trabajo del ADSP y corren fuera de los tokens de núcleo (`kernel_thread_off_cores`):
  el juego también usa el núcleo 3, porque el kernel informa la máscara 0xF.
- La mezcla final es un comando DeviceSink (id 0x14), que el procesador del `sdk` salta (en la consola lo toca el
  ADSP): un hook después de `CommandListProcessor::Process` lee sus buffers (int32 en la escala de int16, 6
  canales FL FR FC LFE BL BR), los baja a estéreo y los manda al stream SDL.
- Medido en el Santuario (Ryzen 5 5600X): unos 190 µs por frame (máximo 0,7 ms), espera del mutex casi siempre
  por debajo de 2 ms, 4 cortes del dispositivo en 150 s con 25 ms en cola, todos mientras carga la escena (el
  `Update` del juego retuvo el mutex hasta 30 ms). Con los hilos dentro de los tokens de
  núcleo y el evento señalado desde el mismo hilo eran 1-2 ms por frame, picos de 50-170 ms y decenas de cortes
  por segundo.
- La idea viene de SuperMarioWonderRecomp (MIT, BelmanteGu), que corre así el renderer del SDK 16 de Wonder; se
  usó su PROGRESS.md como referencia, sin copiar código.
- `SAVAGEWIND_AUDIO_DFC=0` vuelve al mezclador HLE de `audren:u` (heredado de LASRecomp), que sigue en el archivo.
  Sin probar: el reinicio en el lugar (vuelta a la pantalla de inicio) con el renderer abierto, y
  `CloseAudioRenderer`, que el juego no llamó en las pruebas.

## Sondeo del exefs

```
tools/venv/Scripts/python tools/sw_probe.py extracted/exefs --json build/probe.json
```

(En Linux: `tools/venv/bin/python`.) Imprime las direcciones que `tools/layout.py` da a los módulos y
si el runtime puede cargarlos ahí. Para cada módulo imprime:

- tamaños de segmentos y build id,
- funciones encontradas y jump tables,
- instrucciones que el lifter no traduce todavía, agrupadas por mnemónico con un ejemplo,
- tamaño estimado del C que generaría `make gen`,
- las funciones NVN que el juego nombra contra las que implementa `runtime/nvn` (faltantes y stubs).

El entorno Python se crea con:

```
python -m venv tools/venv
tools/venv/Scripts/python -m pip install capstone==5.0.9 unicorn==2.1.4 lz4==4.4.5
```

## Toolchain

Para compilar el runtime en Windows hace falta MSYS2 UCRT64 (clang, make, SDL3, FFmpeg, Vulkan,
shaderc), como describe `docs/BUILD-windows.md`. En Linux, los paquetes de `docs/linux.md`.
Comprobación rápida desde una shell UCRT64: `make runtime-objs` (compila el runtime sin enlazar).

## Primera generación y compilación completa (1.8.2)

Medido el 2026-10-14 con el exefs 1.8.2 (`main` build `de0b6ac4efc1dda7`, `subsdk0` `3308c1d216f78839`,
`sdk` `5cf080e800530a7f`) en un Ryzen 5 5600X (6 núcleos, 12 hilos) con 32 GB de RAM, Windows 11,
MSYS2 UCRT64 clang 23.1.3 y Python 3.14 en `tools/venv`. Usa el generador con el layout de módulos,
`DT_GNU_HASH` y `DT_RELR`. La biblioteca del juego (`build/swgame.dll`) compila y enlaza sin errores ni
warnings: nada del generador ni del Makefile la bloqueó. El juego no se corrió con ella (el arranque está
en "Pendiente").

Generación (`make gen`, es decir `gen.py all`: un módulo detrás de otro; `--simd c`, el default en x86-64):

| | `main` | `subsdk0` | `sdk` | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| funciones | 131.322 | 17.790 | 46.563 | 195.675 |
| archivos `.c` (con la tabla) | 384 | 98 | 125 | 607 + `layout.c` |
| C generado | 375,7 MB | 60,2 MB | 115,9 MB | 551,8 MB |
| tiempo | 42 s | 6 s | 13 s | 62 s |

La memoria pico de Python es la de `main`: 1,9 GB. `sw_probe.py` había estimado 449 MB para `main` +
`sdk`; el real es 491,5 MB, un 9 % más. La función más grande ocupa 1,68 MB de C. 114 archivos de `main`,
38 de `subsdk0` y 31 de `sdk` tienen una sola función (`--big-fn`: desde 100 KB de C, cada función va en
su propio archivo).

`DT_RELR` trae 222.402 relocaciones relativas en `main` (198.097 apuntan a código), pero casi todas a
funciones que `gen.py` ya encontraba por `.eh_frame`, `bl` o `adrp` + `add`: suma 2 inicios de función
en `main`, 17 en `subsdk0` y 8 en `sdk`. `runtime/hle/hle_symbols.txt` solo lista `longjmp` (del `sdk`).

Compilación (`make -j12`, con `build/savagewind.exe` ya hecho, que tarda unos 10 s):

- 19 min 1 s (1141 s) para los 608 archivos más el enlace. El enlace (lld) tarda 0,5 s y usa ~0,3 GB.
- Memoria pico: 2,9 GB sumando los 12 clang que corren a la vez; el clang más grande llegó a 731 MB.
- Objetos: 250,6 MB (`main` 188,3 MB, `subsdk0` 20,0 MB, `sdk` 42,3 MB).
- `build/swgame.dll`: 198,8 MB (`.text` 179,2 MB, `.rdata` 10,8 MB, `.pdata` 2,3 MB). Exporta solo
  `swgame_tables` e importa de `savagewind.exe` y del CRT.
- Una primera pasada con las direcciones fijas de antes (`main` y `sdk`, sin `subsdk0`) tardó casi lo
  mismo: 1171 s para 509 archivos y una DLL de 182,3 MB.

El tiempo de compilación no depende del volumen de C sino de unas pocas funciones. Cuando una función
tiene un `br` por tabla (resuelta o no), `emit_function` le pone una etiqueta a cada instrucción y un
`switch` en `L_dispatch` con un `case` por instrucción, por si la tabla emulada no cubrió algún caso.
Con 8.000 a 12.000 casos, clang -O1 se vuelve muy lento:

- Compilando 6 a la vez, `main_104.c` (una función de 1,08 MB de C, 8.089 etiquetas) tarda 553 s (9 min).
  `main_248.c`, más grande (1,7 MB) pero con 2 etiquetas, tarda 31 s.
- De los 145 archivos de una sola función de `main` y `sdk` (4.099 s de CPU, 6 a la vez), los 66 que
  tienen ese `switch` suman 3.972 s (97 %), y los 20 más lentos, 3.238 s.
- Compilados solos: un archivo normal de 1,5 MB con 535 funciones tarda 4,9 s; la tabla de `main`
  (8 MB), 2,3 s.

Bajar ese `switch` (por ejemplo, a solo las instrucciones que pueden ser destino, o despachando por
`rt_dispatch`) es lo que más acortaría la compilación, pero cambia lo que hace el código generado cuando
una tabla no se resolvió bien. (Los tiempos varían mucho con la carga: `main_248.c` tarda 10,5 s sola y
31 s con otros 5 compilando.)

Después de integrar `module-layout`, `gamelib-build` y `jump-tables` en `main` (misma máquina,
2026-10-14): `make gen` tarda 50 s (`main` 122.961 funciones en 428 archivos, `subsdk0` 13.934 en 143,
`sdk` 40.461 en 205) y `make -j12` 969 s (16 min 9 s) sin errores, con un `build/swgame.dll` de
211,7 MB. Una corrida con `savagewind.exe extracted --play` reubica los tres módulos, corre los
constructores del `sdk` y se detiene donde dice "Pendiente" 2: mensajes TIPC 16 y 17 a `sm:` y
`svcBreak(0)` en 0x700251863c.

Arreglos en `tools/sw_probe.py` de esta misma tanda:

- Las importaciones se agrupan por namespace (`nn::os` 85, `nn::audio` 74, `nn::util` 34, ...). Antes,
  402 de las 465 de `main` caían en un grupo vacío porque no se saltaba el prefijo `_ZN`.
- Las funciones NVN que enlaza `runtime/hle` (`nvnBootstrapLoader`, `nvnDeviceGetProcAddress`) cuentan
  como implementadas. Con 1.8.2: el juego nombra 569, el runtime implementa 515 (86 vacías) y faltan 54.

```

`docs/SOFTWARE-KEYBOARD.md`:

```md
# Software keyboard output

The overlay edits UTF-8 text. The `nn::swkbd::ShowKeyboard` HLE returns it using the encoding selected by
`ShowKeyboardArg + 0x3bd` (`IsUseUtf8`): UTF-8 when nonzero, UTF-16LE when zero.
BotW 1.9.0's horse-naming caller leaves this flag zero and reads the result as 16-bit units.

The output `String` contains a pointer and a byte capacity, including space for the terminator. Conversion
keeps complete characters, reserves a one-byte or two-byte terminator, and never splits a UTF-8 sequence
or UTF-16 surrogate pair at the buffer limit. Invalid UTF-8 input bytes become U+FFFD.

Run the regression checks with:

```sh
make test-swkbd
```

The test calls the actual HLE with synthetic guest buffers and a replacement UI prompt. It needs no game
files, renderer or window. Cases include the reported `Talon`, odd/even and nine-letter ASCII names, both
output encodings, Unicode boundary values, surrogate pairs, malformed input, repeated prompts, terminators
and short/odd byte capacities with output guards.

For a live check, register a horse, confirm its full name in the dialogue and horse list, then save and reload.
Check both physical keyboard and controller entry. This exercises the game and UI beyond the synthetic prompt.

```

`docs/STATUS.md`:

```md
# Status

[Back to the README](../README.md)

Estimates of where each part stands, grouped by area. "Tested in game" is how much of the game has been played through on Savage Wind so far.

The overall bar in the README is a weighted average. Each area has its share of the whole (the percentage in its heading). Each part has a weight inside its area: x1 an extra, x2 important, x3 essential. An area's value is the weighted mean of its parts, and the overall value the weighted mean of the areas. After changing a table, run `python tools/status_bars.py` to redraw the bars.

Testing glitches such as windbombs, Bullet Time Bounce (BTB), or inventory tricks? Use the [glitch compatibility tracker](glitch-compatibility.md) to record results by build and frame rate.

✅ done · 🔧 in progress · 🗺️ roadmap

The Champions' Ballad has been played through. |

`docs/VIRTUAL_GYRO.md`:

```md
# The virtual gyro at a shrine apparatus

Some shrines are solved by tilting a platform with the controller's motion sensors (the game's DungeonRotateGyro
mechanisms). A controller with a gyroscope (DualSense, DualShock 4, Switch Pro, Joy-Con, the Steam Deck) works as on
the Switch. Without one, Savage Wind turns a virtual controller instead, while the player controls such a mechanism
(game version 1.9.0):

- **Keyboard**: the gyro keys turn it at 90 degrees per second while held, and it keeps its pose when they are let go.
- **Mouse**: hold the left button and drag, like rolling a ball under the hand; let go to keep the pose and take a new
  grip anywhere on the screen. The tilt key (T) and the mouse work too, as everywhere.
- **A controller without a gyroscope** (Xbox and most XInput pads): the right stick turns the platform (X) and tilts
  it front / back (Y), the left stick banks it (X) and tilts it front / back (Y). R3 or L3 levels it again. The sticks
  move neither Link nor the camera meanwhile. The motion sensitivity and inversion options apply.
- **A controller with a gyroscope**: the gyroscope tilts it as it is held (no sensitivity, inversion or lean). The
  sticks take over once pushed past half way (a gyroscope lying still, a handheld on its dock); R3 or L3 gives it back
  to the gyroscope.

Leaving the mechanism levels the virtual controller and drops any turn still to come.

## Options

Options > Controls:

- **Shrine keyboard gyro** (on): the gyro keys, only while controlling a mechanism. Anywhere else the keys they share
  (I / J / K / L turn the camera by default) work as they always do.
- **Shrine mouse drag** (on): the left-button drag. Off, the left button attacks as usual and the keys still work.

`SAVAGEWIND_PC_GYRO=0|1` and `SAVAGEWIND_GYRO_SCENE=0|1` set the two switches at start.

Options > Keyboard (sticks) binds the gyro keys (`savagewind.ini`: `bind_key_gyro_*`):

| Action | Default |
| --- | --- |
| Gyro tilt up / down | I / K |
| Gyro tilt left / right | J / L |
| Gyro turn left / right | U / O |
| Gyro recenter | P |

A gyro key rebound onto another gyro key's swaps with it; it never takes a camera or movement key's binding away,
since they are only the gyro's during the mechanism.

## The tilt key

T held, the mouse tilts the virtual controller and the wheel turns it (six degrees a step), without the old 50 degree
limit. At a mechanism letting go of T keeps the pose (a clutch: move the mouse back, hold T again, go on). Anywhere
else the tilt levels again within a fraction of a second once T is let go, so it never stays in front of a
controller's own gyroscope for motion aiming.

## How it works

- `tools/game_sites.py` `gyro_scene_actor` (optional; the game code is built with it): the call in which a mechanism
  fetches its input; `tools/patches.py` adds a heartbeat after it. `runtime/pc_gyro_scene.c` turns the heartbeat into
  "the player controls a mechanism" (held through a pause; reset on a reboot).
- `runtime/hle/motion.c`: the virtual controller is kept as continuous angles, so whole turns keep their winding, and
  delivered to the game at the Switch's 200 Hz at a bounded speed (`runtime/pc_gyro.h`). The drag and the sticks are
  rotations in the table's axes, composed as quaternions and then turned back into those angles (`virtual_turn`), so
  any axis works at any pose.
- `runtime/hle/input.c`: the gyro keys and the sticks; `runtime/ui/gyro_drag.h`: the drag (nothing is drawn).

`make test-gyro` runs the tests: the keys through the bindings, the two switches saved and loaded, turns at polling
rates from 30 to 1000 Hz, full and fast turns, the drag's and the sticks' composition, the mechanism's heartbeat,
pause and reboot, and the patch's instruction check. None needs the game files.

```

`docs/cheats-and-assists.md`:

```md
# Cheats, assists and amiibo

Savage Wind adds options that make the game easier, cheats that hand you items or change the world, a teleport, and
a virtual amiibo reader. None of them is on until you turn it on, and none of them changes your game files.

| What | Where | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| [Colour vision](#colour-vision) | The game's Options > Accessibility | Nothing |
| [Assists](#assists) | The game's Options > Accessibility | Nothing |
| [Cheats tab](#cheats-tab) | Savage Wind menu (F1) > Cheats | Being in game |
| [Teleport and console cheats](#teleport-and-console-cheats) | The console (` or F12) | The `DEV` launch option |
| [amiibo](#amiibo) | Savage Wind menu (F1) > amiibo | Your own figure dumps |
| [Save profiles](#keep-a-separate-save-for-cheats) | Savage Wind Configuration > Settings > Saves | The game closed |

## Colour vision

For colour-blind players. Open the game's own menu, then **Options > Accessibility**; Colour vision is at the top.
It shifts the colours of the whole picture, the game's HUD and menus included, so colours that look alike to you come
apart: a red Chuchu from a green one, the stamina wheel turning red when it runs out. The change shows at once, so you can try each type and strength while the menu is open.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| Colour vision | Off, or the kind of colour blindness you have: **Protanopia** (red looks dark and close to green), **Deuteranopia** (green and red look alike, the most common), **Tritanopia** (blue and green, and yellow and pink, look alike). |
| Correction strength | How strongly the colours are shifted: 10% to 100%. Milder colour blindness often needs less; lower it if the picture looks too changed. |

Notes:

- It works with HDR, the upscalers and frame generation, and adds no extra pass: the frame rate stays the same.
- The Savage Wind menu (F1) and the photos you take with the camera rune keep their real colours. Screenshots and
  recordings of the window (Steam, OBS) show the corrected picture.
- Savage Wind's colour look and the Video > Colour settings still apply; the correction comes after them.

## Assists

Open the game's own menu, then **Options > Accessibility**. Changes apply at once, while you play, and are saved with
your settings.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| God mode | Link takes no damage. |
| One-hit kill | Enemies go down in one hit. |
| Damage taken | How much damage Link takes: 25% to 400%. 100% is the game's own. |
| Damage dealt | How much damage enemies take: 25% to 400%. 100% is the game's own. |
| Weapon wear | How fast weapons, bows and shields wear out: Fairy (never), Peter Pan (0.5x), Hylian (1x, the game's own), Hero (1.5x), Master (2x), Legend (2.5x), Dude, are you ok? (3x). |
| Infinite arrows | Shooting a bow uses up no arrows. You still need one arrow to shoot. |
| Infinite stamina | The stamina wheel never runs out. |

## Cheats tab

Open the Savage Wind menu (**F1**, **Esc**, the controller's Home / Xbox / PlayStation button, or Back + Start) and
go to the **Cheats** tab. The tab only shows up while you are in game, not on the title screen.

### Items

1. Pick a **Category** (weapons, bows, shields, arrows, armour, materials, critters and fairies, or all), or type part
   of a name in **Search**. The list stays empty until you do one of the two.
2. Set the **Amount** (1 to 99). Stackable items such as arrows and materials take the whole amount at once.
3. Press **Add** next to the item. It goes into your pouch through the game's own item pickup.

If the pouch is full, you get as many as fit, and the tab says how many were added. If you are in a menu or a
cutscene, the request waits until you are back in play. The item list comes from your own game files; nothing of the
game is shipped with Savage Wind.

### Rupees and weather

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| Infinite rupees | Keeps your wallet at 9999 rupees, topped up every few seconds. |
| Set rupees | Sets your wallet to an exact number (0 to 999999). Turn off Infinite rupees first. |
| Weather | Holds the weather you pick (clear, cloudy, rain, heavy rain, snow, heavy snow, thunderstorm, thunder rain, rain in sunshine), or keeps out rain or thunderstorms. Automatic is the game's own. Cutscenes keep their weather. |

## Teleport and console cheats

The teleport and a few more cheats are console commands for developers. To use them:

1. Add the launch option `DEV` with the value `1` on the Savage Wind start screen. How to add one:
   [Launch options](launch-options.md).
2. Start the game and load your save.
3. Press **`** (the key under Esc) or **F12** to open the console. The game gets no input while it is open; press the
   same key to close it.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `tp shrine 5` | Teleport to a shrine, a tower, a stable, a village, a landmark or a Korok, by number or name: `tp tower 3`, `tp stable wetland`, `tp hateno`, `tp korok 10`, `tp nearest korok`. `goto` works the same. Every place with its number: [Teleport places](teleport-places.md). |
| `places` | Lists the kinds of places and how many there are. `places shrine` lists the shrines with their numbers and names, and more words narrow the list: `places shrine akkala`. |
| `tp <x> <y> <z>` | Teleport to coordinates. |
| `pos` | Shows where Link is and copies a line you can give to `tp` later to come back. |
| `give <name> [count]` | Puts an item in the pouch, the same as the Cheats tab: `give arrow 20`. With several matches it lists them. |
| `time <0-24>` | Sets the hour of the day. `time freeze` stops the clock and `time unfreeze` starts it again. |
| `help` | Lists every command. |

Known limits of the teleport:

- Some places, Koroks above all, can land a little low or off to one side.
- After a long jump the camera can look odd for 1 to 3 seconds while the area loads.
- Rarely, the game crashes after long jumps. Save before you teleport often; restarting the game fixes it.

Developer mode also turns on other developer tools. If you only want the items, rupees and weather, use the Cheats
tab, which needs no launch option.

## amiibo

Savage Wind has a virtual amiibo reader: the game's amiibo rune finds the figure you choose in the Savage Wind menu.
It reads dumps of your own amiibo figures. Savage Wind does not include any amiibo data and never will.

1. Turn on the amiibo rune in the game, as on the console.
2. Put your figure dumps (`.bin` files) in the `amiibo` folder of Savage Wind's data folder: next to
   `savagewind.exe` on Windows, and `~/.local/share/savagewind/amiibo/` on Linux and the Steam Deck. Folders inside it
   work too, for example one per series.
3. For the figures to give game data (their rewards, the nickname, Wolf Link's hearts), also put the amiibo keys file
   `key_retail.bin`, dumped from your own console, in the same folder. Without it the reader still finds the figure,
   but the game gets no data from it.
4. Open the Savage Wind menu (F1) and go to the **amiibo** tab. Pick a figure from the list; Search and the series
   filter help with a big collection. The figure you pick stays on the reader until you pick another one or **None**.
5. In the game, use the amiibo rune as usual. The game finds the figure on the reader.

The game's own limits apply: each figure gives its rewards once a day.

## Keep a separate save for cheats

Cheats change your save for good: items you add stay in the pouch, and a teleport can skip parts of the story. To
keep your own playthrough clean, use a second save profile for cheating. A save profile is a whole set of saves, with
its own slots, options, Hero's Path, album and compendium, and profiles never touch each other.

1. Close the game. Profiles are only on the start screen, because the game must not be running while saves change.
2. Open **Savage Wind Configuration** and go to **Settings > Saves**. The **Profiles** section is at the top. Your
   existing saves are the profile called **Default**; they are not moved or changed.
3. To cheat on a copy of your playthrough: select **Default**, type a name in **Name for a new profile** (for example
   `Cheats`) and choose **Copy this profile**. To start from scratch instead, type the name and choose **Create empty
   profile**.
4. Select the new profile and choose **Use this profile**, then press **Play**. The game now loads and saves only in
   that profile.
5. To go back to your own playthrough, close the game, select **Default** and choose **Use this profile**.

Switching only changes which profile the game uses: no save is copied, moved or deleted. Renaming, deleting, where the
files are and the naming rules are in [Save profiles](save-profiles.md).

```

# Controls

[Back to the README](../README.md)

Any controller SDL knows works, by button position; one with a gyroscope (DualSense, DualShock 4, Switch controllers,
Steam Deck) also aims and tilts by motion.

Controller buttons, sticks and motion only control the game while its window has focus. Switching away releases
held inputs; returning reads the controller's current state.

Keyboard and mouse defaults:

| Action | Key | Action | Key |
|---|---|---|---|
| Move | W A S D | Camera | Mouse (or I J K L) |
| Walk (hold) | C | Crouch | Left Ctrl |
| Jump (X) | Space | Sprint / back (B) | Left Shift |
| Interact / confirm (A) | E | Attack (Y) | Left click |
| Shield / lock on (ZL) | Right click | Bow (ZR) | F |
| Rune (L) | Q | Throw (R) | R |
| Look (right stick press) | Middle click | Weapons / shields / runes / whistle (d-pad) | 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 |
| Inventory (Plus) | Tab | Map (Minus) | M |
| Tilt the controller (hold, motion puzzles) | T + mouse | | |

Every game action has its own key and its own controller button, set on the Key bindings page of the game's Options
(a keyboard/mouse button and a controller button per row; see [ACTIONS.md](ACTIONS.md)). Mouse sensitivity
(horizontal and vertical), Y inversion and motion sensitivity and inversion are on the Controls page. The game's
button prompts show the keys you bound, or your controller's own buttons (Controls > Button icons: Automatic follows
the device you use). The mouse turns the camera directly, as in a PC game: 0.022° per count at 100% sensitivity (as
Quake and Source count it), on both axes (the vertical one scaled by Controls > Mouse vertical sensitivity), with no
acceleration or top speed, the same at any frame rate. The bow's and the scope's own slower speeds stay, and so do the
game's camera speed setting and its camera axis inversion options. Esc frees the cursor, a click in the window takes
it back. F10 cycles the performance overlay (off, FPS, full). Full also shows Link's XYZ coordinates from the game's
position copy, in game units, with one decimal place. The line is hidden on the title screen, while loading,
during movies and scripted events (cutscenes, talks, item pickups), or when the position is unavailable.

```

`docs/data-folder.md`:

```md
# Moving the data folder

Set `SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT` to choose where Savage Wind keeps its game files, saves, settings and caches. This
already works on Windows and Linux; it is an environment variable, not an option in the configuration screen.
Use an absolute path to a writable folder. The destination drive must be available whenever you start the app.

## Copy your existing data

1. Close the game and Savage Wind Configuration.
2. Find the current data folder. The startup log prints it as `[paths] data: ...`. By default it is the folder of
   `savagewind.exe` on Windows, or `~/.local/share/savagewind` on Linux (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/savagewind` if
   `XDG_DATA_HOME` is set to an absolute path). Source builds started in a folder containing `extracted/` use that
   starting folder instead. An existing `SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT` takes precedence over these defaults.
3. Copy your data into an empty destination folder, keeping the same structure: `extracted/`, `save/`, `save-profiles/`, `save_profile.txt`, `cache/`,
   `fonts/`, `savagewind.ini` and `launch-flags.txt` (the start screen's launch options), where present, along with any custom files such as `splash.png`.
   The destination should contain `extracted/` and `save/` directly, not another enclosing copy of the old folder.
   Copy the whole `save/` folder, including `save_0` and its contents.
4. Start Savage Wind with the variable set, using one of the examples below. Replace the example paths with your
   own application and destination paths.
5. Check `[paths] data: ...` in the new startup log, then check your settings and load your existing save.
   Keep the old data until you have verified the copy. Afterwards, you can remove the old data you copied to free
   space; keep the original application, its DLLs and helper tools in place.

The variable does not move or import anything by itself. An empty destination starts with no saves or settings
and asks you to set up the game files. Your original data stays in the old folder.
If you also set `SAVAGEWIND_SAVE_DIR` for testing, it overrides the save location separately: unset it or update it
when moving the whole data folder.

## Windows

For one PowerShell session:

```powershell
$env:SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT = 'D:\Games\Savage Wind Data'
& 'C:\Games\Savage Wind\savagewind.exe'
```

To use the same folder each time, save this as a `.cmd` file and launch it instead of the executable:

```bat
@echo off
set "SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT=D:\Games\Savage Wind Data"
"C:\Games\Savage Wind\savagewind.exe" %*
```

Both examples leave the executable, DLLs, `zig/` and `swgen/` in the application folder. Add `--config` when
launching to open Savage Wind Configuration with the same data folder. The variable in a PowerShell session or
`.cmd` file does not automatically apply when you launch the executable another way.

## Linux / Steam Deck

For one launch:

```sh
SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT="/mnt/games/Savage Wind Data" "/path/to/Savage_Wind.AppImage"
```

For repeated launches, save this as `run-savagewind.sh` and make it executable with `chmod +x run-savagewind.sh`:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
export SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT="/mnt/games/Savage Wind Data"
exec "/path/to/Savage_Wind.AppImage" "$@"
```

Run `./run-savagewind.sh --config` to open configuration with the same data folder. If you launch through a desktop
entry or Steam, point it at the wrapper or set the variable in that launcher's environment too. Launching the
original AppImage directly does not inherit the wrapper's variable. You can keep the AppImage in its original
location; it does not need to be copied into the data folder.

## Returning to the original folder

Launch without the override, or change the path in your wrapper. In a PowerShell session,
`Remove-Item Env:SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT` unsets the variable; in a Linux shell, use `unset SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT`.
This only changes which folder the next launch uses: saves and settings are not synchronized between folders.
If you want to keep newer progress when switching back, close the game and copy it back first, keeping a backup
of the destination's saves.

```

`docs/game-files.md`:

```md
# Game files

[Back to the README](../README.md)

- Your own *Breath of the Wild* (cartridge or digital) and its **1.9.0 update**, the latest, extracted from your own
  console:
  - the **ExeFS** of that version (`main`, `main.npdm`, `rtld`, `sdk`, `subsdk0`)
  - the **RomFS** with that update applied (base game and update merged)
- Optional: the DLC, *The Master Trials* and *The Champions' Ballad*, from your own copy: the **RomFS** of each of
  the two DLC, version 3.0 (see [The DLC](#the-dlc) below).
- Windows 10 or later or Linux, on x86-64 (a CPU with SSE4.2; without AVX2 / FMA the game code runs in a slower
  compatible mode), and a GPU with Vulkan 1.3.

Keep them in one folder like this one. The setup asks for it, and its name and place don't matter; a source build
reads `extracted/` next to the program (git ignores this folder):

```
extracted/
  exefs/   main, main.npdm, rtld, sdk, subsdk0
  romfs/   the complete RomFS (base game + the 1.9.0 update merged)
  aoc1/    optional: the first DLC's RomFS (11 folders, about 7,000 files, 1.4 GB)
    Game/  Map/  Movie/  NavMesh/  Pack/  Physics/  Sound/  System/  Terrain/  UI/  Voice/
  aoc2/    optional: the second DLC's RomFS (1 folder, 1 file)
    System/AocVersion.txt
```

The `main` module's build id tells the exact version; `python tools/sw_probe.py` (it reads `extracted/exefs`)
prints it and what the recompiler will find there.

## The DLC

Each DLC's RomFS goes in a folder of its own, named `aoc1/` and `aoc2/` as above, with its folders right inside it
(`aoc1/System/AocVersion.txt`). Keep the two DLC apart: the second one's RomFS is a single file, and extracting both
into one folder leaves only one DLC.

Do not merge the DLC into the game's `romfs/` either. A `romfs/` with the DLC inside (about 47,700 files instead of
41,062) lets the game start, but the loading screen after a Divine Beast boss then never ends
([#438](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/438), [#570](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/issues/570)):
the same save loads on to the inside of the beast with a `romfs/` of 41,062 files and the DLC in `aoc1/` and `aoc2/`.
The game files page tells you when the DLC is merged.

- **With the game:** keep them in the same folder as `exefs/` and `romfs/`, and choose that folder at the first
  setup. The DLC is set up together with the game.
- **Later:** in Savage Wind Configuration's game files page, choose a folder that holds just the DLC folders and set
  up. The DLC is added to the game files already set up, without building the game code again.

The setup tells the game's RomFS (it has `System/Version.txt`) from a DLC's (`System/AocVersion.txt`) and copies the
DLC as `aoc1/` and `aoc2/` into the data folder. A folder the game reads in place (an `extracted/` folder next to the
program) is not copied, so there the DLC folders must already be named `aoc1/` and `aoc2/`. The game files page shows the DLC set
up (for example "1 + 2 (3.0)") and removes it; your saves stay.

The DLC are optional: the whole game plays without them. What you get depends on what you set up:

| Set up | What you get |
|---|---|
| No DLC | The whole game, as on a console without the DLC |
| Only the first or only the second DLC | The whole game, without DLC content: the game uses the DLC only when it finds both |
| Both DLC | The whole game plus Master Mode, the Trial of the Sword, the Travel Medallion and The Champions' Ballad; the title screen shows "DLC Ver.3.0" |

The two packs came out months apart in 2017, both part of the Expansion Pass. In the version the game has now (DLC
3.0), the first DLC holds the data of both packs, *The Champions' Ballad* included, and the second only tells the
game that you have the second pack. So setting up only one of them never breaks your game: it runs as without DLC.
To unlock the DLC content, set up both, from your own console and your own Expansion Pass.

## Setting up without a window

A launcher that already has your game folder (RecompLauncher passes the one you picked) can run the same setup with no
window:

```
savagewind --prepare --game <folder with exefs and romfs>
```

It copies the game files and builds the game code, printing `progress <0 to 1> <step>` lines, and exits with 0 when
they are ready. The shader pipelines need a window, so they are left out and compile the first time they are drawn.
`--game` on its own is unchanged: it is the Steam entry that goes straight into the game.

```

# Glitch compatibility tracker

Use this checklist to record which Breath of the Wild glitches and speedrun techniques behave like the
Nintendo Switch **1.9.0** game in Savage Wind. Only include glitches with a documented working 1.9.0
baseline or a successful test using the supported 1.9.0 game in the recomp. `Untested` refers to the
recomp result, not whether the glitch exists in 1.9.0.

Savage Wind targets **Switch version 1.9.0**. Record the exact Switch version used as a baseline: an older
video or a Wii U result alone does not establish expected behavior on the supported version.

## Filling in the tables

- Replace `Untested` with `Works`, `Partial`, `Fails`, or `Retest` for each frame rate you test.
- `Works` means the expected effect was reproduced; `Partial` means it differs or only some variants work.
  `Fails` means the documented setup was attempted without the expected effect. `Retest` means an earlier
  result needs checking on the current build. A failed attempt alone does not establish a regression.
- In **Switch baseline**, link the working 1.9.0 reference. Recomp evidence alone must be labeled as
  such; it does not establish console parity. Do not add patched or unverified techniques to the tables.
- In **Build / report**, add the recomp commit or release and a link to a test record below, clip, or issue.
- Use **Notes** for the exact variant, limitations, and other frame rates (90, 120, uncapped, etc.).
  Add separate rows when variants or builds give different results.

Start at 30 FPS, then repeat the same setup at 60 FPS and any higher cap you use. Record the cap and actual
FPS when possible. Keep the location, equipment, input device, and setup consistent between runs.

## Movement, launches, and clipping

| Glitch / technique | Switch baseline | 30 FPS | 60 FPS | Build / report | Notes / other FPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Windbomb (general test; variant not recorded) | [1.9.0 reference][baseline-190] | Works | Works | Built from `test` branch commit [`ac47f65e3f9ee05641fff35f8d683fd36c306513`](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/commit/ac47f65e3f9ee05641fff35f8d683fd36c306513); [video evidence](https://youtu.be/7JGTN7cCYoY) | **120 FPS: Works.** Tester reports that higher FPS makes execution harder because the trick is timing-sensitive; expected behavior, not an issue. |
| Bullet Time Bounce (BTB) | 1.9.0 recomp confirmed; console baseline not recorded | Works | Works | Built from `test` branch commit [`ac47f65e3f9ee05641fff35f8d683fd36c306513`](https://github.com/Revivedx/SavageWindRecomp/commit/ac47f65e3f9ee05641fff35f8d683fd36c306513); [video evidence](https://youtu.be/A6n5opLTVng) | **120 FPS: Works.** |
| Whistle sprint | [1.9.0 reference][baseline-190] | Untested | Untested | — | — |
| Skew storage / shield clipping | [1.9.0 reference][baseline-190] | Untested | Untested | — | Record wall and skew setup. |
| Extended shield clip (ESC) | [1.9.0 reference][baseline-190] | Untested | Untested | — | Record location and setup. |
| Moon jump | [1.9.0 reference][baseline-190] | Untested | Untested | — | Record mounted archery setup. |

The [1.9.0 compatibility guide][baseline-190] reports the retained console-baseline techniques as working
on original Switch 1.9.0. Its Switch 2 Edition results are separate: plain shield clips differ, while the

Copy this template for each test session. Back up your saves before testing inventory or progression

`docs/hdr.md`:

```md
# HDR output

Savage Wind presents in HDR10 when **Video > HDR** is `on`, or `auto` while the display is in HDR. The display must
offer an HDR10 swapchain format (`VK_EXT_swapchain_colorspace`, ST 2084 / Rec. 2020); otherwise the picture stays SDR.
The HDR present path is the Vulkan backend (Windows and Linux); the calibration-profile read below is Windows-only.

## How BOTW's picture reaches the display

BOTW renders the 3D scene and its bloom into two **B10G11R11 float** images at the internal resolution (1600x900
docked). Its scene tonemap (fragment shader `72cb7ff600`, the engine's `hdr_compose` pass) adds them, applies the
game's own `1 - e^-x` curve and saturation grade, and writes a 1600x900 `A2B10G10R10` image. The game's upscale/FXAA
pass (`72caebd800`) brings that to the 1920x1080 final image, the HUD is drawn into it, and the game copies it
sRGB-encoded into the 8-bit image it presents. That copy clips everything above white.

With HDR on:

- `runtime/nvn/vulkan/textures.c` creates the 1600x900 scene tonemap target **and** the 1920x1080 final image as
  **RGBA16F**, so the extended curve's highlights reach the game's upscale/FXAA pass and the HUD. The B10G11R11
  scene and bloom sources are already float; small 10-bit scene targets (effects/copies) stay as they are.
- `runtime/nvn/vulkan/exec.c` (`hdr_make_tonemap_prog`) recognises the tonemap at its first draw by its own fragment
  shader constants (`0.2989`, `-1.442695`, `10000`, `2/3`) and its two float scene/bloom textures, then replaces its
  fragment shader with the HDR tonemap: RenoDX's **extended vanilla** curve (the game's own `1 - e^-x` up to a pivot,
  continued along its tangent above it, keeping BOTW's exact luminance/per-channel mix and saturation grade), the
  MacLeod-Boynton hue/purity transfer, and then either the RenoDX BOTW mod's **PsychoV test17 + per-channel Neutwo**
  (the default) or the game's own clipped tonemap (Vanilla). The output is linear, with 1.0 at the HUD's white.
- `exec.c` (`hdr_record_draw`, `hdr_record_copy`) remembers the float image the game's final copy reads. The present
  then uses that image instead of the clipped 8-bit copy.
- `device.c` draws the game's picture into an RGBA16F window-size image, PQ-encodes it to the HDR10 swapchain
  (`hdr_pq`), draws the overlay menu into an RGBA8 image and blends it on at the paper white (`hdr_ui`), and sends
  `VkHdrMetadataEXT` with the configured peak.

The in-game HUD is part of the game's picture. The 3D scene and the HUD/menu have separate whites (`hdr_game_nits`
and `hdr_ui_nits`, both 203 by default); the peak is the final cap for both.

BOTW's shader archives (`Bootup_Graphics.pack` → `uking_sys` / AGL `hdr_compose`) and its embedded shader names
(`HDRCompose`, `hdr_compose`, `HDR_TONEMAPPING`, `HDR_BLOOM_COMPOSE`) confirm this pass; the `72cb7ff600` program
is the one the game draws into the 1600x900 scene target.

The **main-menu background** is not this 3D pass: it is the static 2D layout art in `Layout/Title.sblarc`
(`timg/__Combined.bntx`, with `blyt/Title_00.bflyt` for the logo and menu). It is drawn after the scene tonemap and
therefore does not use the extended curve. The layout texture can itself hold values slightly above 1.0 (the current
menu art measures up to ~1.7x paper white), so it is not clamped exactly to paper white; that is the 2D layout's own
range, not a 3D scene highlight. `TitleBG.pack` holds the separate 3D title scene (terrain, Link, `WorldMgr`); when that scene
is drawn, it uses the same scene path as the game.

## Settings

| INI key | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `hdr` | `auto`, `on`, `off` | `auto` |
| `hdr_peak_nits` | the display's peak: the scene's roll-off target **and** the final cap for every element; on Windows the first start fills it from the monitor's HDR calibration profile (1000 nits if none), then it is editable; other platforms default to 1000 and it is set manually | Windows: ICC peak / 1000; elsewhere 1000 |
| `hdr_game_nits` | the 3D scene's white (paper white), capped by the peak | `203` |
| `hdr_ui_nits` | the HUD and menu white, capped by the peak | `203` |
| `hdr_tonemapper` | `0` Vanilla (the game's own tonemap, clipped at white), `1` RenoDX (PsychoV + per-channel Neutwo; the BOTW mod's "RenoDRT" option) | `1` |
| `hdr_exposure` | PsychoV exposure, percent of the scene's own | `100` |
| `hdr_highlights` | PsychoV highlight contrast (0..100; 50 neutral) | `50` |
| `hdr_shadows` | PsychoV shadow contrast (0..100; 50 neutral) | `50` |
| `hdr_contrast` | PsychoV contrast around mid-grey (0..100; 50 neutral) | `50` |
| `hdr_saturation` | PsychoV saturation (0..100; 50 neutral) | `50` |
| `hdr_highlight_saturation` | PsychoV highlight colour (0..100; 50 neutral, below desaturates toward white) | `50` |
| `hdr_flare` | PsychoV flare/glare compensation (0..100; 0 neutral; the mod's steep `0.10 * pow(value, 10)` mapping) | `0` |
| `hdr_gamma` | the mod's `ToneMapGammaCorrection`: `0` none, `1` 2.2, `2` BT.1886 (2.4); it adjusts the per-channel Neutwo peak for gamma-encoded output. `0` is correct for this linear/PQ path; the mod defaults to `1` (2.2) for its gamma-encoded output | `0` |
| `hdr_look1`..`hdr_look3` | the three saved HDR looks (`Video > HDR preset`), 18 space-separated values: tone mapper, exposure, highlights, shadows, contrast, saturation, highlight saturation, flare, hue, blowout, SDR blend, vanilla saturation, bloom, clamp, peak, game, UI, gamma | the mod's defaults; peak/game/UI start as 0 (keep the current display setup): on Windows the first start fills the ICC peak, elsewhere they stay 0 until a preset is saved (a saved preset stores the effective nits) |
| `hdr_preset` | `0` Preset Off (the mod's OnPresetOff; it leaves SDR blend, vanilla saturation and gamut clamp as they are), `1`..`3` the selected saved slot; `4` is Custom, derived by the UI when the values match no state and never stored | `1` |
| `hdr_hue` | highlight hue/purity transfer: how much of the game's SDR hue the extended colour takes, in MacLeod-Boynton space, percent (`0` off) | `70` |
| `hdr_blowout` | SDR blowout: how much of the game's SDR highlight desaturation/purity the transfer keeps, percent | `65` |
| `hdr_sdr_blend` | extended-curve pivot: where the curve leaves the game's `1 - e^-x` and continues straight, percent of scene white | `18` |
| `hdr_vanilla_saturation` | the game's own saturation grade strength, percent | `100` |
| `hdr_bloom` | the game's bloom strength in HDR, percent (`0` removes it) | `100` |
| `hdr_clamp` | the clamp after the grade: `0` BT.709 (the game's own), `1` BT.2020 | `0` |
| `hdr_clip_nits` | legacy, ignored; the final cap is always `hdr_peak_nits` | — |
| `hdr_paper_white` | old SDR fallback key, used only if the game and UI whites are both `0` | Windows' SDR white |

The peak, game and HUD brightness, the tone mapper, the PsychoV sliders and the rest of the HDR look controls (hue,
blowout, SDR blend, vanilla saturation, bloom, clamp, presets) are in the HDR menu and the game's own Options screen;
the peak slider moves in 10-nit steps, the hue in 5% and the others in 1%. The HUD and menu default to 203 nits (HGIG
reference white), and the 3D scene's paper white also defaults to 203.

`Video > HDR preset` saves and recalls three complete looks: the tone mapper, every look control, the display peak,
game and UI whites, and gamma (the mod's presets do the same). `Preset Off` is the mod's OnPresetOff: Vanilla tone
mapper, peak/game/UI 203, neutral grading, hue 100, blowout 0 and bloom 100; SDR blend, vanilla saturation and gamut
clamp stay as they are, as the mod's OnPresetOff leaves them. It starts on Preset 1, which matches the RenoDX BOTW mod's
defaults. `Save HDR preset` writes the current look into the last selected slot (Preset 1 when Off or Custom); the
values apply live, as in the mod. `Custom` is shown but not selectable: it means the current values differ from the
selected slot. Select Preset 2, adjust the sliders and Save to write that look back into Preset 2; with no slot
selected, Save uses Preset 1.

The overlay/launcher HDR group keeps the tone mapper, peak, game (paper white) and UI brightness visible and folds
the rest, from HDR exposure through Save HDR preset, under `Advanced (show)`; it starts collapsed. The game's own
Options screen keeps its flat page.

A fresh settings file has no peak value. On Windows, the first start reads the display's **ICM profile association**
(`ICMProfileAC`) for the monitor the game window is on, and uses the last valid profile's **MHC2** tag
`max_luminance` — the display's small-area peak. It writes that value into the settings and logs the ICC file and
peak. The standard `lumi` tag is the maximum full-frame luminance, not the highlight peak. The group for the window's
monitor is used, not another display's profile; if that group has no profile with an `MHC2` tag, the monitor's default
profile is tried, and the result is 0 (no profile) if that has none either. On other platforms there is no Windows
calibration profile: the peak defaults to 1000 and is set manually.

The value is then a normal editable setting; on Windows the setting's description shows the current ICC profile and
peak, or says no profile was found. If no profile is found, the first start writes **1000 nits** and the description
says so (`No Windows HDR calibration profile found; peak defaults to 1000 nits.`). There is no 0/automatic value in the
UI.

The scene's tonemap rolls off at the peak, and the present clamps the final signal — scene, flashes, particles, HUD and
menu — to that same peak. The peak also caps the game and UI whites: if either is set above it, the effective white is
the peak. The game and HUD whites are separate so the 3D scene can be brighter or dimmer against the HUD; both default
to 203.

The picture is PQ-encoded at the HUD/paper white; the opening awakening cutscene is rendered in real time; the
`Movie/*.webm` files are the memories and other demos, not that sequence.

The highlight hue correction (`hdr_hue`) is a compact port of RenoDX's MacLeod-Boynton hue/purity transfer: the
extended colour takes the hue angle and purity of the game's own SDR result while keeping its HDR luminance, so a
fire's core reads yellow-white as in SDR instead of staying deep red. `hdr_blowout` is the purity strength (the SDR
blowout); `hdr_hue` is the hue strength, weighted by the SDR donor's chroma. The defaults, 70 and 65, are RenoDX
BOTW's.

`hdr_sdr_blend` is the extended curve's pivot (RenoDX BOTW's 18%). `hdr_vanilla_saturation` scales the game's own
saturation grade (100 is the game's look); the grade is normalized by RenoDX's Neutwo max-channel scale
(`1/sqrt(max^2+1)`), as the mod does. `hdr_bloom` scales the bloom the game's tonemap adds (100 is the game's own
bloom; 0 removes it in HDR). `hdr_clamp` clamps negative channels after the grade in BT.709 (the game's own) or
BT.2020.

The default tone mapper is the RenoDX BOTW mod's **PsychoV test17** path: its `ApplyTest17BT2020` (exposure, highlights,
shadows, contrast and flare on the Yf luminance, saturation and highlight saturation in MacLeod-Boynton purity, with
the mod's post gamut compression) and then its per-channel `neutwo` fit to the display peak. `runtime/nvn/vulkan/hdr_psycho.c` is a GLSL
port of the game-local `psycho_test17_custom.hlsli`, limited to the path the mod's `BuildPsycho17Config` uses (no LMS
tonemap, bleaching, hue emulation, pre-gamut compression or dechroma). The mod's generic template labels this
`ToneMapType = 1` option "RenoDRT", but the shader runs PsychoV, not RenoDRT; this UI names it "RenoDX (PsychoV)".
Vanilla (`0`) uses the game's own tonemap and grade, clipped at white, so it has no scene detail above white.

`hdr_saturation` is the PsychoV purity scale, and `hdr_highlight_saturation` is the mod's `ColorGradeHighlightSaturation`
(the `purity_highlights` term): below 50% it desaturates highlights toward white, above 50% it adds highlight colour.
The neon-like shifts of the per-channel PsychoV path are why the mod's `hdr_blowout` transfers the SDR purity first.

The HDR look (tone mapper, sliders, hue/blowout/SDR blend/vanilla saturation/bloom/clamp, gamma and the presets,
including peak/game/UI) is read from a push-constant block on every HDR tonemap draw, and the HDR metadata is re-sent
when the peak or scene white changes, so changes apply live, as in the mod. Only `hdr` itself still needs a restart:
turning HDR on or off changes the game's target formats (RGBA16F) and the swapchain, which happen at start. `auto`
follows the display's HDR state at the next start.

## Debugging

- `SAVAGEWIND_HDR_RT8=1`: keep the final image 10-bit (no HDR float path).
- `SAVAGEWIND_HDR_TONEMAP=0`: keep the game's tonemap (the float path still presents its output, without the extended
  curve; the game's own 8-bit copy would clip it).
- `SAVAGEWIND_SAVE_MSL=1`: save translated GLSL under `build/glsl/`.
- The log says whether the tonemap was replaced and whether the present found the float picture:
  `[hdr] the game's tonemap runs as the HDR tonemap (fs 72cb7ff600)`, `[hdr] presenting the game's float picture`,
  `[hdr] HDR10 output, but the game's float picture was not found`. On Windows the first start logs the ICC profile and
  peak (`[hdr] Windows HDR calibration profile: "<profile>.icc", <peak> nits`, then
  `[hdr] peak brightness set to <peak> nits (from the ICC profile)`), or
  `[hdr] no Windows HDR calibration profile found` / `[hdr] peak brightness set to 1000 nits (no ICC profile)`; the
  first present logs the paper white and the peak/final cap:
  `[hdr] present: paper white <UI white> nits, peak <peak> nits (final cap)`.
- `SAVAGEWIND_WINDOW_SHOT=<frame>` saves the presented HDR float picture as an SDR PNG and logs its true range, e.g.
  `[hdr] float picture: max <x> (<nits> nits), mean <y> (<nits> nits)`; the raw float image can exceed the peak (the
  HUD/menu at their own white, or post-tonemap effects), and the present clamps it to the peak. (The control
  endpoint's `shot` saves the game's clipped 8-bit copy instead, so highlights there are white.)

## Limitations

- AMD FSR 3 frame generation is off while HDR is on: its intermediate copies are 8-bit and would clip the picture.
- FSR 1 on the final image is off while HDR is on (it expects a gamma-encoded signal). The scene upscaler and TAA run;
  the grade and sharpening passes preserve values above 1.0, so the extended highlights survive them.
- The PsychoV port is the subset the RenoDX BOTW mod actually runs (`ApplyTest17BT2020` with its fixed configuration);
  the mod's unused full-observer `psychotm_test17` (LMS Naka-Rushton response, bleaching, hue emulation) and its
  advanced controls (dechroma, hue shift, adaptation) are not ported. The mod's generic template labels this option
  "RenoDRT", but its shader runs PsychoV; this UI names it "RenoDX (PsychoV)".
- The Windows ICC first-start read selects the monitor's profile group by its `\\.\DISPLAYn` number; Windows exposes no
  stable mapping between display numbers and those groups, so on an unusual multi-monitor setup the description may
  name another display's profile. The log and the setting's description name the profile used. On Linux and macOS the
  peak is set manually.
- The overlay menu's translucent parts blend in PQ code values, so their edges can be slightly off; opaque menu
  pixels are exact.
- The extended curve needs the scene's 1600x900 (docked) tonemap target; at the game's 1280x720 handheld resolution
  that target stays 10-bit and highlights clip at white, as without HDR.
- The optional **Video > Colour** grade, including its LUT, still runs on the HDR scene (`exec.c` `scene_post`,
  `shaders.c` `grade_lut.frag`): the LUT is applied to the SDR part of the linear scene (0..1) and the part above 1 is
  added back, but an SDR-authored LUT can still shift HDR colours. If a scene shows an unexpected tint — the reported
  teal cliffs in Gerudo — turn the LUT off first. The HDR tonemap replacement itself samples only the game's scene and
  bloom, not a LUT.

## Credits

The approach comes from the RenoDX TotK port by ProSep
([totk-pc-recomp#281](https://github.com/valentderah/totk-pc-recomp/pull/281)), which credits the RenoDX TotK mod:

- game mod by souperman9
- tonemapper by Musa
- RenoDX by ShortFuse (Carlos Lopez Jr.)
- RenoVK fork by Ritsu

Sources: [RenoDX](https://github.com/clshortfuse/renodx), MIT; the curve follows its BOTW mod (`src/games/botw`). From
it come two ideas: replacing the tonemap and keeping the game's curve below a pivot, and the observation that the
passes after the tonemap keep values above 1. The MacLeod-Boynton matrices and the hue/purity formula are adapted
from that mod's `macleod_boynton.hlsli` (`CorrectHueAndPurityMBBT709WithBT2020`, MIT); the PsychoV test17 path and the
per-channel Neutwo fit are a GLSL port of its `psycho_test17_custom.hlsli` (`ApplyTest17BT2020`, the gamut-compression
and purity helpers, MIT); the rest of the shader and the runtime code here are new. The PQ (SMPTE ST 2084) and
Rec. 709 -> Rec. 2020 (BT.2087) constants are from the standards.
