`docs/launch-options.md`:

```md
# Launch options

Sometimes we ask you to test with an extra setting turned on, for example "start the game with `SAVAGEWIND_FSR3`
set to 1". These settings are called launch options (programmers call them environment variables). You do not need
a terminal or a batch file: you can set them on the Savage Wind start screen.

## Add a launch option

1. Open the start screen (Savage Wind Configuration) and stay on the first page, the one with Game files and Game
   font. Scroll down to **Launch options**. The list is empty until you add something.
2. Click the first field and type the name, for example `FSR3`. You can leave out the `SAVAGEWIND_` start. While you
   type, matching suggestions appear below the fields; click one to fill in its name and an example value. You can
   also type any name we gave you that is not in the suggestions.
3. Click the second field and type the value we asked for, for example `1`. If you leave it empty, `1` is used.
4. Press Enter, or click **Add**. The option shows up in the list. With a controller, press A on a field to get the
   on-screen keyboard.
5. Press **Play**. Savage Wind restarts once by itself and then starts the game with your options. You may see the
   window close and open again; that is expected. Starting the game directly with `savagewind.exe` (or the AppImage)
   uses your launch options too, with the same quick restart.

Launch options stay until you remove them, also after you close and reopen Savage Wind.

## Change or remove one

- To change the value, edit the value field in the list and press Enter.
- To change the name, remove the option and add it again.
- To remove an option, click **Remove** next to it. The next time you press Play it is gone.

## Switches are on or off, not 0 and 1

Many options are plain switches: they are on when they are in the list and off when they are not. For those,
writing `0` does **not** turn them off (the game only checks that the option exists). To turn a switch off, remove
it from the list. Savage Wind refuses `0`, `off`, `false` and `no` for the switches it knows about, and shows a
message instead.

## Warnings

- Only add options you were asked to add. A wrong option can make the game slower, glitchy or crash at start.
- Options shown in orange are for developers. Some of them make the game much slower or write very large files.
- Savage Wind does not accept options that would lock you out of this screen or break the start (for example
  `SAVAGEWIND_NO_LAUNCHER`), or system settings such as `PATH`.
- If the same variable is also set outside Savage Wind (in a shortcut or a terminal), the value in this list wins.

## If something goes wrong

The start screen opened with `--config` (what Savage Wind Configuration does) always starts **without** your
launch options, so you can always get back in and remove a bad one.

To start the game ignoring all saved launch options once, start it with `--no-launch-flags`, for example
`savagewind.exe --no-launch-flags`.

To clear them completely, close Savage Wind and delete the file `launch-flags.txt` in the data folder (the same
folder as `savagewind.ini`; the log line `[paths] data: ...` shows where it is).

## For testers who like details

- The options are kept in the text file `launch-flags.txt` in the data folder, one `NAME=value` per line. Lines
  starting with `#` are comments. It can be edited by hand while Savage Wind is closed; lines that are not valid
  are ignored.
- The names of the suggestions come from the program itself: `tools/gen_launch_flags.py` collects every
  `SAVAGEWIND_` name that the code reads into `runtime/launch_flags_table.c`, and `make test-launch-flags` fails
  when that list is out of date. The short descriptions of the suggested options are in
  `tools/launch_flags_curated.txt`.
- A name you type that is not in the list still works; it is passed to the game as it is.

```

`docs/linux.md`:

```md
# Savage Wind on Linux (x86-64, aarch64)

Status (inherited from LASRecomp): builds and runs on Vulkan on x86-64. aarch64 is **experimental**: cross-compiled, its start screen checked under emulation,
the game itself untested on real hardware - community reports decide (see the end). `make appimage` / `make appimages`
package the release AppImages.

## Running the AppImage
    chmod +x Savage_Wind-0.3.0-alpha.3-x86_64.AppImage
    ./Savage_Wind-0.3.0-alpha.3-x86_64.AppImage

Needs: a distribution with glibc 2.35 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Fedora 36, Arch, ...), a Vulkan 1.3 driver
(Mesa RADV / ANV / NVK / Turnip / Asahi Honeykrisp, or NVIDIA's), and on x86-64 a CPU with SSE4.2 (2008 or newer;
without AVX2 / FMA the game code is built in a slower compatible mode).
The start screen asks for the folder with your own game files and sets them up; from then on the game starts
straight away. `--config` (`./Savage_Wind-*.AppImage --config`) opens the configuration screen: Play, Settings, the
game files, Quit. Once the AppImage is in your applications menu (AppImageLauncher, Gear Lever, or your desktop's own
AppImage integration), its entry has a **Savage Wind Configuration** action (right-click it) that does the same. A picture of your own as `splash.jpg` / `splash.png` in the data folder below replaces the start
screen's art.

Everything the app writes lives in `~/.local/share/savagewind` (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/savagewind`): game files (`extracted/`),
saves, settings (`savagewind.ini`), shader caches, imported fonts. Started without a terminal the log is
`~/.local/share/savagewind/savagewind.log` (from a terminal it prints there instead). `SAVAGEWIND_DATA_ROOT=<dir>` uses
another folder. See [Moving the data folder](data-folder.md) for copying existing data and setting up a launch
wrapper, including on Steam Deck.

Controllers work as on the other systems (SDL3's gamepad support, bundled): Xbox, PlayStation (DualShock 4,
DualSense), Switch Pro / Joy-Con, 8BitDo and other pads through the kernel's drivers, plugged in or paired while the
game runs. For SDL's own drivers (rumble, LEDs and gyro on PlayStation /
Switch pads) the user needs access to `/dev/hidraw*`, which most distributions give with Steam's udev rules
(`steam-devices`, or Steam installed); without them the controller still works through the kernel driver. Started from
Steam with Steam Input on, the game sees Steam's virtual Xbox controller.

If the AppImage won't start with a FUSE error, install your distribution's `fuse3` package (the AppImage runtime
needs `fusermount3`), or run it as `./Savage_Wind-....AppImage --appimage-extract-and-run`.

### Updating

Savage Wind Configuration offers a new release when there is one. Its Update entry downloads the AppImage for this
machine (x86_64 or aarch64) with the system's `curl`, checks its signature and replaces the running file under the same
name, so shortcuts and Steam entries keep working. The previous file stays next to it as `<name>.old` until the new
version has finished setting up. The AppImage's folder must be writable.

### Steam Deck motion in Gaming Mode (DSU)

Keep Steam Input enabled for buttons and sticks. On Linux the game automatically prefers fresh native SDL gyro
**and** accelerometer samples, then falls back to a Cemuhook DSU server at `127.0.0.1:26760`. If neither source
works, the existing still-controller / mouse-tilt fallback remains. This is native game motion (bow aiming and
motion puzzles), not gyro-to-mouse; the game's own motion-controls option still decides when aiming uses it.
Controls-page motion sensitivity and inversion apply to either sensor source. No root access is needed by the game.

1. Install [SteamDeckGyroDSU](https://github.com/kmicki/SteamDeckGyroDSU) separately in Desktop Mode. Follow its
   current **Install/Update** instructions: download and run the official **Update GyroDSU** desktop shortcut.
   The game does not install or start the service. Follow the project's installer instructions if it requests
   device permissions. Updating an existing installation uses the same shortcut.
2. Check in Konsole: `systemctl --user status sdgyrodsu.service`. It should be active. The service runs in Gaming
   Mode too. `journalctl --user -u sdgyrodsu.service -n 30 --no-pager` shows its startup and device errors.
3. Add the patched Linux AppImage to Steam as a non-Steam game (native Linux execution; do not force Proton).
   Leave Steam Input enabled and use a normal gamepad layout. No Steam gyro-to-mouse mapping is required.
4. Return to Gaming Mode and launch. DSU fallback is automatic; no launch option is required. To enable DSU
   explicitly, use Steam launch options:

       SAVAGEWIND_DSU=on %command%

5. Enable the game's motion-controls option, hold the Deck still briefly for bias calibration, then check bow
   aiming and a tilt shrine. Motion should only affect the contexts where the game normally uses it.

`SAVAGEWIND_DSU=auto` is the Linux default: contact DSU only when fresh SDL motion is unavailable.
`SAVAGEWIND_DSU=off` disables DSU completely. `SAVAGEWIND_DSU=on` keeps discovery/subscription active even when SDL
works, with SDL still taking priority. An optional `SAVAGEWIND_DSU_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:26760` accepts a numeric IPv4
address and port (no DNS lookup on the game thread). Windows has the same DSU client (see the
[FAQ](FAQ.md#does-gyro-work)); macOS keeps its SDL motion path. A controller sensor SDL gives no data rate (a
handheld's own sensor lent to its gamepad by SDL's sensor fusion) comes after a DSU server that answers.

Look in `~/.local/share/savagewind/savagewind.log` (or terminal output; custom data roots use their own log) for
`[motion]` and `[dsu]`. SDL availability is logged when opening a controller; `[dsu] connected: slot ...` means
valid motion packets were received; `[motion] source: none -> DSU` means they are being used. `enabled` alone
means the client is trying, not that the server was detected. `SAVAGEWIND_MOTION_LOG=1` adds the existing periodic
fusion/orientation diagnostic. Logs are never emitted per sample by default.

Troubleshooting:

- Buttons working with no gyro is expected when Steam exposes a virtual Xbox pad: check for a DSU connection.
- If DSU stays unavailable, check the service above and its port. If you changed `SDGYRO_SERVER_PORT` on the
  server, set the matching `SAVAGEWIND_DSU_ENDPOINT` on the game. Check that localhost UDP is permitted.
- A timeout means no advancing, valid motion for 500 ms. The client drops stale data and retries discovery and
  subscriptions every second; starting/restarting the service later needs no game restart. A still controller
  remains valid if packets/timestamps keep advancing. Duplicate and out-of-order packets do not refresh it.
- Invalid-packet messages are rate limited: check the endpoint really serves Cemuhook DSU. The known 2.1
  SteamDeckGyroDSU padded version reply is supported explicitly; motion packets still require valid CRC/lengths.
- One DSU controller is selected and retained by slot/MAC until disconnected. With multiple controllers,
  automatic selection cannot infer which physical controller Steam's virtual pad represents; stop unrelated
  DSU sources or use `off` for an external controller without motion. Fresh SDL sensors always take priority.
- After suspend or a source switch, allow a brief stationary period for calibration. Device changes reset fusion
  and timestamps; no stale angular velocity is integrated. Saves and settings do not need to be changed.

Developer validation (no game assets): `DEPS=/absolute/path/to/deps tools/test_dsu.sh`, or omit `DEPS` with SDL3
installed through pkg-config. `SANITIZE=1` enables ASan/UBSan when the compiler's sanitizer runtimes are installed.
Tests exercise CRC against zlib, malformed packets, axis/unit conversion, UDP discovery/subscription, sequence wrap,
server restarts, timeouts, source priority and game-facing source-switch angular velocity. A live diagnostic can be
built separately: `cc -Iruntime tools/dsu_probe.c runtime/dsu.c -lm -o /tmp/dsu_probe`; `/tmp/dsu_probe` checks the
real endpoint for three seconds without SDL or game data. It reports acceleration in the runtime's Switch axes
(flat, face upward: approximately `0 0 -1`) and angular velocity in rad/s.

Protocol/axis references: [Cemuhook reference](https://v1993.github.io/cemuhook-protocol/),
[SteamDeckGyroDSU MIT implementation](https://github.com/kmicki/SteamDeckGyroDSU/blob/master/src/sdgyrodsu/cemuhookadapter.cpp),
and [SDL Steam Deck sensor mapping](https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL/blob/main/src/joystick/hidapi/SDL_hidapi_steamdeck.c).
The client uses G and rad/s directly in the existing fusion axes.

### Steam Deck (first test, 2026-10-23)
SteamOS 3.8, Mesa 26.2 RADV (VANGOGH). The setup works: copying the game files, generating and compiling the game
code (~16 minutes on the Deck's 8 threads), precompiling the shaders (~7 minutes). Known problems:

- (Fixed) The GPU hung within the first frames: black screen, and a process that only a restart of the Deck cleared.
  The game draws point lists with vertex shaders that write no point size, which is undefined without
  `VK_KHR_maintenance5`. The renderer enables it now, so that size is 1.0.
- (Fixed) 15 fps in the open world. Two causes:
  - RADV has no `VK_KHR_unified_image_layouts`, so the renderer copied each target a draw samples while drawing
    into it, ~200 times a frame. Those targets now spend their passes in the `ATTACHMENT_FEEDBACK_LOOP_OPTIMAL`
    layout.
  - amdgpu revisits every page of an imported host-memory buffer at each submission: ~4 ms a submit for the 3 GB
    guest heap. The heap is now GPU memory, exported as a dma-buf and mapped at the heap's addresses
    (`SAVAGEWIND_VK_HEAP_IMPORT=1`: the import, as before).

  Measured standing on the Great Plateau after Continue: about 40 fps with the 60 fps cap, a steady 30 with the 30
  fps cap.
- Shadow resolutions above Console show graphical glitches on RADV.
- Started in Desktop Mode, Steam's desktop controller layout also sends keys and mouse motion. Gaming Mode is untested.

## Building from source
Ubuntu 25.04+ / Debian 13 packages (other distributions: the same libraries under their names; clang 18 or newer - the
lifted FP/SIMD code needs `__builtin_elementwise_*` - and SDL3 3.2 or newer):

    sudo apt install clang lld make pkg-config python3-venv libsdl3-dev libavformat-dev libavcodec-dev \
        libavutil-dev libswscale-dev libvulkan-dev libshaderc-dev zlib1g-dev glslc vulkan-tools

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and older, Debian 12 and openSUSE Leap have no SDL3 package (SDL3 arrived after their freeze):
build SDL3 from source there, or use the AppImage. Vulkan headers older than 1.4.321 (Debian 13, Ubuntu 25.04, Fedora
42 ship 1.4.304 - 1.4.313) build too: feedback loops then use the `ATTACHMENT_FEEDBACK_LOOP_OPTIMAL` layout, as on
drivers without `VK_KHR_unified_image_layouts`.

`tools/linux/distro_build.sh` builds the app (start screen only, no game code) natively in each of Debian 13, Ubuntu
26.04, Fedora 44, Arch and openSUSE Tumbleweed, in containers, with each distribution's own clang, SDL3, FFmpeg,
shaderc and lld; CI runs the same script (`.github/workflows/linux-distros.yml`). That is the check for "does it build
on my distribution": a container reproduces exactly what differs (package names, library sonames, header versions),
where a virtual machine would only do it slower.

(The Vulkan Memory Allocator header the renderer uses is bundled in `third_party/vma`, as are stb_image and
stb_image_write in `third_party/stb`.)

Then from the repo root:

    python3 -m venv tools/venv && tools/venv/bin/pip install lz4 capstone unicorn
    make -j         # the start screen only (no game code yet): set up the game files there, or put extracted/ here
    make gen        # once: recompile the game from your own game files
    make -j         # -> build/savagewind and the game code library build/swgame.so

Run `./build/savagewind` from the repo root: with `extracted/` in the starting folder it uses that folder for
everything (dev mode) instead of `~/.local/share/savagewind`.

`ARCH` picks the target, separately from the OS: the generated code differs per arch (aarch64 runs the guest's
FP/SIMD as inline asm, like Apple Silicon; x86-64 lowers it to C with `-march=x86-64-v3`, like Windows, or for CPUs
without AVX2 / FMA `GENARCH_COMPAT`'s `-march=x86-64-v2`: the start screen builds the one the CPU runs, `make` the
`GENARCH` one). `make gen` passes the matching `--simd`. A cross build (`ARCH=aarch64` on an x86-64 machine, `SYSROOT=<arm64 root filesystem>`)
keeps its own `generated-aarch64/` and `build/aarch64/`. The build detects whether shaderc is named
`libshaderc.so` or `libshaderc_shared.so`; override it with `SHADERC=-l<name>` if neither is found.

## AppImages
Needs podman, and for aarch64 QEMU user emulation with binfmt (`sudo apt install podman qemu-user qemu-user-binfmt`).

    make appimage                # this machine's arch -> build/dist/Savage_Wind-<version>-<arch>.AppImage
    make appimage ARCH=aarch64   # cross-compiled from x86-64
    make appimages               # both

Everything is built in Ubuntu 22.04 containers (`tools/linux/Containerfile`), so the result runs on glibc 2.35+:
SDL3, an LGPL-only FFmpeg (only the movie codecs, as on Windows / macOS), and shaderc from pinned sources
(`tools/linux/build_deps.sh`), then the game against them (`tools/linux/package.sh`). aarch64 is cross-compiled in
the amd64 container against the arm64 image's root filesystem (`build/linux/aarch64/sysroot`). The game code
generator helper (`tools/linux/gen_helper.sh`, PyInstaller) is frozen in a container of its own arch (on arm64 under
QEMU).

The AppImage holds `savagewind`, `swgen/`, `zig/`, the start screen font and the bundled libraries (SDL3,
FFmpeg, shaderc). Not bundled: glibc, libstdc++, zlib, the Vulkan loader and the GPU drivers (always the system's). No game
files or fonts.

## Differences from macOS / Windows
- Platform layer `runtime/platform/linux.c`: like macOS, the guest window (0x70_0000_0000..0x73_2000_0000) is one
  read/write mapping (`MAP_NORESERVE`), crashes are caught with `sigaction` on an alternate stack.
- The HLE / service / reset tables are ELF sections found through the linker's `__start_` / `__stop_` symbols.
- Renderer: the Windows Vulkan backend unchanged.
- Without the user's Switch fonts the game text uses DejaVu Sans (TrueType; the game's font engine can't use CFF
  fonts such as Noto Sans CJK). For Chinese or Korean text set `SAVAGEWIND_CJK_FONT` to a TrueType CJK font (e.g.
  `wqy-microhei.ttc`), or install one where the game looks for it; see `fonts/README.md`.
- Pages: 4K and 16K kernels (Asahi) work; 64K-page kernels (some ARM servers) are not supported.

## Testing on ARM (aarch64): what to report
The aarch64 AppImage is experimental: built on x86-64, only its start screen has run (emulated): reports from real hardware
(Asahi Linux, Snapdragon laptops, Raspberry Pi 5 and other boards) are what tells whether it works. Please include:

1. **Distribution and kernel**: `cat /etc/os-release | head -3; uname -r; getconf PAGESIZE`
2. **GPU and Vulkan driver**: `vulkaninfo --summary` (package `vulkan-tools`); at least the devices section with
   `deviceName`, `driverName` and `driverInfo`.
3. **What happened**: start screen? extraction? in game? where it stopped, any visual problems (screenshots help).
   With a controller: its model, and whether it works (the log names it: `[input] gamepad: ...`).
4. **The log**: `~/.local/share/savagewind/savagewind.log` (or the terminal output when started from a terminal).
   A crash writes `*** signal ...` and a backtrace there; attach the whole file. Opened again since? The run before is
   `savagewind.prev.log` next to it.
5. **A crash backtrace with gdb** when the log's isn't enough:

       ./Savage_Wind-0.3.0-alpha.3-aarch64.AppImage --appimage-extract    # -> squashfs-root/
       cd ~/.local/share/savagewind
       gdb -batch -ex 'handle SIGSEGV nostop noprint pass' -ex run -ex 'thread apply all bt 20' \
           --args ~/squashfs-root/usr/bin/savagewind > gdb.txt 2>&1

   (Adjust the `squashfs-root` path to where you extracted it. The game itself uses SIGSEGV for memory watches, hence
   the `handle` line; a real crash still ends in the backtrace. Attach `gdb.txt`.)

`docs/menu-language-packs.md`:

```md
# Menu language packs

Savage Wind's own menus (the start screen and the in-game Options) come in 14 languages, built into the program
(`runtime/ui/i18n/<lang>.inc`). A **language pack** lets a player fix or finish one of them without waiting for a new
build: a text file in the data folder that the menus read over the built-in table.

- **Where:** `lang/<language>.txt` in the data folder (next to `savagewind.ini`). `<language>` is the menu language's
  code: `en`, `de`, `es`, `fr`, `it`, `nl`, `pt`, `ru`, `ja`, `ko`, `zh-Hans`, `zh-Hant`, `th` or `he`.
- **Format:** UTF-8, one text per line: the English text exactly as in the program, a tab, then the translation.
  `\n` stands for a line break, `\t` for a tab and `\\` for a backslash. Lines starting with `#` and empty lines are
  skipped. A line without a tab is skipped too (the log says so).
- **Formats:** some texts hold numbers or names, such as `%d x %d` or `%s`. The translation must have the same `%`
  codes in the same order (`%%` is a percent sign and doesn't count). A line where they differ is skipped and the
  log names it, since the menu would otherwise show garbage or crash.
- **Which texts:** the English side is the first string of each `T("English", "...")` line in
  `runtime/ui/i18n/<language>.inc`. A text the pack doesn't name keeps the built-in translation.
- **When:** the pack is read the first time its language is shown, so restart Savage Wind after changing it. The log
  shows `[i18n] lang/<language>.txt: <n> texts`.

The game's own texts (items, dialogue, the game's menus) aren't part of this: they come from the game files.

Better translations are welcome back in the built-in tables, so every player gets them: see `tools/i18n_check.py`.

```

`docs/motion-vectors-spike.md`:

```md
# Per-object motion vectors: what BOTW's draws give us (spike, 2026-10-25)

A temporal upscaler (AMD FSR 3.1, NVIDIA DLSS, Intel XeSS) or frame generation needs, per pixel, where that pixel was
in the previous frame. Vectors from the depth buffer and the camera alone are right only for things that don't move by
themselves; Link, enemies, horses, NPCs, wind-swept grass, water and particles would smear. This spike measured what
Savage Wind's renderer sees of BOTW's scene draws, to choose how to make vectors for everything.

The idea being tested: almost everything that moves in BOTW moves because of the vertex shader's inputs (an object's
matrix, a bone palette, a time or wind value), not because its vertices are rewritten. If each scene draw can be given
the previous frame's inputs, a second copy of its vertex shader computes where each vertex was, and the difference is
the motion vector, with no knowledge of what the object is.

## Method

Instrumentation (`runtime/nvn/vulkan/mv_spike.c` plus one call in `exec.c` `draw_`, `SAVAGEWIND_MV_SPIKE=1`; a throwaway
commit, see "Reproducing") recorded the **scene draws** (depth or first color target in the RS_SCENE
scale group: the 3D scene's targets at the internal resolution) of two consecutive frames every 240 presented frames.
Each draw of the second frame was matched to one of the first by a **key**: vertex and fragment shader code addresses,
the addresses of the non-instanced vertex streams the vertex shader reads, the index buffer address, index count,
first index and base vertex; draws repeating a key in a frame were told apart by their order (ordinal). For each
matched draw it compared:

- each vertex shader constant buffer (hardware slot 3+): same guest address or not, same contents or not (hash of up
  to 64 KB);
- the non-instanced vertex streams' bytes (same key: rewritten by the CPU between the frames?);
- the instanced streams (divisor > 0): address, bytes, instance count;
- whether the vertex shader reads global memory (`uses_gmem`) or textures (`ntex`).

Run: the Alpha 3 build (5173d27) with only the runtime swapped, on the ROG Ally (RADV, Z1 Extreme), 1.8.2,
the owner's save (a scratch copy, `SAVAGEWIND_SAVE_DIR`), Great Plateau. Scripted input (`SAVAGEWIND_INPUT`): Continue,
then still, walking forward (`STICK_90`), a camera pan (`RSTICK_RIGHT`), walking sideways while panning, still again.

## Results

In the world from frame ~2880 (before that, the title and loading: 13 scene draws or none).

| Phase (frame pair) | Scene draws | Matched | Keys repeated in the frame | Instanced | VS reads textures | VS cbuf >= 2 KB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Still (3120) | 3114 | 98.4% | 1766 (57%) | 50 | 1603 (51%) | 240 |
| Walking (4080) | 3935 | 95.4% | 2472 (63%) | 82 | 1942 (49%) | 280 |
| Camera pan (4800) | 2359 | 93.0% | 1329 (56%) | 107 | 1395 (59%) | 250 |
| Walk + pan (5520) | 2637 | 93.1% | 1587 (60%) | 47 | 1331 (50%) | 235 |
| Still again (6480) | 2368 | 98.8% | 1405 (59%) | 116 | 1573 (66%) | 255 |

Constant buffers of the matched draws:

| Phase | cbuf slots | Same address | Moved | Moved, same contents | Draws with every cbuf at the same address | Draws with any cbuf contents changed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Still (3120) | 10097 | 31.3% | 6933 | 5102 (74%) | 8.3% | 54% |
| Walking (4080) | 11966 | 28.4% | 8573 | 1834 (21%) | 6.7% | 99% |
| Camera pan (4800) | 7840 | 23.4% | 6002 | 1534 (26%) | 11.5% | 99% |
| Walk + pan (5520) | 8208 | 23.6% | 6269 | 1510 (24%) | 10.3% | 99% |
| Still again (6480) | 8790 | 31.8% | 5992 | 2046 (34%) | 10.8% | 99% |

Every pair: **0** draws read global memory in the vertex shader; **0** draws had their (non-instanced) vertex data
rewritten between the frames; the cbuf slots that stay at one address and change contents are always the same 231
(per-frame globals). Instanced draws keep their instance stream address (45-116 of 47-117 draws) and instance count
(0-2 changed), but their instance **data** changes every frame for most of them (30-87 draws), standing still too.

The raw log lines are in the appendix.

## What this means

1. **Constant buffers are re-allocated every frame.** Only 23-32% of the slots keep their address, and three quarters
   of the moved ones (standing still) carry the same bytes as before: the game writes its constants into fresh memory
   each frame. "The previous frame's data at this address" doesn't exist; the previous inputs must be kept **per
   draw**: a copy of each scene draw's constant buffers, found again next frame by matching the draw.
2. **Matching draws by key works for 93-99% of them.** Standing still, 98.4-98.8%; moving, 92-95% (objects streaming
   in and out, LOD changes, culling). The unmatched rest (1-8%) is mostly a handful of shaders (the log's "unmatched"
   lists) and needs a fallback: camera-only reprojection, or the reactive mask.
3. **Over half the draws share their key with other draws in the same frame** (the same mesh drawn for several
   objects, told apart only by their constants). The ordinal is a weak identity: when culling adds or removes one of
   them, every later one would take its neighbour's previous constants, and get a wrong vector. These need a stronger
   tie-break, for example the nearest previous object matrix (the per-object constant slot is the one whose contents
   differ between the repeated draws).
4. **The constants carry the camera too.** Moving or panning, 99% of the draws had some constant change, so the
   per-object constants hold view-dependent matrices (or the game's camera block changes address with them). Running
   the vertex shader with the previous constants gives the whole motion, camera and object, in one go; the camera's
   own matrices are needed only for the unmatched fallback and for the jitter.
5. **Everything the vertex shaders read besides vertex streams and textures is in constant buffers.** No global memory
   reads, so bone palettes are constants too (the ~240 draws with a constant buffer of 2 KB or more, most of them one
   shader, `72cb2fb900`, 222 draws in every frame). Skinned characters need nothing beyond the constant copies.
6. **No CPU-built geometry in the scene passes.** No draw's vertex data changed between frames: no CPU skinning, no
   CPU-written cloth or particle vertices there. (Particles may come from instancing, or from passes outside the
   RS_SCENE targets, not checked.)
7. **Instance data is rewritten every frame** for most instanced draws (grass, foliage, effects), at the same address
   and with the same count. The previous instance data must be kept like the constants (a copy per draw), and its
   order may change between frames (open question below).
8. **About half the scene draws sample textures in the vertex shader** (terrain heights, grass and wind
   displacement...). Static textures need nothing; any that the game rewrites each frame (a displacement or interaction
   map) would need its previous version kept, or those draws marked reactive.

## Design this points to

- **Draw identity:** key = shaders, non-instanced vertex streams, index range (as measured) + a tie-break for repeated
  keys by the nearest previous per-object constants; unmatched draws fall back to camera reprojection.
- **Previous inputs:** Savage Wind already copies each draw's constant buffers per submission (`cbuf_info` ->
  `guest_copy`); keep last frame's copies alive one more frame and remember them by draw identity. Same for instanced
  streams.
- **Motion vertex shader:** a variant of each scene vertex shader from the translator (`maxwell/translate.c` emits GLSL
  reading `cbN[i][j]`): the position computed a second time from the previous-frame constants (and instance data),
  both clip positions passed to the fragment stage, the jitter removed from both.
- **Where the vectors go:** first a replay pass (the scene's opaque draws drawn again into a motion target, depth-tested
  against the scene depth: isolated, easy to check), later an extra output of the game's own geometry passes.
- **Masks:** blended / transparent draws and unmatched or texture-animated draws into the reactive and transparency
  masks.
- **Debug view:** a colour-coded vector overlay and a reprojection error measure (the previous frame warped by the
  vectors compared with this one).

## Open questions (next measurements)

1. **Instance order:** are a draw's instances in the same order frame to frame (only their data changing), or re-sorted
   / re-culled? Compare instance records between the two frames (count of equal records at equal and at other indices).
2. **Vertex shader textures:** which of the textures vertex shaders sample are render targets written in the same or
   the previous frame (GPU-made), and which are static?
3. **Repeated keys:** which constant slot differs between draws sharing a key, and does the nearest-matrix tie-break
   make the matching unambiguous (measure: matches whose tie-break disagrees with the ordinal)?
4. **Unmatched draws:** what the shaders in the "unmatched" lists are (they include some that are unmatched even when
   standing still: alternate-frame updates?).
5. **Passes outside RS_SCENE:** particles and effects drawn into other targets, and how the scene's transparent passes
   are ordered.
6. **Cost:** bytes of constants and instance data kept per frame (memory for one extra frame of copies).

## Answers from the implementation (TAA, desktop, Great Plateau)

Measured with TAA on (Video > Anti-aliasing), a reprojection error view (the previous frame warped by the vectors,
minus this one, x4) and the jitter off (`SAVAGEWIND_JITTER=0`), so only vector errors show.

- **Vectors:** the error is lowest at the vectors' own scale and sign (mean 0.39 against 0.53-0.57 at -1, 0 and 2);
  sky, far terrain, rocks and Link are near zero. What is left is thin grass blades and leaves uncovering what was
  behind them (no vector can say what was there; TAA's neighbourhood clamp is what handles it) and outlines.
- **Vertex shader textures (2):** ~1450 of ~2100 scene draws a frame have vertex shaders that sample textures; the
  only other buffer they read outside slots 3-16 is slot 1 (the shader's own compiler constants: static). Seven
  textures they read are drawn by the GPU every frame (a 512x512 RGBA8 linear target, a 256x256 RG8 one, 128-192
  RGBA8 / RGBA16 levels). Giving the previous frame's copy of the vertex shader those textures' previous contents (a
  copy before each frame's first pass into them, 8 a frame, 63% of the lookups) changed the error by nothing beyond
  noise, standing still (grass in the wind) and moving: the grass's motion comes from its constants, which the history
  already has. Not kept.
- **Instance data (1):** ~3 instanced draws a frame get a motion program, 1-2 of their streams (~2 KB) change from
  frame to frame. Not worth previous-frame vertex inputs (a second vertex binding and attribute set in every pipeline
  of those draws).
- **Matching (3):** the fingerprint is the first 12 floats of the draw's first 4 constant buffers after the camera
  block (slot 3, which every scene draw shares). With the camera block in it, no fingerprint equalled its match's
  while the camera moved and the search never stopped early; without it, recording costs 0.68 ms of CPU a frame for
  ~2300 draws (was 0.90) and matches to another object (a world position jump over 1 cm) are 5-9 a frame in a pan, 0
  standing still.
- **Cost (6):** ~2.3 MB of constants a frame go through the history, ~240 KB copied (the rest shared within a
  submission), a few KB of instance data; the history slots (5, one per frame in flight) start at 2 MB (0.2-0.5 MB
  used) and grow when a frame fills one. Uncapped at 4K: 81.6 fps with TAA, 94.1 with SMAA; the GPU side is ~0.6 ms a frame (the geometry pass's doubled vertex work and the motion target),
  the rest is CPU (recording, the motion program lookup, push constants).
- **Shader compiles:** the motion variants go into the precompile key log like any other; with the cache warm, a TAA
  run compiles nothing in play and world entry peaks at 67-108 ms (75-191 without TAA).

## TAA: FSR 3.1's temporal reconstruction at 1x

The first TAA (one fragment pass: Catmull-Rom history in a fixed 1.25 sigma YCoCg box, one blend weight for every
pixel) flickered on foliage at about twice AMD FSR 3's rate. It is now the reconstruction of FSR 3.1's upscaler
(the vendored SDK's shaders were the reference, not copied), at the scene's own size, as seven compute passes
(`shaders.c` `taa_*.comp`, `exec.c` `mvec_taa`):

- **Dilation:** each pixel's vector and depth are the nearest surface's in its 3x3, so silhouettes move with the
  foreground.
- **Disocclusion from depth:** this frame's nearest depths are scattered (atomic min) to where they were last frame;
  a surface behind what landed in its place was hidden. No previous depth buffer is kept.
- **Per-pixel accumulation:** 1/3 more a frame, 0 on a shading change, two frames of the new image alone after a
  disocclusion. The blend is the new sample's own weight (how close its jittered samples fall to the pixel) against
  it: about 1/23 on a converged still pixel.
- **Shading change:** this frame's 5-luma neighbourhood against last frame's as sorted sets (jitter and sub-pixel
  motion reorder values but don't change them), over three sizes.
- **Anti-flicker:** a pixel whose luma matches an older frame better than the last one (it oscillates with the
  jitter) and thin features (luma ridges filling no 2x2 quadrant) keep their history from the clamp.
- **Clamp:** an ellipsoid around the 3x3's Gaussian mean, 1-3 standard deviations by confidence, motion and distance.
- **Around it:** the game's own textures in the jittered passes get a -1 mip bias (`log2(render / output) - 1` under
  an upscaler); Video > Sharpening is RCAS after TAA, as under FSR 3 (CAS sharpened the residual flicker up); the
  jitter steps once per presented frame (paused, the game updates twice a frame and only half the phases were used).

Measured at 4K on an RTX 3080 Ti, still view, flicker (temporal second difference of luma, 75th percentile of the
region) against AMD's own FSR 3 at the window's size (the same algorithm in AMD's code: the FSR 3 upscaler that builds
on this, with its `fsr3-native` test mode) in the same run, interleaved: trees 0.23-0.29 against 0.27-0.30, grass
0.40-0.47 against 0.39-0.48, far field 0.23-0.25 against 0.23-0.25. GPU time 2.0 ms a frame (FSR 3 native: 2.3), plus
0.09 ms of RCAS; the old TAA was 0.6.
`SAVAGEWIND_TAA_VIEW=<frame>:<1-7>` shows its masks (disocclusion, accumulation, shading change, instability, locks,
motion divergence, no vector); `SAVAGEWIND_MIP_BIAS=<levels>` replaces the bias.

## Reproducing

The instrumentation (`SAVAGEWIND_MV_SPIKE=1`, `[mv]` log lines) was a throwaway commit, not part of this branch: the
runtime built in the Linux container (`make B=build/linux/x86_64/game DEPS=... build/linux/x86_64/game/savagewind`), run
with a scripted input such as
`900:A:8,1400:A:8,1900:A:8,3500:STICK_90:900,4500:RSTICK_RIGHT:600,5200:STICK_0:700,5200:RSTICK_LEFT:700`.

`docs/profiler-internals.md`:

```md
# Profiler internals

How the profiler in `runtime/prof.c`, `runtime/prof_sampler.c` and `tools/swprof.py` works, and the rules it relies on. For
using it, see [profiling.md](profiling.md). No game files, generated code or captures belong in issues or pull requests.

## Capture ownership and producer completion

Every capture has a generation number. A timed scope (`SW_ZONE`, `SW_ACC` and the renderer's manual draw spans) keeps
the generation it started in. When it ends, a scope from another generation is dropped, so a scope that crosses a stop
and a start cannot charge its time to the later capture. Recording checks admission again before it touches its cursor.

The recorder has 256 bounded thread slots. A thread-local key identifies a thread's slot. When the thread exits, its
destructor releases ownership and keeps that capture's final totals. Slots are not reused within a capture. The first
event of a thread takes the registry mutex; after that, a record only touches the calling thread's cursor and its
write-in-progress flag.

The ordering between producers and the writer, in `prof.c:enter` and `writer_main`:

1. A producer publishes `busy = 1` with sequential consistency, then checks its generation and admission, also with
   sequential consistency. It touches capture data only after the check succeeds.
2. Stop closes admission with a sequentially consistent store. The writer drains the GPU results, closes GPU admission,
   and then checks every busy flag under the registry mutex.
3. A producer that passed its check before admission closed finishes and publishes `busy = 0` before the writer reads
   its slot. A producer that arrives after the writer's scan fails the check and never touches capture data.

The flag covers the short recording operation, not the scope being measured, so a long scope cannot hold the writer.
Final accumulator totals are streamed as extra chunks, so they survive a full event pool and the exit of a worker.
If a frame flush fills the pool partway through, only stored sites are cleared. The remaining totals keep their
original frame for the writer; the new frame's addition that encountered the full pool is rejected as admission closes.
Thread ids are compacted for the file, and slots left over from earlier captures are omitted.

Normal shutdown and an in-place game reboot wait for the writer, so the file is finished before guest thread handles or
the game library are replaced. A full buffer requests a stop after leaving the recording critical section and logs the
reason. If the file cannot be opened, written or closed, no new path is published, and a partial file is removed.

## Linux sampling

Named threads register a lifetime slot even while capture is off. The sampler snapshots these slots before asking
the kernel for its running threads, then validates the slot generation and holds the lifetime mutex across
`pthread_sigqueue`. The thread's TLS destructor takes the same mutex before releasing its slot, so exit, detach and
join cannot reclaim pthread storage during signal delivery. Reused slots and unregistered threads are skipped.
The mutex is released before waiting for a signal response; the handler never takes it.

The handler for a sample must be async-signal-safe. glibc's `backtrace()` is not (it can take heap and loader locks), so
the Linux sampler does not unwind. It reserves `SIGRTMIN + 6` once for the lifetime of the process, and refuses to run
if that signal is already in use instead of replacing someone else's handler. `SIGPROF` is not touched.

Each request carries an id that is never reused. The handler claims the matching request atomically, reads the
interrupted program counter and the OS thread id, preserves `errno` and acknowledges. A request that times out is
cancelled only if the handler has not claimed it; otherwise the sender waits for the short handler to finish before it
reuses the storage. A cancelled request that arrives late does nothing. The handler stays installed after the capture
ends, so a signal that was blocked or delayed at stop time is harmless.

As a result, Linux samples hold a single program counter. Module classification and self time in the runtime work;
caller and inclusive time do not. Windows suspends the thread and unwinds with the x64 unwind data, with structured
exception handling around the unwind, and the module snapshot is bounded by its allocation if modules appear while it
is enumerated.

References: [glibc backtrace safety](https://www.sourceware.org/glibc/manual/latest/html_node/Backtraces.html),
[signal handler safety](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal-safety.7.html).

## Frame and GPU boundaries

Stop writes a closing frame mark separately from the event pool, so a one-frame capture has both boundaries even when
the pool is full. A manual stop closes the last partial frame at the time of the stop.

GPU admission stays open while the writer runs the backend drain. Under the renderer mutex, the backend submits pending
work and collects the timestamp results; CPU and GPU instrumentation for new work is off during the drain, and pending
events keep their generation so they are still written. Collecting does not wait on a query. Stopping can briefly
contend with rendering while the drain holds the renderer mutex.

GPU timestamps are aligned to the CPU clock by calibration: the device and an advertised host time domain are queried
together (the performance counter on Windows, `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on Linux), and the host timestamp is correlated with
the profiler's cycle counter. The capture stores the driver's reported deviation and the bracket around the host read.
Without `VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps`, the submission timestamp is used and the report labels the alignment as
estimated. Captures without calibration data show it as unknown. The metadata uses the existing counter record with bit
8 set, so it can be written during the drain; the record kind and the file version are unchanged.

Reference: [VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps](https://docs.vulkan.org/features/latest/features/proposals/VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps.html).

## Offline attribution

`swprof` builds the nesting of zones first and then subtracts the direct children's intervals from each zone, which
gives its self-time intervals. Each interval is intersected with the frame boundaries, so a zone that spans several
frames is split between them. CPU and GPU intervals are clipped to a selected frame window, and an empty selection
reports no work. Counts include every operation that touches the window; times are clipped.

Accumulators are totals per thread and per observed frame. Their individual intervals are not stored, so they are not
split across frames. Scopes still open at stop are discarded rather than invented.
Accumulator self time subtracts direct children in the slash-separated hierarchy within each thread and frame.
To avoid counting accumulated work again as zone self time, its total is deducted proportionally from non-wait zone
self time on that same thread and frame, capped at the available zone time. Inclusive zone times are unchanged.
This is an estimate: ACC records carry neither intervals nor parent links, so unrelated zones sharing the frame can
lose self time too, and accumulator work beyond the recorded zone coverage remains separate. Wait zone self time is
preserved. Without complete frame boundaries the same estimate applies to the whole capture.

## Tests

```sh
make test-prof
```

This builds and runs the recorder test (`tools/test_prof.c`: the recorder and the sampler, several threads, a full
buffer), the report tests (`tools/test_swprof.py`) and the lifecycle tests (`tools/test_prof_lifecycle.py`, which drive
`tools/test_prof_lifecycle.c` as a subprocess). The lifecycle tests cover a scope that crosses a stop and a start, a
delayed `SIGPROF`, final totals of an exited worker, a one-frame capture, repeated captures with concurrent producers
and a failing writer. Macros that are off cost a branch; the finest zones can be removed with `-DSW_PROF_DISABLE`.

Not covered by the automated tests: GPU driver behaviour, the macOS sampler and Metal GPU timing, other GPU vendors,
and long captures.

## Points worth checking in review

- The admission and busy ordering, slot reuse, and the interaction of the thread-local destructor with a game reboot
- Delayed signal cancellation, the permanent ownership of the reserved signal, and the program-counter-only limit on Linux
- Vulkan query lifetime and reuse, renderer locking while stopping, and how frame boundaries are interpreted
- The calibration time domains, timestamp wrap, and the labelling and uncertainty of the fallback
- Self-time attribution for deep nesting, clipped boundaries and empty selections

`docs/profiling.md`:

```md
# Profiling Savage Wind

SWR has one profiler. It is off until you ask for a capture, costs about one branch per marker while off, and writes
one file per capture. A tool (`tools/swprof.py`) turns that file into text, JSON or CSV. Nothing is sent anywhere and
no viewer is needed.

## Taking a capture

| How | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `F6` in the game | Starts a capture; `F6` again stops it. After a full buffer stops it automatically, the next press only acknowledges the stop; the press after that starts a new capture. Ignored while a menu captures input or F6 is assigned to a game control. |
| `SAVAGEWIND_PROF=<first>[:<frames>]` | Starts at frame `<first>`; stops after `<frames>` frames (without a count: stays on until stopped). |
| `prof start`, `prof stop`, `prof status` | The same, from the command layer (once it is merged). |

A capture also ends by itself when its buffer is full (`SAVAGEWIND_PROF_MB`, default 256, 8 to 4096). The file is
written in the background to `profile/swprof-<date>-<time>.swprof`. This logs `[prof] buffer full, stopping capture`;
there is no on-screen notification. The next F6 press only acknowledges that stop, and the press after that starts
a new capture once writing is finished. Stopping first closes CPU recording, then drains
pending GPU timestamps on the writer thread. A capture started while the last file is still
being written is refused; wait for `prof status` to say `idle`.

While a capture runs the game is slightly slower. Keep captures short (5 to 30 seconds) and take them at the moment
the problem happens.

Normal exit and an in-place game reboot finish the file. Force termination and `_exit` test hooks bypass this.
The buffer remains allocated for reuse, plus about 6 MiB of bounded thread slots. A scope crossing a capture boundary
is discarded; it cannot contribute to a later capture. Completed final accumulator totals are retained.

## Reading it

```
python3 tools/swprof.py                      # the newest capture in ./profile
python3 tools/swprof.py FILE --exe PATH      # name the runtime's functions (PATH = the binary that was running)
python3 tools/swprof.py FILE --frames 120:240 --top 40 --slow 25
python3 tools/swprof.py FILE --json out.json --csv frames.csv
```

The report has, in this order:

- **Frames**: rate, average, p50, p95, p99, max, how many were over 33 and 50 ms.
- **Top places by self time**: the zones and added-up work with the most time of their own, per frame.
- **GPU**: busy and idle time, then every pass, dispatch and copy by GPU time. GPU rows are aligned to the CPU clock,
  so a slow frame can be matched to what the GPU was doing. The report labels alignment as calibrated, estimated
  (submission-time fallback), or unknown for an older capture, and includes calibration uncertainty when available.
- **Sampler**: where each thread was, by stack sample: game code, the SWR runtime, the driver and system, or waiting
  (inside one of the wait zones). Then the runtime's hot functions by self time, by inclusive time, and the runtime
  functions that were calling into the driver or system. Without `--exe` the functions show as `runtime+0x...`.
- **Threads**: zone tree per thread, then the added-up work (`SW_ACC`) tree.
- **Counters** and the **slowest frames** with the places that took the most time in each (and the sample split).

All times are milliseconds per frame unless a heading says otherwise. The sampler takes one stack per thread per
millisecond (`SAVAGEWIND_PROF_SAMPLE=<microseconds>`, 100 or more, `0` = off).
This is a requested interval, not a guaranteed rate. The report shows the observed interval. Linux records one
interrupted program counter per sample, rather than a stack. Runtime caller/inclusive attribution requires Windows
stack samples; Linux can classify waits only where a completed wait zone covers the sample.

Zone self time is split at child and frame boundaries. A frame selection clips CPU/GPU intervals to that window;
an empty selection reports no work. Operation/call counts include operations touching the window, while their times
are clipped. Accumulators are assigned to the frame observed by that thread; they do not retain individual intervals.
Their self time is deducted proportionally from non-wait zone self time on the same thread and frame, up to the
available zone time. This prevents duplicate self-time totals, but the missing ACC intervals mean the enclosing zone
cannot be identified exactly; unrelated zones in that frame can also be reduced. Zone inclusive time is unchanged.
Accumulator self totals also appear in slow-frame causes and CSV cells, assigned by the frame number in each ACC
record rather than its later flush timestamp. Slash-separated accumulator children are subtracted within that frame.

The recompiled game code is deliberately one total. The tool never looks up or prints a game function, and the
sampler section ends with a reminder: do not put game addresses, game names or generated code into pull requests or
issues. Runtime function names are fine.

## Adding markers

Include `prof.h`. Pick the cheapest marker that answers the question:

| Marker | Use it for | Cost while capturing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SW_ZONE("name")` | A stretch of work that happens up to a few hundred times a frame. One event each. | one event |
| `SW_ACC("a/b")` | Work done thousands of times a frame (a draw's steps). Summed per thread and frame; `/` nests. | two clock reads, no event |
| `SW_TALLY("name")` | Only how often something happens (cache misses). | a counter bump |
| `SW_COUNT("name", n)` | A number now: draws, bytes, queue depth. | one event |
| `prof_site_dyn(name)` | A name only known at run time (a pass's size). Cached, copied. | once per name |

Steady-state literal markers do not allocate or take a mutex. First use registers a name and claims a bounded thread
slot; dynamic GPU labels format text, intern names under a mutex and may allocate. Names should be string literals; put the finest zones
behind `-DSW_PROF_DISABLE` if they sit in the hottest loops. This disables the SW_* macros, not direct recorder calls
or the renderer's manual span markers. Wait zones that should count as waiting in the sampler are
listed in `WAIT_ZONES` in `tools/swprof.py`.
The Vulkan semaphore wait is recorded as the `gpu_wait` interval zone so samples inside it count as waiting, including
Linux's single-PC samples. With runtime symbols and stack samples, `vk_wait_seq` also identifies waits whose zone
has not completed or began before capture. Older captures containing only a `gpu_wait` accumulator require that
stack-based fallback; an accumulator cannot locate a wait in time.

## Platforms

- **Windows**: the sampler suspends each guest thread, reads its context and unwinds with the x64 unwind data.
  GPU time comes from Vulkan timestamps, aligned with `VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps` when the driver has it.
- **Linux**: the sampler reserves `SIGRTMIN + 6` if its disposition is still default, and sends tagged requests with
  `pthread_sigqueue`. The handler reads the interrupted PC from `ucontext`; it never unwinds or allocates. The handler
  stays installed for the process lifetime so blocked, delayed requests remain harmless after stopping. If that signal
  is already in use, sampling is skipped with a log message; zones and counters still work. SIGPROF is untouched.
- **macOS**: zones, added-up work and counters work; GPU timing (Metal) and the sampler are not there yet.

## Tests

On Linux, `make test-prof` builds the recorder/sampler and lifecycle harnesses, and runs report tests on synthetic
captures. It covers delayed signals, scopes spanning captures, final totals, repeated start/stop with concurrent
producers, normal exit, writer-open failure, the final frame boundary, GPU draining and interval attribution. It also
prints synthetic marker costs with recording off and on. These numbers are not gameplay overhead measurements.

See [profiler internals](profiler-internals.md) for the capture lifecycle, the thread ordering rules and the limits.

The older tools stay: `SAVAGEWIND_VK_PROF`, `SAVAGEWIND_TIMELINE`, `SAVAGEWIND_GPUPROF_AT`, the `sample`, `vkprof`, `gpuprof` and
`threads` control commands and `tools/profile_samples.py` are unchanged, and `tools/perf_routes.py` still uses them. `prof` is
separate from them. FNPROF and the F10 player overlay remain separate.

## File format

`SWPROF01` version 1; `runtime/prof.c` has the layout in its header comment. The tool refuses files with another
magic or version.
Short chunk headers and payloads are rejected with a message naming the chunk and the expected and available byte
counts, including truncation on a complete record boundary. The command exits unsuccessfully and writes no reports.

`docs/research/colour-vision.md`:

```md
# Colour vision options: design

2026-11-15, BotW 1.9.0. **Status:** phase 1 implemented the same day, on the user's request, as the first rows of
Options > Accessibility (runtime/colour_vision.c, the present shader variant). The game-specific help under "Later"
is not started. Player docs: [Cheats and assists](../cheats-and-assists.md#colour-vision).

## Goal

Players with a colour vision deficiency (CVD) can tell apart the game's colour cues: Chuchu and Keese elements, enemy
tiers, the stamina wheel's exhausted state and the like. The option sits at the top of Options > Accessibility, so it
is one of the first things a player finds, and it can also be offered at the first setup.

About 8% of men and 0.5% of women have red-green CVD (protan or deutan, most of them the milder "anomalous" forms);
tritan (blue-yellow) is rare. Red-green is the case that matters most.

## Colour cues in BOTW

Approximate, from knowledge of the game; the rows marked "verify" must be checked in game with the simulation mode
below before relying on them.

| Cue | Colours | Other cue the game gives | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chuchu, Keese, Wizzrobe elements; Chuchu Jelly | red fire, yellow shock, white-blue ice, green-blue normal | flames, sparks, frost close up; the jelly's name in the pouch | High (red / yellow / green) |
| Enemy tiers: Bokoblin, Moblin, Lizalfos, Lynel, Hinox | red, blue, black, silver, gold | none besides how hard they hit | High (red looks dark to protans: red vs. black) |
| Lizalfos elements | red fire, yellow shock, white ice | breath effects | Medium |
| Stamina wheel | green, red when exhausted, yellow extra | Link pants, the wheel empties | Medium |
| Hearts | red, yellow extra hearts | extra hearts come last in the row | Low |
| Temperature gauge | blue cold, red hot | needle position, flame icon | Low |
| Shrines and towers | orange glow not done, blue done | map icon (verify whether it differs) | Low |
| Guardian laser | red-pink laser and dot | sound, music | Low |
| Map pins and beacons | verify | | verify |
| Weapon comparison in the pouch | verify whether better / worse is colour only | | verify |

## What the player sees

Options > Accessibility gets a "Colour vision" group as its first rows, above God mode:

| Row | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Colour vision | Off; Protanopia (red looks dark, red and green look alike); Deuteranopia (green and red look alike); Tritanopia (blue and yellow look alike) | Off |
| Correction strength | 10% to 100% in 10% steps (always shown; no effect while Colour vision is Off) | 100%, to be revisited with testers |

Changes apply at once. The game's own Options screen is drawn by the game and corrected like the rest of the
picture, so the player sees the effect while changing it.

Placement decisions for the user:

1. The two rows at the top of Accessibility (proposed).
2. Accessibility moved up in the main Options list, for example right after Gameplay (it is 8th today).
3. A "Colour vision" row in the launcher's first setup ("Set up" section, next to "Savage Wind colour look").
4. The main page's Accessibility description changes to "Colour vision and assists that make the game easier."

A "World only" choice (HUD keeps its colours) is cheap to add later, because the colour grading pass already runs on
the scene before the HUD. It is left out of the first version to keep the page simple.

## How it works

### Colour science

- Simulation: Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (2009) matrices at severity 1.0, in linear RGB. The paper also gives
  milder severities; the implementation uses only the 1.0 matrices, and the strength slider scales the correction
  (k in runtime/colour_vision.h), which also suits the milder anomalous forms. Chromium's developer tools use the same model for their vision deficiency emulation; Unreal Engine offers a
  similar "type plus severity, simulate or correct" option, which is the usual pattern players know from games.
- Correction ("daltonize"): the colour difference the player cannot see, `c - S c`, is moved into channels they can
  see: `c' = c + E (c - S c)`. For protan and deutan, E moves the lost red-green difference into green and blue
  (`[[0,0,0],[0.7,1,0],[0.7,0,1]]`); for tritan, the lost blue-yellow difference into red and green
  (`[[1,0,0.7],[0,1,0.7],[0,0,0]]`).
- Both fold into **one 3x3 matrix** per type and strength, `M = I + E (I - S)`, computed on the CPU when the setting
  changes. The GPU cost is one matrix multiply per pixel.

Correction matrices at full strength (linear RGB, rows = output R, G, B):

```
protan  [ 1.0000  0.0000  0.0000 ] [ 0.4789  0.4769  0.0442 ] [ 0.5973 -0.6887  1.0914 ]
deutan  [ 1.0000  0.0000  0.0000 ] [ 0.1628  0.7250  0.1122 ] [ 0.4547 -0.6454  1.1907 ]
tritan  [ 0.7412 -0.4072  0.6660 ] [ 0.0751  0.5852  0.3397 ] [ 0.0000  0.0000  1.0000 ]
```

Synthetic check: colour difference (CIE76 ΔE; above ~10 is easy to tell, below ~5 hard) between approximate cue
colours, as a CVD player sees them before and after the correction. Colours picked by eye, not measured in the game.

| Pair | Normal | Protan: before, after | Deutan: before, after | Tritan: before, after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fire Chuchu red / normal green | 110 | 27, 60 | 18, 52 | 119, 100 |
| Shock Chuchu yellow / normal green | 60 | 39, 43 | 47, 44 | 57, 41 |
| Heart red / extra heart yellow | 85 | 68, 66 | 38, 74 | 73, 64 |
| Stamina green / exhausted red | 121 | 43, 66 | 18, 59 | 129, 104 |
| Shrine orange / blue | 126 | 113, 75 | 126, 77 | 101, 62 |
| Red / black Bokoblin | 67 | 37, 42 | 55, 37 | 77, 56 |
| Ice Chuchu light blue / normal green | 76 | 72, 76 | 63, 73 | 29, 47 |

The red-green pairs, which are the real problem, get two to three times further apart. Pairs that were already far
apart lose some distance but stay easy to tell. At full strength the whole picture shifts (green-tinted for protan
and deutan), which is why the strength slider exists. Demo pictures of two screenshots (simulated, corrected,
corrected as seen) were made with a scratch script; they are kept outside the repository, in
`issue-logs/alpha6-colour-vision/` of the working folder.

### Where in the renderer (as implemented)

The correction runs on the final picture, after the game has drawn its HUD and menus:

- `vk_present_draw` (runtime/nvn/vulkan/exec.c) draws the game's image into the window with `present.frag`, after
  `post_process` (SMAA, FSR 1). With the option on it uses `present_cvd.frag` (runtime/nvn/vulkan/shaders.c) instead:
  the matrix rows as fragment push constants after the vertex shader's 32 bytes (the present pipeline layout gained
  that range). With the option off the pipeline is the same as before.
- **SDR:** the game's 8-bit image is read raw, so it holds sRGB-encoded values: the shader decodes them, applies M and
  encodes again.
- **HDR10:** the game's float picture (RGBA16F, linear, HUD included) also goes through `vk_present_draw` before the
  PQ pass in device.c, so the same shader applies M to it directly (a flag in the push constants says the picture is
  linear). The ImGui menu is drawn separately and keeps its colours.
- **Frame generation:** generated frames are also drawn with `vk_present_draw`, so they are corrected the same way.
  The generator's own HUD-less input is untouched.
- **Not corrected, on purpose:** the Savage Wind menu and overlays (ImGui, drawn after the present), and Album photos
  taken with the camera rune (runtime/hle/photo.c captures the game's image before the present), so photos keep the
  game's real colours. Window captures (Steam, OBS) show the corrected picture.
- **macOS / Metal:** not done; the build is unmaintained and macOS has its own system colour filters.

### Code

- `runtime/settings.h` / `settings.c`: `colour_vision` (`off`, `protanopia`, `deuteranopia`, `tritanopia` in the ini)
  and `colour_vision_strength` (percent, 10 to 100), saved in savagewind.ini like the other Accessibility rows.
- `runtime/colour_vision.c/.h`: the three Machado matrices and `colour_vision_matrix(float m[9])`, false when off.
- `runtime/ui/game_options.mm`: the two rows at the top of the `P_ACCESS` items (before God mode). The type's
  description names the chosen type; the strength row is always shown.
- Translations in all 13 `runtime/ui/i18n/*.inc` tables (`tools/i18n_check.py`: none missing).
- Player docs: the "Colour vision" section of docs/cheats-and-assists.md, a README line and a CHANGELOG entry.
- Not done: a row in the launcher's first setup, and moving Accessibility up in the main Options list.

### Testing

- Developer simulation mode: `SAVAGEWIND_CVD_SIMULATE=protan|deutan|tritan[:<percent>]` shows the picture as a
  dichromat sees it, after the correction if one is on. It is meant for auditing the cues above (the rows marked
  "verify") and for before / after screenshots.
- Done 2026-11-15 (Windows, hidden runs, Great Plateau, 60 fps cap): the setting is read and saved back; the run
  reaches the world at a steady 60 fps; window shots show the corrected picture with the HUD corrected (deuteranopia:
  the red hearts turn pink) and the F10 overlay untouched. The pictures are in `issue-logs/alpha6-colour-vision/` of
  the working folder.
- Still to do: HDR checked by eye on an HDR display, one Steam Deck run, frame time on and off at 4K, and testers
  with colour blindness on the Discord to set the default strength.

## Later: game-specific help

Not needed for the first version; considered after testers try the filter.

1. **Name on lock-on.** While Z-targeting, a short label with the enemy's name from the game's own texts (for
   example "Electric Chuchu", "Blue Bokoblin"). It covers element and tier without relying on colour at all. It needs
   reverse engineering of the lock-on target and the actor's localised name (none exists in the runtime yet), new
   1.9.0 sites in tools/game_sites.py, and a way to draw the label (overlay or the game's own layout). Medium to
   large.
2. **Targeted recolouring** of specific shaders (shrine and tower glow, guardian laser) by shader hash. Fragile and of
   little value once the full-picture correction exists.
3. **High-contrast HUD** and bigger icons: a separate accessibility topic.

## Risks

- The models are approximations, and real CVD varies from person to person; the strength slider and tester feedback
  cover this.
- At full strength the picture looks different from the game's art; some players will prefer a lower strength.
- The correction runs after the colour grading and the Savage Wind LUT, which are on by default; the two compose,
  but testers should judge them together.
- Off by default, and the Off path is unchanged, so players who do not use it are not affected.

## Later work

The game-specific help above is not Alpha 6 work. The launcher setup row and moving Accessibility up in the main
list are small and can follow if the user wants them.
